lead: 144 decision support tools for metal additive manufacturing, scored on whether each accounts for four costs and four benefits of adopting it. Filter by columns in the cost and benefit matrix; select a table row to read the rating notes, the tool link and sources.
foot: Scope: commercial software, academic models, government and consortium tools, and methods or standards, published 2010 onward, all metal AM processes, with a defense sustainment lens. Ratings reflect public documentation as of November 2026, checked against the written rating rules in the report. No means a full description of the tool was read, or its documented scope plainly excludes the item; Unknown means the public evidence is too thin to tell, which is common for internal government tools and products described only in press releases. Where a tool was released more than once, only the newest release is listed and earlier ones are named under What it is. A tool is included only if metal AM is in scope: it models, screens for or supports metal processes or materials, or was applied to metal parts. Polymer-only and process-agnostic tools are excluded. Tool links and ratings were re-checked in November 2026.

tools.name: NIAR Additive Manufacturing Techno-Economic Analysis cost model and TEA module (America Makes IMPACT project 5554.007)
tools.developer: Wichita State University National Institute for Aviation Research (NIAR), VALDOS group (team listed in the briefing: Brady Williams, R. Andrulonis, M. Shaw, L. Tubesing, C. Combemale, P. Funk; no PI is labeled). Funded by OSD ManTech through AFRL agreement FA8650-20-2-5700 and administered by America Makes (project 5554.007; IMPACT Topic 8, Project 2).
tools.year: 2023–2025 (period of performance Nov 14, 2023 to May 14, 2025; no final deliverable found publicly as of Oct 2026)
tools.context: DoD-wide, not Air Force-only. It targets sourcing gaps where castings and forgings are hard to get. Advisory board: Army DEVCOM AvMC, NAVSEA, AFLCMC (the only Air Force member, Beth Dittmer), DLA R&D, NASA, Boeing, GE Additive, BAE Systems and America Makes. No Air Logistics Complex or RSO member is listed.
tools.processes: L-PBF, laser/electron-beam DED, wire-arc AM, additive friction stir deposition (AFSD)
tools.availability: Deliverables go to America Makes and DoD: a 4-modality cost model with a TEA module, a value-proposition framework, a manufacturing readiness report and a manuscript. No public release, final report or newer description was found.
tools.description: A cost model for four metal AM modalities, plus a techno-economic analysis (TEA) module 'to be used by DoD personnel to aid in the decision of when to leverage AM'. The stated objective is to 'deliver a framework for when, where, and how to utilize metal AM technologies to bridge gaps in component sourcing.' The team compared 13 existing cost models and used advisory-board and government interviews to find omitted cost elements; the stated future work is to 'implement the gaps into a tool.' This update re-read the Jan 2024 interim briefing and searched for other NIAR tools built for the Air Force. None were found. NIAR's other Air Force work is B-1/F-16 digital twins, WAM materials data and scanning/reverse engineering. The ratings describe the planned cost structure in the interim briefing, not a verified final tool.

NRE.note: 'NRE (DFAM, engineering salary, etc.)' is listed only as a gap item for the planned LPBF model, and CAD/DFAM/machine-setup appear as rows in the literature-review cost-element matrix; no values or formulas are published (interim briefing, Jan 2024).

Production.note: Per-modality cost elements (feedstock, build plate, machine cost, depreciation, labour, energy, gas, build time, post-processing) are listed from a review of 13 existing models as the basis for a planned 4-modality cost model, with no calculation or values public (interim briefing).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification appears only as 'supplier learning curve/common qualification', a planned industry-maturation factor, with no qualification cost element (interim briefing).

QA_Insp.note: 'Quality control' is a row in the literature-review matrix and 'inspection rate per part application' a gap item for the planned LPBF model; no inspection-cost method or values are public (interim briefing).

Storage.note: The advisory board flagged 'packaging and storage' as a cost element omitted from traditional models, to be considered in the TEA module; nothing is quantified (interim briefing).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine depreciation, machine and labour wrap rates and a build-plate packing factor are listed as planned elements, but no amortisation or utilisation calculation is shown (interim briefing).

Shared_Capacity.note: The objective says 'when, where, and how', but the briefing has no site, capacity or utilisation content, and a 2025-26 search found no final tool, report or manuscript (interim briefing; web search).

Speed.note: 'Readiness/AOG', 'costs associated with inoperable equipment and/or vehicles' and 'supply chain alleviation' are listed as factors for the planned TEA module; lead time is not modelled in the briefing (interim briefing).

tools.name: Part Assessment and Cost Tool (PACT)
tools.developer: US Air Force Rapid Sustainment Office (RSO) Advanced Manufacturing Program Office (AMPO), AFLCMC; contractor not named in public sources
tools.context: US Air Force sustainment; for System Program Offices (SPOs)
tools.processes: Additive manufacturing (unspecified), cold spray repair, directed energy deposition
tools.availability: Government internal (Air Force Cloud One; to be built into the AGORA digital thread)
tools.description: A decision support application on Air Force Cloud One. It grades a supply chain part on 'supply chain impact', compatibility with or feasibility of advanced manufacturing, and return on investment (ROI), so SPOs can decide whether to start an advanced manufacturing project. AFLCMC describes it as performing 'cost-benefit analyses to determine ROI' for AM parts.

NRE.note: PACT 'assesses uploaded part files', but the press articles do not say whether reverse engineering, redesign or TDP cost enters the ROI grade (AFLCMC news; 3DPrint.com).

Production.note: Each candidate is graded on return on investment, but no cost inputs or elements are documented (AFLCMC news; 3DPrint.com).

QA_Qual.note: The press articles do not say whether qualification or airworthiness effort enters PACT's grades.

QA_Insp.note: The press articles do not list PACT's cost elements, so whether inspection is costed is not known.

Storage.note: The press articles do not say whether the 'supply chain impact' grade includes inventory; 'inventory' appears only in a comparison to other firms' digital inventory platforms (3DPrint.com).

Shared_Capital.note: The press articles do not say whether equipment investment enters the ROI grade.

Shared_Capacity.note: The press articles describe no capacity or site analysis.

Speed.note: Parts are graded on 'supply chain impact', a screening proxy for supply problems, but lead time or availability is not named and how it enters the grade is not documented (AFLCMC news; 3DPrint.com).

tools.name: SEEKR advanced manufacturing data analytics
tools.developer: EXPANSIA (SDVOSB), in partnership with the Air Force AMPO, under a Rapid Sustainment Office contract
tools.year: Unknown (the session page is undated; it reports results from the RSO contract awarded in March 2023)
tools.context: US Air Force sustainment (RSO); B-1, B-52, E-3 and KC-135 part assessments
tools.processes: Polymer and metal AM (library of 667 AM materials); specific metal processes not documented
tools.availability: Contractor tool used under Air Force RSO contract
tools.description: Combines DoD logistics data with technical part data to prioritize part needs, flag parts affected by diminishing manufacturing sources and material shortages (DMSMS), and match part requirements to likely AM solutions. It reportedly assessed more than 6,000 Air Force parts and found about 900 viable for AM; under the RSO contract, 689 of 1,100 parts evaluated per airframe were found viable.

NRE.note: The undated session listing and 2023 contract press describe part prioritisation and matching to AM solutions but do not say whether reverse-engineering or redesign effort is assessed; no product documentation was found.

Production.note: The session listing and contract press give no cost figures or method and do not say whether part cost is estimated.

QA_Qual.note: Steers parts toward 'commercial airworthiness-certified' printing processes, a qualitative consideration of qualification burden with no qualification effort or cost (session listing; ExecutiveGov 2023).

QA_Insp.note: The session listing and contract press do not mention inspection or testing.

Storage.note: Flags DMSMS (obsolescence) parts as a screening criterion; there is no inventory or holding-cost calculation (session listing).

Shared_Capital.note: The contract press mentions characterising AM part families, but neither it nor the session listing mentions equipment investment or how capital is shared.

Shared_Capacity.note: The press mentions building organic AM capability but neither source mentions capacity, site allocation or pooling in the tool.

Speed.note: Prioritises part needs and claims reduced DMSMS and lead time, with no lead-time calculation (session listing).

tools.name: DLA Legacy Parts AM Prescreening Tool (DLA prototype AM candidate selection tool)
tools.developer: LMI with XSB Inc., Penn State (T. Simpson) and Virginia Tech (C. Williams), for the Defense Logistics Agency Weapon System Sustainment Program
tools.context: DLA-managed Class IX legacy spare parts (all services)
tools.processes: All metal and polymer AM (matched against the Senvol machine/material database)
tools.availability: Government internal prototype; method published in LMI report DL501T1 (DTIC)
tools.description: A database query tool that narrows about 4.5 million DLA-managed parts to about 43,000 that fit an AM build envelope and exactly match a common AM feedstock, assuming no redesign. Users then filter by FSC, weapon system, criticality, lead time, unit cost, dimensions, material and machine, with engineering review of each candidate's technical data package (TDP) required before any decision.

NRE.note: TDP availability is a displayed attribute, a proxy for reverse-engineering need, and each candidate goes to engineer-in-the-loop TDP review; NRE is not costed and no redesign is assumed (LMI DL501T1, Ch. 3-4).

Production.note: Current unit price from FLIS/EBS is used only as a filter (cost ranges); no AM production cost is computed (LMI DL501T1, Ch. 3-4).

QA_Qual.note: Criticality codes are a filter in the prototype, and acceptance, test and qualification requirements (QAP, FAT) are discussed as decision considerations left to engineering review; no qualification burden is estimated (LMI DL501T1, Ch. 2-4).

QA_Insp.note: Production lot testing is listed in Chapter 2 only as a general consideration; it is not among the nine collected logistics attributes, the prototype filters or display, or the proposed functional requirements (LMI DL501T1, Ch. 3-4).

Storage.note: Annual demand and backorder status are proposed filters and stock on hand is a listed consideration, but there is no inventory or holding-cost analysis (LMI DL501T1, Ch. 2-4, Table 4-1).

Shared_Capital.note: Printer investment is not discussed; AM systems are recorded only by build envelope and feedstock (LMI DL501T1, Ch. 3, full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Shared capacity and production networks are not discussed; point-of-need production is mentioned only in passing (LMI DL501T1, Ch. 1, full text).

Speed.note: Combined administrative plus production lead time (long lead/overage ranges) is a filter, with backorder filters requested; lead time is not computed or valued (LMI DL501T1, Ch. 4).

tools.name: NAVSEA AM part risk triage and TDP approval framework (with NAMPIE part identification events)
tools.developer: Naval Sea Systems Command (NAVSEA 05T, AM Technical Warrant Holder)
tools.context: US Navy surface ships and submarines; shipboard and waterfront AM
tools.processes: Polymer and metal (L-PBF and DED technical publications referenced)
tools.availability: Government internal (described in a public NRC workshop briefing)
tools.description: Parts are sorted into color-coded risk boxes: Yellow (under triage), Green (low criticality; can be approved at the waterfront or aboard ship), Blue (requires NAVSEA HQ review) and Red (cannot or should not be made by AM). Low-risk applications are delegated to local chief engineers, and others go through technical-authority approval that results in a TDP. NAMPIE events identify candidate shipboard parts, and a 'buy or print' Mission Impact Analysis uses the NAVSUP Price Fighter cost tool.

NRE.note: The framework produces technical data packages in a NAVSEA AM TDP format, and NAMPIE events aim to 'influence creation of associated technical data' for candidate parts, but TDP effort is not costed (NRC briefing, Dec 2020).

Production.note: NAVSUP N25's Price Fighter AM cost/part tool is being integrated into TDP development to project AM part cost, a planned feature with no documented inputs (NRC briefing).

QA_Qual.note: Risk box sets the approval level (green: waterfront or shipboard; blue: NAVSEA HQ; red: not AM capable), a criticality gate with no class-specific test requirements (NRC briefing).

QA_Insp.note: Neither the briefing nor the DoD IG audit mentions inspection or NDE in triage or TDP approval, and the internal criteria are not public (NRC briefing; DODIG-2020-003).

Storage.note: Approved TDPs are shared digitally, a parts repository is part of the digital strategy, and AM parts are to be catalogued in logistics databases for buy-or-print, but physical stock is not addressed (NRC briefing; DODIG-2020-003 on JTDI).

Shared_Capital.note: Neither the briefing nor the DoD IG audit mentions equipment cost or sharing, and the framework's internal criteria are not public.

Shared_Capacity.note: Low-risk approvals are delegated to ship and waterfront chief engineers, and a digital enclave for ship-shore data transfer is meant to facilitate distributed manufacturing, but no capacity analysis is described (NRC briefing).

Speed.note: Readiness through production of 'obsolete or long-lead items' is the stated aim, and a logistics database is planned to evaluate mission impact and readiness for buy-or-print, but lead time is not quantified (NRC briefing).

tools.name: NAVAIR AM Candidate Assessment Tool (Navy STTR topic N23B-T032)
tools.developer: Solicited by NAVAIR (transition targets: PEO-CS Digital Thread team and NAWCAD Lakehurst Digital Enterprise Tools Branch); no awardee found
tools.context: US Navy/Marine Corps aviation sustainment (readiness degraders)
tools.processes: Laser powder bed fusion and material extrusion (FDM) first; architecture to extend to other processes
tools.availability: STTR solicitation; no delivered tool found publicly
tools.description: A requested tool that uses expert-guided active machine learning on Technical Data Package and supply data (material, GD&T, acceptance criteria, criticality, demand, FSC) to screen out unsuitable parts, then estimate production cost and delivery schedule, building on an 'existing cost and time estimation tool' (possibly AMCAT; inference). The scores reflect the solicitation's requirements.

NRE.note: The topic requires CAD, TDP and PLM knowledge but does not mention reverse engineering, redesign or TDP creation as a tool function, and no delivered tool is public (Navy STTR N23B-T032 topic and Q&A).

Production.note: Phase I requires refining existing cost and time tools to predict production cost estimates for AM part candidates, a listed requirement; no awarded or delivered tool is public, so nothing is shown to be modelled (Navy STTR N23B-T032).

QA_Qual.note: Acceptance criteria and criticality are TDP and supply inputs and the aim is 'producing qualified end use parts', but no qualification process, test set or cost is specified (Navy STTR N23B-T032 topic and Q&A).

QA_Insp.note: The topic requires that production cost estimates 'consider all post-processing operations' including inspection, a requirement for an undelivered tool rather than a modelled cost element (Navy STTR N23B-T032, Phase I).

Storage.note: Demand is listed among supply data the tool would draw on and obsolescence is a stated motivation, but the topic does not mention inventory or say demand is a screening criterion, and no delivered tool is public (Navy STTR N23B-T032 topic and Q&A).

Shared_Capital.note: The topic and Q&A do not mention machine or equipment investment, and no delivered tool is public (Navy STTR N23B-T032).

Shared_Capacity.note: The topic and Q&A do not mention capacity or multiple sites, and no delivered tool is public (Navy STTR N23B-T032).

Speed.note: Predicting AM delivery schedules is a listed Phase I requirement and readiness through shorter lead times is the stated aim, but no delivered tool shows lead time computed (Navy STTR N23B-T032).

tools.name: Joint Additive Manufacturing Model Exchange (JAMMEX)
tools.developer: Defense Logistics Agency and America Makes; development overseen by the Joint AM Working Group
tools.context: Joint DoD (all services and DLA), including warfighters in the field
tools.processes: All AM; also cold spray procedures
tools.availability: Government internal (CAC-enabled web portal, jammex.dla.mil)
tools.description: A secure web repository for storing, managing and sharing 3D AM models, cold spray procedures and metadata across the services and DLA. It is an enabling digital-inventory system, not an analytical decision tool.

NRE.note: JAMMEX is meant to let the services and DLA share approved AM technical data, and the DoD IG says a single sharing method 'could eliminate duplicative AM efforts and result in cost savings', but engineering effort is not quantified (DoD IG DODIG-2020-003, pp. 7, 12, 16).

Production.note: DLA says parts printed through JAMMEX avoided costs that 'would have otherwise cost more and taken longer to procure' and that it aims at 'decreasing costs', but the repository computes no part cost (DLA news 2020 and 2023).

QA_Qual.note: DLA states it ensures 'models that go on JAMMEX are approved models' and the DoD IG says it will share approved data and parts awaiting approval, an approval gate rather than a qualification analysis (DLA news 2020; DoD IG DODIG-2020-003, p. 16).

QA_Insp.note: The flyer, DoD IG audit and DLA articles say JAMMEX stores models, cold-spray procedures and metadata but none says whether testing or acceptance requirements are included, and the CAC-only portal cannot be opened (JAMWG flyer 2024; DoD IG; DLA news).

Storage.note: DLA says JAMMEX provides 'a catalog of alternate sources for hard-to-procure and obsolete parts', a digital-inventory benefit stated without any inventory or holding-cost calculation (DLA news 2020 and 2023).

Shared_Capital.note: JAMMEX is a model and technical-data repository; machine capital is outside its documented scope (JAMWG flyer 2024; DoD IG).

Shared_Capacity.note: JAMMEX shares models and data across services, not printing capacity; no source describes pooling printers through it (JAMWG flyer 2024; DLA news 2020 and 2023).

Speed.note: DLA says JAMMEX aims at 'reducing readiness risks' and 'improving responsiveness', with interim parts printed for battle-damaged equipment while users wait for the real part, but no lead time is computed (DLA news 2020 and 2023).

tools.name: Selection of Additive Manufacturing Equipment (AMRDEC TR-RDMR-WD-16-87)
tools.developer: US Army AMRDEC Weapons Development and Integration Directorate (L. Hall)
tools.context: US Army aviation and missile R&D lab, including aviation part repair
tools.processes: Blown-powder DED, metal powder bed fusion, multifunctional (conductive) printing, polymer FDM
tools.availability: Published method (DTIC technical report)
tools.description: A narrative justification for choosing three AM machine types based on capability gaps from a workforce survey, part size and complexity (DED for large near-net parts, PBF for small complex parts), functional integration, and input from other labs. There is no scoring or cost model.

NRE.note: The report plans for process characterization to be done at AMRDEC and then transitioned to a contractor and discusses design freedom (topology optimisation, part-count reduction), with no cost (DTIC AD1031372).

Production.note: Fabrication cost is discussed in words; the only figure is that a first powder-bed build may need $10K-$50K of powder, falling with reuse, with no per-part cost (DTIC AD1031372).

QA_Qual.note: Material characterization is to be performed in-house and transitioned to a contractor, and current systems are said not to allow structural components for system testing, but no qualification steps or costs are given (DTIC AD1031372).

QA_Insp.note: The full report specifies no inspection, NDE or testing of parts (DTIC AD1031372).

Storage.note: The full report gives no spare-part, inventory or obsolescence content (DTIC AD1031372).

Shared_Capital.note: No machine prices are given and equipment sharing or utilisation is not addressed; only information sharing with vendors under CRADAs is mentioned (DTIC AD1031372).

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity is discussed only as build-envelope size, with no pooling across sites or users (DTIC AD1031372).

Speed.note: Cites decreased fabrication time and faster material delivery for blown-powder DED qualitatively, with no lead times; repairs would go to a contractor (DTIC AD1031372).

tools.name: Techno-economic performance metrics for large-format metal DED (ORNL MDF)
tools.developer: Oak Ridge National Laboratory Manufacturing Demonstration Facility (A. G. Stevens, P. Mhatre, L. Heinrich, C. Masuo, A. Shanafield, T. Feldhausen, B. K. Post)
tools.context: DOE national lab; domestic production of high-mix, low-volume casting replacements for 'energy and defense industries'
tools.processes: Large-format metal DED (several mature and emerging variants)
tools.availability: Published method (SFF Symposium 2024)
tools.description: Techno-economic and life-cycle metrics (build rate, volume, resolution, feedstock cost, embodied energy and CO2e) for several large-format DED processes, compared with conventional manufacturing. It is a set of comparison metrics, not a decision tool.

NRE.note: The conference abstract does not mention design or engineering effort, and no proceedings paper was found in searches (SFF 2024 abstract).

Production.note: Feedstock cost and build rate are reported as metrics for each DED process against conventional routes, but no per-part cost build-up is described (SFF 2024 abstract).

QA_Qual.note: The conference abstract does not mention qualification, and no full paper was found (SFF 2024 abstract).

QA_Insp.note: The conference abstract does not mention inspection, and no full paper was found (SFF 2024 abstract).

Storage.note: The conference abstract does not mention inventory, and no full paper was found (SFF 2024 abstract).

Shared_Capital.note: The abstract lists build-rate, feedstock-cost and energy metrics but not equipment capital; the later Shanafield and Stevens (2026) DED cost model does include capital cost but is a separate paper, so it does not settle this (SFF 2024 abstract; ORNL publication record).

Shared_Capacity.note: The conference abstract does not mention capacity sharing, and no full paper was found (SFF 2024 abstract).

Speed.note: The abstract gives build rate as a machine metric but does not say whether time to part or lead time is computed (SFF 2024 abstract).

tools.name: Project TAMPA additive manufacturing accelerator (spiral-based part adoption)
tools.developer: UK MOD Defence Support / UK Strategic Command with DE&S; industry framework: Babcock, NP Aerospace, RBSL, Thales, AMFG
tools.context: Defence spares and obsolescence across land, sea and air platforms, UK
tools.processes: Metal AM (specific processes not named); AMFG workflow software/digital catalogue
tools.availability: Programme; method not published; outcomes via DE&S 'recommended for adoption' decisions
tools.description: Accelerator that sequences parts in spirals by safety criticality and material (spiral 1: 11 non-safety-critical metallic NSN parts; spiral 2: safety-critical metallic parts) and takes successful parts to a DE&S recommendation for adoption into the defence inventory.

NRE.note: Re-engineering parts with no drawings is a named step (Babcock re-engineered a 1960s 4.5-inch naval gun part before printing it), but it is not costed (Operations Engineer July 2023).

Production.note: MOD sources only expect 'significant cost savings' and hope to 'reduce costs'; no per-part cost assessment is described (DE&S news page; Eureka; TCT 2024).

QA_Qual.note: Spirals are ordered by safety criticality and material, certification and qualification is one of four problem areas, safety-critical parts are certified by the producer, and parts go to a DE&S adoption recommendation; no qualification cost or counts (DE&S news page; Operations Engineer 2023; TCT 2024).

QA_Insp.note: Babcock X-rayed the original cast part to show its flaws and says porosity is controlled by governed print parameters, but no per-part inspection scope or cost is given (Operations Engineer July 2023).

Storage.note: Reduced need to stockpile is cited as a benefit and 'robust inventory management' as a problem area, not quantified (DE&S news page; fw-mag).

Shared_Capital.note: Only MOD news and trade press describe the programme, and none says whether machine investment or sharing is assessed.

Shared_Capacity.note: Vision of global hubs that print and dispatch assured parts for the UK and allies, plus secure transmission of print files for remote production; not modelled (DE&S news page; Babcock news 2024).

Speed.note: Periscope clamp produced in 'days instead of months' and a Mastiff carrier with an estimated 60% faster turnaround are quoted case results, not computed by the programme (Eureka; TCT 2026 via pulse.bot).

tools.name: AM in military logistics assessment for the Finnish Defence Forces and Millog (SWOT/AHP and depot-placement recommendation)
tools.developer: Finnish National Defence University (S. Rautio, doctoral thesis 2023); journal article by I. Valtonen, S. Rautio and M. Salmi, 'Capability Development in Hybrid Organizations - Enhancing Military Logistics with Additive Manufacturing', Progress in Additive Manufacturing 7 (2022) 1037-1052 (authors confirmed by the thesis record, which lists it as one of the four constituent articles)
tools.context: Defence spares and depot maintenance, Finland
tools.processes: Metal L-PBF (EOS M 100 costed) and AM generally
tools.availability: Doctoral thesis (2023, Finnish) and Springer journal article (DOI 10.1007/s40964-022-00280-z); qualitative
tools.description: Integrative review, case study, SWOT and AHP with experts (journal article) on how AM fits the FDF-Millog hybrid maintenance model; the thesis concludes industrial AM is best placed in repair-depot maintenance or for civilian components.

NRE.note: The article notes printing needs a 3D CAD model and that configuration management should hold baseline design data for spares, but design or digitisation effort is not costed (Valtonen, Rautio & Salmi 2022, Aalto open copy).

Production.note: The commercial partner's business case and payback are discussed in words, and responsiveness is ranked above direct manufacturing cost, with no per-part cost (Valtonen et al. 2022).

QA_Qual.note: Quality issues are listed among key barriers, with no qualification steps or costs (Valtonen et al. 2022).

QA_Insp.note: The article notes coordinate measuring machines are still needed in the printing workflow, without cost or scope (Valtonen et al. 2022).

Storage.note: Local production could reduce the supply chain to 'merely a supply of raw materials such as powder and wire', a qualitative claim with no stock calculation (Valtonen et al. 2022).

Shared_Capital.note: Quotes an EOS M 100 at about EUR 300k (EUR 500-700k with facilities) and says payback could take decades with one customer and few parts, but these are cited figures with no sharing or amortisation model (Valtonen et al. 2022).

Shared_Capacity.note: Notes capacity utilisation is 'significantly lower' in a decentralised model but more resilient, compares centralised and distributed printing, and the thesis places industrial printing in repair maintenance or civilian component production; no capacity model (Valtonen et al. 2022; thesis summary, Doria).

Speed.note: Responsiveness is emphasised and waiting time is said to be no more than machine cycle time plus post-processing, qualification and assembly, with no lead-time figures (Valtonen et al. 2022).

tools.name: FFI field AM trial assessment and component-suitability analysis (Norwegian Armed Forces)
tools.developer: Norwegian Defence Research Establishment (FFI) with Norwegian Special Forces (NORSOF)
tools.context: Deployed field spares and prototypes, Norway
tools.processes: Field unit used FDM polymer; titanium part printed by external partner (Tronrud Engineering) from transmitted files; powder-bed metal discussed
tools.availability: Public FFI report 16/01008 (Norwegian)
tools.description: Report on a containerised 3D printing capability at exercise Cold Response 2016; it references a prior FFI analysis of which components suit AM (Norberg and Oestereng, not located) and sketches distributed vs centralised production.

NRE.note: Notes the Armed Forces have no electronic spare-parts database with design files and recommends one holding CAD files, strength analyses for critical parts and printer-specific parameter sets; engineering effort is not costed (FFI 16/01008 full text).

Production.note: Reports the trial's total cost (~NOK 800k incl. NOK 450k printer) and build times over 40 h as case figures, with no per-part cost model (FFI 16/01008 full text).

QA_Qual.note: States material quality must be tested, standardised and certified, and the production process quality-assured, before AM parts or commercial AM services are used; no qualification steps are costed (FFI 16/01008 full text).

QA_Insp.note: The full report notes the trial parts were not tested but judged usable, and gives no per-part inspection step; its testing call concerns material qualification (FFI 16/01008 full text).

Storage.note: Argues AM can reduce inventory needs and transport costs, without figures (FFI 16/01008 full text).

Shared_Capital.note: The full report gives the trial's own printer cost (Fortus 250mc, NOK 450k, containerised) but does not discuss sharing machines between units (FFI 16/01008 full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Sketches distributed vs centralised production and civilian partners, and a titanium part was printed by an external firm from transmitted files, but no capacity is modelled (FFI 16/01008 full text).

Speed.note: Quick field repairs are reported as case results (a spacer designed and printed in ~30 min), and lead-time savings are described only qualitatively (FFI 16/01008 full text).

tools.name: AM-powered aircraft logistic support business model (Leonardo Aircraft Division)
tools.developer: Politecnico di Torino (G. Viano, MSc thesis) with Leonardo S.p.A. Aircraft Division
tools.context: Aircraft logistic support and spares (aerospace/defence), Italy
tools.processes: Metal powder bed fusion (Ti6Al4V per Leonardo spec NTA55952); FFF for polymers
tools.availability: Public MSc thesis
tools.description: Cost and business model for an AM-based logistic support service with fixed, variable, compliance/certification and per-client costs under a performance-based fixed-fee SLA; uses criticality, make/buy and obsolescence data as selection inputs.

NRE.note: One-time engineering is an explicit cost term in the service cost study: starting costs for candidate selection (fixed assessment times times a success rate), redesign and validation (fixed times plus safety margin), procedure development and catalogue development (preparing part designs for printing), though the numerical values are withheld as confidential (full thesis, 6.5.1.4, 6.7.1, 6.7.5).

Production.note: The thesis's own service cost model has a production cost term (estimated maximum printable material per job plus a margin for transport and wastage, plus five-year hardware depreciation), but values are withheld and there is no full per-part build-up (PoliTo thesis, cost chapters).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification effort is an explicit cost term: procedure development and testing (destructive and non-destructive tests, material cost plus safety margin) as a starting cost, per-client hardware integration and qualification estimated from effort and historical cost, and a compliance and certification cost category, with values withheld (full thesis, 6.5.3, 6.7.1, 6.7.3).

QA_Insp.note: Radiography, tomography and destructive testing of every PBF part (visual, radiography and tensile samples for FFF) are listed as operating cost items, but no inspection cost, count or estimation method is given (full thesis, 5.3.1-5.3.2, 6.5.3).

Storage.note: Inventory reduction is argued qualitatively and warehousing appears as an unvalued logistics cost; AM's effect on stock levels or holding cost is not computed (full thesis, 1.1, 6.2, 6.5.2).

Shared_Capital.note: Internal and client hardware is depreciated straight-line over five years and fixed starting costs are set against per-client costs in a six-year breakeven (year 3-4), but no utilisation or parts-per-machine input is used (full thesis, 6.7.1-6.7.5).

Shared_Capacity.note: Leonardo-owned hubs and a supplier network are described as reducing lead time and transport cost, but no capacity, pooling or utilisation is modelled (full thesis, 5.3.2-5.3.3).

Speed.note: AOG downtime cost and SLA uptime and delivery-time guarantees are discussed without figures; lead time, downtime and availability are not computed (full thesis, 1.1, 5.2, 6.6.2).

tools.name: Deutsche Bahn AM part identification and business-case process (with 3YOURMIND AM Part Identifier)
tools.developer: Deutsche Bahn AM team; vendor platform 3YOURMIND (Agile PLM, AM Part Identifier)
tools.context: Rail rolling-stock spares and obsolescence, Germany
tools.processes: 12 AM technologies incl. metal (aluminium, steel, titanium); WAAM/3DMP (GEFERTEC) for large metal parts
tools.availability: Internal process; described in vendor case study and DB interviews
tools.description: Combines bottom-up idea submission from ~200,000 employees and top-down automated scanning of inventory/stock lists (AMPI and AI) to flag candidates, then prioritised assessment and per-part business cases. Reported results: 74% faster assessments and 50-70% savings vs conventional procurement.

NRE.note: DB notes it lacked CAD data, has parts reconstructed from 3D scans and re-engineered (e.g. the gear housing), and keeps digitised documentation in a database, but no source shows this cost entering the business case (DB 3D printing page; EOS blog 2025).

Production.note: Per-part business cases compare AM with conventional procurement and report 50-70% savings, but the cost method is not disclosed (casestudies.com 3YOURMIND case).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification and testing are named as the main bottleneck, all printed parts are extensively tested before use, and DB/MGA worked with DIN on a production-site capability guideline (cited as DIN 52920), but no qualification effort or cost enters the assessment (EOS blog 2025; DB 3D printing page).

QA_Insp.note: DB says every printed component is extensively tested before use, but it is unclear whether this is per-part inspection or type testing, and no inspection scope or cost is given (DB 3D printing page).

Storage.note: AMPI scans stock lists, and the 'Road to 100 Million' target (EUR 1.8bn warehouse, about 10% printable) and avoided minimum order quantities are cited, but stock or holding cost is not modelled per part (EOS blog 2025; casestudies.com).

Shared_Capital.note: The case study, Automation Alley report, DB page, EOS blog and press mention DB's own industrial printers, but none shows whether machine investment or its sharing is assessed.

Shared_Capacity.note: DB prints in its own works and through external providers and the Mobility goes Additive network (used, e.g., for the gear-housing sand moulds), described qualitatively with no capacity modelling (DB 3D printing page; EOS blog 2025; heise).

Speed.note: Shorter lead times and avoided train standstills are savings streams (gear housing: 2-year quoted lead time vs 2 months; roll-stop 10 to 5 months), but no valuation method is published (EOS blog 2025; Automation Alley report).

tools.name: MPA/NAMIC/SSA maritime AM Joint Industry Programme part screening (Phase 1)
tools.developer: Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore, NAMIC, Singapore Shipping Association; DNV GL lead research performer; 10 SSA members incl. Wilhelmsen; collaborators Waertsilae, Sembcorp Marine, SpareParts3D, Ivaldi
tools.context: Merchant ship spares, Singapore
tools.processes: AM generally; worked examples mostly polymer plus steel and stainless parts; no metal process specified
tools.availability: Public report (public version PDF)
tools.description: Four-stage screening of ~600,000 part-order lines using a scoring matrix of commercial drivers (unit cost, quantity, lead time), AM supply chain benefits (lead-time reduction, stockyard inventory, TCO) and technical aspects; shortlisted 100 parts in three feasibility categories.

NRE.note: Reverse engineering and digitisation are not costed, but part identification relies on drawings, the digital inventory is CAD-based and partner cases describe digitalisation and redesign (MPA public report, pp. 12, 17, 38).

Production.note: Cost saving is defined as conventional minus AM cost (feedstock, process, post-processing, evaluation, certification) and unit purchase cost is a scoring criterion, but no per-part build-up is shown and the savings in Table D1 and the guide-bar case (USD 2,000 vs 1,250) are quoted without method (MPA public report, pp. 18-19, 38-39).

QA_Qual.note: Parts are sorted into feasible-with or feasible-without class certification and certification is named as an AM cost element, but certification needs are assumed rather than verified and are not costed (MPA public report, pp. 18, 26).

QA_Insp.note: Part evaluation is named in the AM cost and destructive or non-destructive evaluation is mentioned as a confidence factor, with no inspection cost or scope (MPA public report, pp. 13, 18).

Storage.note: Inventory portfolio is a shortlisting criterion and reduced stockyard inventory is a scored benefit, but no holding cost or stock level is calculated (MPA public report, pp. 11, 17-19).

Shared_Capital.note: Upfront machine and facility capex is called considerable, partnering with a third-party AM company or forming a consortium is suggested, and ROI/TCO are discussed without numbers (MPA public report, pp. 13, 29).

Shared_Capacity.note: Distributed printer networks, port and shipboard printing and service-provider networks are described, but capacity is not modelled (MPA public report, pp. 7, 29, 36, 38).

Speed.note: Delivery lead time and reduced procurement lead time are scoring criteria and the guide-bar case quotes under 72 h vs up to 12 weeks, but lead time is not computed (MPA public report, pp. 19, 38).

tools.name: Wilhelmsen DAVAMS on-demand spare part service model and Digital Asset Review Tool (DART)
tools.developer: Wilhelmsen Ships Service (lead) with Ivaldi Group, Pelagus 3D and SINTEF; demo parts from Valland, Kongsberg Maritime, Kawasaki Heavy Industries
tools.context: Merchant ship OEM spares, Norway/Singapore
tools.processes: Polymer and metal AM; specific metal processes not stated
tools.availability: Commercial service; DART described only in a Research Council of Norway project summary
tools.description: Service model for local on-demand production of genuine OEM spares with a part identification and feasibility step, DART (automatic GHG, cost and lead-time estimates for AM vs conventional, designed for sparse data), and a cloud digital warehouse holding design files, qualification rules and inspection records.

NRE.note: Parts pass a 'digitization and certification process' and a part identification and feasibility step before on-demand production, but this effort is not costed (Maritime Executive 2019; Prosjektbanken DAVAMS summary).

Production.note: Downgraded: DART is said to give automated cost estimates for AM vs conventional manufacturing designed for sparse data, but the project summary documents no inputs or method, which the rubric treats as costing mentioned without documented inputs (Prosjektbanken DAVAMS summary).

QA_Qual.note: The digital warehouse stores qualification requirements and qualification processes were demonstrated, and early adopters started with parts not needing class approval; no qualification effort or cost is modelled (Prosjektbanken; Maritime Executive 2019).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection information is held in the digital warehouse and the demonstrator chain included testing, but inspection is not costed or scoped (Prosjektbanken DAVAMS summary).

Storage.note: The digital warehouse aims at 'eliminating the need for physical inventory storage' with reduced inventory and transport costs claimed but not quantified (Maritime Executive 2019; Prosjektbanken).

Shared_Capital.note: The project summary and 2019 press do not mention machine investment or how printers are shared among customers, and no DART documentation was found.

Shared_Capacity.note: Local micro-factories and partner tech centres (thyssenkrupp Singapore and Muelheim) produce near demand for subscribing vessels, described as a service network without a capacity model (Maritime Executive 2019; 3DPrint.com 2019).

Speed.note: DART provides automated lead-time estimates for AM vs conventional manufacturing; downtime value is not shown (Prosjektbanken DAVAMS summary).

tools.name: DNV Digital Warehouse JIP quality-assurance framework for distributed on-demand spare parts
tools.developer: DNV with 18 JIP companies (incl. Saudi Aramco, ConocoPhillips, Vallourec, Ramlab, Norsk Titanium, Immensa, 3YOURMIND); DNV AM Energy group
tools.context: Oil & gas, energy and maritime spares, global (Norway, Singapore)
tools.processes: Metal and polymer AM (member firms include WAAM and DED suppliers)
tools.availability: JIP outputs to members; DNV AM standards (e.g., DNV-ST-B203) published separately
tools.description: JIP to create a quality-assurance framework for distributed, on-demand printing of spare parts close to where they are needed; DNV also developed a digital-inventory standard with Immensa and the AM qualification standard DNV-ST-B203.

NRE.note: DNV's JIP pages do not mention digitisation or design effort; the separate DNV-RP-B205 (2025) covers digitising parts but is paywalled and is not stated to be the JIP output (DNV JIP pages; RP-B205 page).

Production.note: The JIP pages and press do not say whether production cost is assessed, and no JIP deliverable is public (DNV JIP pages; JPT).

QA_Qual.note: The JIP's stated output is a quality-assurance framework so the end user gets 'the right part, with the right properties', but no qualification steps or costs are public (DNV JIP pages).

QA_Insp.note: The JIP pages do not say whether per-part inspection or testing is covered, and no deliverable is public (DNV JIP pages).

Storage.note: Motivated by spares that are never used and tie up value plus warehouse upkeep cost, with no figures (DNV JIP pages).

Shared_Capital.note: The JIP pages do not mention machine investment or sharing, and no deliverable is public (DNV JIP pages).

Shared_Capacity.note: The premise is sending a digital file through the cloud to print close to operations instead of shipping parts, with no capacity model (DNV JIP pages).

Speed.note: Long lead times and vulnerable supply chains are the stated motivation and AM is said to significantly reduce lead time, with no quantification (DNV JIP pages).

tools.name: Equinor digital inventory / Digital Supply Network programme
tools.developer: Equinor with TotalEnergies, Shell, ConocoPhillips, Vaar Energi and Fieldnode (Fieldmade spin-off); separate Siemens Energy-Equinor-Fieldmade JIP
tools.context: Offshore oil & gas spares, Norway
tools.processes: Metal (steel, Inconel) AM incl. robotic weld-based printing; polymer
tools.availability: Corporate programme; no public decision method
tools.description: Programme to replace physical inventory (about EUR 2.5bn) with digital files printed near point of use, targeting 25% inventory reduction in five years and 50% in ten; no part screening method is published.

NRE.note: The programme describes combining 3D scanning and 3D modelling to reconstruct obsolete metal or plastic parts, but this effort is not costed (Equinor magazine).

Production.note: Equinor describes comparative analyses and an LCA comparing AM with conventional practice and claims cost reductions (e.g. screws that 'save Equinor 10M USD'), with no documented cost model (Valve World; Equinor magazine).

QA_Qual.note: Offshore applications are said to normally require product qualification and certification, a DNV collaboration and earlier R&D on AM component reliability/safety are mentioned, but Equinor's qualification steps are not described (Formnext fonmag; Equinor magazine; Valve World).

QA_Insp.note: The articles mention a polymer replica to check a 3D model and testing alternative materials, but not inspection of printed parts, and no programme documentation is public.

Storage.note: States targets of 25% (5 years) and 50% (10 years) reduction of a ~EUR 2.5bn inventory, of which ~80% is said never to be used, as goals rather than model outputs (Formnext fonmag; Valve World).

Shared_Capital.note: The articles say a mobile micro-factory was hired from Fieldmade and that service providers download recipes, but none discusses machine investment or its sharing.

Shared_Capacity.note: A multi-operator Digital Supply Network with printing near demand, planned hubs (Hammerfest, Helgeland, Bergen) and service providers producing from downloaded recipes is described, with no capacity modelling (Equinor magazine; Valve World).

Speed.note: Lead-time cuts are quoted as case results or goals (40 to 10 weeks for a flange; 3-6 months to 4 weeks), not computed (Equinor magazine; Valve World).

tools.processes: Metal AM (process not named in fetched source)
tools.availability: Corporate practice; described in trade press
tools.description: Shell defines digital part documentation with suppliers and a repeatable qualification process for AM spare part vendors so parts can be bought on demand; first case was AM impellers for a seven-stage centrifugal pump made by Baker Hughes.

NRE.note: Shell defines the digital documentation of parts with suppliers and reverse-engineers parts (within IP law) when no qualified OEM supplies them, but this effort is not costed (Metal AM 2022; The Fabricator).

Production.note: Shell's authors claim in words that 3D printing will reduce the cost of making spare parts, with no cost figures or estimation method (The Fabricator).

QA_Qual.note: A repeatable qualification process for AM spare-part vendors is designed and Baker Hughes' Talamona facility was qualified, with part specifications and the printing process qualified jointly, but not costed (Metal AM 2022; The Fabricator).

QA_Insp.note: The pump underwent intensive pre-installation testing and the impeller was heat treated and tested within the 40-day cycle, but inspection is not costed or scoped (Metal AM 2022; The Fabricator).

Storage.note: Claims about one hundred thousand dollars avoided per stocked pump and reduced need to hold spare inventory, stated as claims rather than computed (Metal AM 2022; The Fabricator).

Shared_Capital.note: Press notes Shell owns about 15 printers at its Amsterdam and Bangalore technology centres for emergency in-house printing, but no source says whether or how machine investment is weighed or shared (The Fabricator).

Shared_Capacity.note: Describes a digital warehouse supplied on demand by qualified OEMs and local partners, with in-house printers for emergencies, as a supplier network without any capacity or lead-time model (The Fabricator).

Speed.note: Baker Hughes aims to reduce lead time, and an LNG pump impeller was printed, heat treated and tested within 40 days, 85% less than normal delivery; these are case figures, not tool outputs (Metal AM 2022; The Fabricator).

tools.name: Onboard metal AM implementation roadmap and part filter (Heerema Marine Contractors)
tools.developer: TU Delft (M.J. Kolthof, MSc thesis) with Heerema Marine Contractors; vendor partner Layertec
tools.context: Offshore construction vessel spares, Netherlands
tools.processes: Bound-metal extrusion with debind/sinter (Desktop Metal Studio System); FDM polymer
tools.availability: Public MSc thesis
tools.description: Phased roadmap (research, plastic then metal printing, opportunities) for onboard AM with part filters (geometry, vendor check, application check, cost comparison) and a Harris-profile evaluation; quantifies machine investment, inventory and downtime context.

NRE.note: On-board engineers modelling parts is listed as a man-hour cost, and model sources (manufacturer, 3D scanning, open databases, office modelling support, field measurement) are discussed, but no hours or costs are estimated (TU Delft thesis, ch. 2-4).

Production.note: Cost comparison is the last part-filter step, using vendor case studies (e.g. CNC $980 vs Studio System $148 per part) rather than a per-part cost model; an interviewee's 'What are the costs per unit?' stays open (TU Delft thesis, field study and appendices).

QA_Qual.note: Critical parts must be certified by bodies such as Lloyd's or DNV and the Chief Engineer approves prints, used as gates without costing (TU Delft thesis).

QA_Insp.note: Lloyd's suggests NDT, lab tests (bend, notch, tensile, hardness) and certified material, and the author ran tensile and hardness tests and recommends on-board trials and monitoring, but no inspection scope or cost is set (TU Delft thesis, ch. 4 and recommendations).

Storage.note: Illustrates that a 5% cut in the ~USD 13M on-board stock saves ~USD 650k and that a 1.8% cut equals the printer investment, an assumed reduction rather than a modelled effect on stock or holding cost (TU Delft thesis, ch. 5 and conclusion).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine investment (Studio System ~EUR 220k, Ultimaker EUR 6k) is entered and set against stock value for one vessel, while an interviewee notes one printer for all vessels would be logical; sharing is not modelled (TU Delft thesis, ch. 5 and appendix 4).

Shared_Capacity.note: The roadmap extends printing to other vessels and proposes an onshore 'external factory warehouse' with globally connected printers, described without any capacity or lead-time model (TU Delft thesis, roadmap and ch. 2).

Speed.note: Cites project downtime of about USD 1M per day, part delivery of up to 4-5 months and vendor print times of 4-5 days as context, and computes only an air-freight saving (~USD 27k/yr); lead time is not computed per part (TU Delft thesis, ch. 5 and appendices).

tools.name: AMDSP 2.0 AM cost and lead-time calculator
tools.developer: Aalto University (within the VTT/Aalto digital spare parts projects)
tools.context: Digital spare parts for Finnish industry (energy, marine, elevators)
tools.processes: 10 system/material combinations incl. metal L-PBF and polymer SLS
tools.availability: Online tool; reuse requires developer permission
tools.description: Online calculator estimating AM part cost and lead time versus production volume and machine utilisation, using hexagonal close-packing nesting and support generation.

NRE.note: The only description (one section of the VTT/Aalto 2020 report) covers STL upload, automatic orientation, support generation and nesting but does not say whether build preparation or design effort is costed; the tool itself (amdsp.org.aalto.fi) is blocked and no paper documenting AMDSP 2.0 was found (VTT/Aalto 2020 report, Sec. 3.1).

Production.note: From an uploaded STL, the chosen machine (10 systems), material and production volume, the tool outputs part cost over production volume, with orientation, supports and nesting computed (VTT/Aalto 2020 report, Sec. 3.1).

QA_Qual.note: The report section lists no qualification element, but it is a short summary of the tool rather than its documentation, so absence cannot be confirmed (VTT/Aalto 2020 report, Sec. 3.1).

QA_Insp.note: Neither the 2.0 description nor the earlier version's description (costs split into machine amortisation, work and material) names any inspection cost, but both are short summaries and the tool itself could not be opened (VTT/Aalto 2020 report, Sec. 3.1; DIVA 2018 report, Sec. 3).

Storage.note: The 2.0 description does not mention storage, while the earlier MATLAB version accepted conventional piece, mould, storage and transport costs as comparison inputs (DIVA 2018 report, Sec. 3); whether 2.0 kept these inputs is not documented and the tool itself is blocked (VTT/Aalto 2020 report, Sec. 3.1).

Shared_Capital.note: The tool outputs 'the cost associated with the machine's utilisation percentage (max. 100%)' and cost over production volume with hexagonal close-packing nesting of multiple parts per build, so machine cost is spread by utilisation, volume and multi-part builds; sharing across users or sites is not modelled (VTT/Aalto 2020 report, Sec. 3.1).

Shared_Capacity.note: One selected machine's capacity is modelled (lead time grows with production volume and cost varies with utilisation percentage), but no contention among users or pooling across sites sets lead time (VTT/Aalto 2020 report, Sec. 3.1).

Speed.note: The tool computes 'the lead time over the production volume' as a stated output; it is not dollarised (VTT/Aalto 2020 report, Sec. 3.1).

tools.year: Unknown start (36-month FP7 project); final report January 2012

tools.availability: Public final report (CORDIS); tools not public
tools.description: Management-level knock-out flowchart plus a six-area constraint model (engineering, material, process, economic, quality, ecological) and a questionnaire-based cost analysis tool for on-demand, on-location spare part production; a knowledge-based AM technology selector was planned.

NRE.note: Design and redesign are discussed, including an FEA-based 'Copy Original Part' method and design-timing options, but no engineering cost is calculated (CORDIS final report).

Production.note: A questionnaire-based cost analysis tool was built from influence parameters summarised in an Ishikawa diagram, but the report shows it only as a figure with no documented inputs or formulas (CORDIS final report).

QA_Qual.note: Product quality is one of six constraint groups, and the report calls for quality management and an 'AM spare parts certificate' process, with no class-specific tests or costs (CORDIS final report).

QA_Insp.note: Quality controls of input data, layering process and end parts are called for and inspection appears in examples (accuracy analysis, visual inspection), with no inspection scope or cost (CORDIS final report).

Storage.note: Cost reduction on stocks and warehousing and a 'balancing end of stock' business model are described, but no holding cost is computed (CORDIS final report).

Shared_Capital.note: The cost tool appears only as a figure and the narrative does not discuss AM machine investment or its sharing, so the public final report cannot settle this; the tools themselves are not public.

Shared_Capacity.note: The report's aim is a network of RTOs and industrial partners offering on-demand, on-location spare-part production, described qualitatively with no capacity model (CORDIS final report).

Speed.note: The knock-out flowchart covers manufacturing cost and time and delivery time is rated as a sector market requirement (e.g., 4.20 automotive), but no lead time is calculated (CORDIS final report).

tools.name: CASTOR (CASTOR Enterprise / automatic part identification)
tools.developer: Castor Technologies Ltd. (described as Israeli in earlier coverage; Fabbaloo 2021 calls it California-based); resold by Siemens (CASTOR Enterprise; Teamcenter-X & CASTOR), integrated into Oqton MOS (Apr 2023), listed on Hexagon Nexus
tools.year: 2020 (earliest coverage); Light/Enterprise/White Label editions by Jun 2021; 2D-drawing analysis Jul 2022; Oqton MOS integration Apr 2023; Siemens Xcelerator Nov 2023; used in NSRP Navy shipbuilding project May 2023-May 2024
tools.context: US Navy submarine sustainment: the NSRP project '3D Printing of Supply Sensitive Parts' (GD NASSCO per NSRP page; NAVSEA and PEO SSBN sponsors; GD Electric Boat observer) used CASTOR to screen Ohio-, Los Angeles- and Virginia-class parts by NIIN. Also general industry (Stanley Black & Decker, Evonik); Siemens lists aerospace & defense and marine among target industries.
tools.processes: Metal and polymer AM with a configurable printer/material library. Metal printers used in the NSRP run: SLM 280 2.0, EOS M400-4, Concept Laser M2 cusing Multilaser, X160Pro (likely ExOne X1 160Pro binder jet; not stated in deck). Metal materials: 316L, 304L, 17-4PH, IN625, IN718, Invar 36, CuNi2SiCr, AlSi10Mg. Polymer: HP Jet Fusion 4200 (PA11/PA12).
tools.availability: Commercial license (enterprise SaaS, cloud or internal server; free trial Jan 2024; Light, Enterprise and White Label editions; Siemens Xcelerator / Teamcenter-X; Oqton MOS integration)
tools.description: Bulk-screens 3D CAD, 2D PDF drawings, BOMs or part metadata spreadsheets. For each part it flags printability (printable / printable with changes / unprintable, with reasons such as threads, metal-support milling, heat deformation and wall thickness) and picks a printer and material. It then estimates AM cost and conventional-manufacturing cost in dollars, plus AM lead time in days. Other outputs: break-even versus CNC and die casting, redesign options (cheapest, best match, weight reduction, consolidation), FEA and CO2. Enterprise adds printer ROI calculations and a customizable calculation structure.

NRE.note: Flags parts 'printable with changes', simulates and grades CNC removal of metal supports, converts 2D drawings and suggests weight-reduction or consolidation redesigns, but none of this engineering effort is costed (NSRP deck 2024; Fabbaloo 2021; 3D ADEPT).

Production.note: Outputs per-part AM and traditional-manufacturing cost estimates in dollars on a suggested printer/material (e.g. check valve AM $368.98 vs TM $868.17) plus break-even versus CNC and die casting (NSRP deck 2024; Fabbaloo 2021).

QA_Qual.note: The NSRP output tables have no qualification or criticality field (the project itself calls shipboard certification undefined) and marketing mentions only a mechanical-property comparison, but the Enterprise cost structure is customizable and not public, so qualification handling cannot be settled (NSRP deck 2024; 3D ADEPT; Hexagon page).

QA_Insp.note: No source read, including the NSRP output tables and vendor pages, mentions inspection or testing, and the full cost model is not public (NSRP deck 2024; Hexagon page; 3D ADEPT).

Storage.note: CASTOR Enterprise lets users set 'operational costs from various points of the supply chain, such as inventory, shipment, labour costs' within its customizable cost estimate, and Hexagon says it identifies inventory cost savings, but no holding-cost or stock-level model is documented (3D ADEPT Enterprise launch; Hexagon page).

Shared_Capital.note: CASTOR Enterprise includes 'ROI calculations for 3D printers' and in-house printers can be set, but no amortisation, utilisation or volume inputs are documented (3D ADEPT interview; NSRP deck 2024).

Shared_Capacity.note: CASTOR says it has 'a network of service bureaus' and connects manufacturers to a bureau that can print the part, but no capacity or queue model is documented (3D ADEPT interview; G2 listing).

Speed.note: Outputs 'AM lead time estimation [days]' and 'AM time saving' per part (e.g. check valve 19-23 days), though no traditional lead time or readiness value is shown (NSRP deck 2024).

tools.description: Screens part inventories (3D CAD, 2D drawings via AI drawing analysis, or metadata only) for technical and economic AM suitability and recommends technologies. With optional economic inputs (current price, lead time, annual demand) it reports unit-cost comparison and savings broken into manufacturing cost, stock avoidance, downtime avoidance and lead-time reduction.

NRE.note: Gives DfAM optimisation suggestions, redesign recommendations and AI extraction of data from 2D drawings, but no NRE cost (3YOURMIND software FAQ; product page; 2D drawing analysis page).

Production.note: The Economics tab shows per-unit cost and savings for each suggested technology broken into material, labour and overhead, compared against the entered original part price (How to find 3D printable parts fast; 2D drawing analysis page).

QA_Qual.note: Builds catalogues of 'qualified parts' and SNCF's qualified inventory uses tailorable material and tolerance criteria, but qualification is a screening label with no cost or effort modelled (product page; SNCF case; software FAQ).

QA_Insp.note: Product pages, FAQ and the USMC case study do not mention inspection or testing, and no help documentation or screening-model description is public.

Storage.note: The savings report includes an explicit 'stock avoidance' component alongside manufacturing cost, and users can define inventory scores as KPIs (2D drawing analysis page; software FAQ).

Shared_Capital.note: Public pages name material, labour and overhead in the per-unit economics but do not say whether machine depreciation or utilisation enters; the printer database can be customised with own machines (How to find 3D printable parts fast; software FAQ).

Shared_Capacity.note: Part Identification pages describe no capacity model (machine utilisation and scheduling belong to the separate MES product), and the full method is not public (software FAQ; How to find 3D printable parts fast).

Speed.note: Takes the original lead time as an optional input and reports lead-time reduction and 'downtime avoidance' savings within total savings (2D drawing analysis page; How to find 3D printable parts fast).

tools.context: US Navy (ONR STTR Phase I/II, NAVSEA, NAVAIR), US Air Force (AFRL; America Makes allowables project 2022), US Army (ARL/AMMP missile-part qualification with Lockheed Martin, 2020-2022); commercial aerospace, oil & gas, medical

tools.description: Machine-learning software linking process parameters, process signatures (in-situ monitoring) and material properties to optimize parameters, predict properties and generate statistically substantiated allowables with fewer test builds. NRE.note: Directly supports parameter development ('rapidly optimize parameters & develop materials') and claims to cut the time and cost of process development, but does not estimate NRE cost (Senvol ML product page; 3D Printing Industry 2021).

Production.note: Senvol ML's documented scope is machine-learning models linking process parameters, process signatures and material properties, which plainly excludes per-part production cost (Senvol ML product page).

QA_Qual.note: Core purpose is to support machine and material qualification and predict allowables with less test data; it claims lower qualification time and cost but does not output the number of tests or the cost (Senvol ML product page; Navy STP spotlight).

QA_Insp.note: Analyses process-signature data from in-situ monitoring sensors to relate the process to properties, but sets no per-part inspection scope or cost (Senvol ML product page; Metal AM 2021).

Storage.note: Senvol ML's documented scope (process-property machine learning) plainly excludes inventory (Senvol ML product page).

Shared_Capital.note: Senvol ML's documented scope (process-property machine learning) plainly excludes machine investment or utilisation (Senvol ML product page).

Shared_Capacity.note: Senvol ML's documented scope (process-property machine learning) plainly excludes production capacity (Senvol ML product page).

Speed.note: Part lead time is outside the documented scope; time savings are claimed only for qualification data generation and 'more rapid implementation of AM' (Senvol ML product page; Navy STP spotlight).

Replique also reviews spare-part inventories for AM suitability and reverse-engineers or converts 2D drawings.

NRE.note: Design, reverse engineering and process adaptation are offered as services when part documentation is missing, with no NRE costing (Replique spare-parts page).

Production.note: Free non-binding quotes are prepared by Replique engineers from an uploaded drawing, CAD file or photo, and the platform lists a Quoting module, but no cost inputs or method are documented (Replique homepage and platform page).

QA_Qual.note: Partners are vetted for repeatable fit-for-purpose parts and series production includes first-article inspection with a documented process, but qualification is not modelled or costed (Replique homepage; ManufacturingTomorrow 2021).

QA_Insp.note: Replique enforces and tracks print and process parameters at service bureaus and stores quality records in a patented quality module, with no per-part inspection scope or cost (AWS blog; Replique platform page).

Storage.note: Digital storage of designs is claimed to replace physical stock and obsolete-stock disposal, and spare-part inventories are screened by material, size, demand frequency and single-supplier reliance, but holding cost is not computed (Replique spare-parts page; ManufacturingTomorrow 2021).

Shared_Capital.note: The company site, AWS blog and trade articles say nothing about machine investment or utilisation, and no product documentation is public.

Shared_Capacity.note: Orders are automatically routed across a partner network (450+ partners per the current site) by capability, capacity and location, with no modelled effect on lead time (AWS blog; Replique homepage).

Speed.note: Vendor claims 3 weeks vs 16 weeks conventional for spare parts and cites a 6-week MAN case, quoted from cases rather than computed (Replique homepage and spare-parts page).

tools.name: aPriori (Additive Manufacturing process group)
tools.developer: aPriori Technologies
tools.context: General manufacturing (medical, consumer, industrial, aerospace, automotive); no defense customer named in fetched pages
tools.processes: DMLS (metal powder bed), SLS, SLA, material jetting
tools.availability: Commercial license (enterprise)
tools.description: Digital-factory should-cost software whose AM process group computes physics-based cycle time, orientation, supports, nesting, post-processing (secondary machining, heat treat, powder recycling) and downstream surface treatment, heat treatment, inspection and packaging. Breakeven reports compare AM with casting across volumes.

NRE.note: Build-job setup is costed as Amortized Batch Setup = Setup Time x (Labor Rate + Direct Overhead Rate) / Batch Size, but no one-time redesign or engineering cost appears in the AM formulas (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2, Metal Sintering and Printing Formulas).

Production.note: Per-part DMLS cost is built from cycle time (preparation, support, part, recoat, powder-removal and cool time divided across nested parts), labour cost (labour time x rate / yield) and downstream heat treatment, surface treatment and inspection (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2).

QA_Qual.note: The AM chapter's documented scope is manufacturing times and costs for AM and subsequent processes, and its 13 formula sections (accounting, yield, printing, sintering, base removal, cleaning, curing, sieving, powder loading) contain no qualification element (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2).

QA_Insp.note: The AM process group estimates time and cost of subsequent inspection processes where applicable (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2, AM chapter intro); the inspection formulas themselves were not visible.

Storage.note: aPriori is a per-part should-cost engine whose documented AM scope is manufacturing time and cost, so inventory holding is outside it (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2).

Shared_Capital.note: Parts are nested to the maximum that fits the build plate and build, preparation and powder-removal time are divided across them, but how machine capital, utilisation or depreciation enter the direct overhead rate is not shown (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2, Metal Sintering Formulas).

Shared_Capacity.note: As a per-part should-cost engine its documented scope does not include capacity shared across sites or users (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2).

Speed.note: Per-part cycle time is computed from preparation, support, part, recoat, powder-removal and cool times, a partial time model; no lead time or availability output is documented (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2, Metal Sintering Formulas).

tools.name: Rickenbacher integrated SLM cost model
tools.developer: L. Rickenbacher, A. Spierings, K. Wegener (ETH Zurich / inspire AG)
tools.context: Industrial SLM job-shop costing; parts from different projects pooled into mixed build jobs
tools.processes: L-PBF (SLM)
tools.availability: Published model (Rapid Prototyping Journal 19(3):208-214); equations in paper, no public software
tools.description: Adapts Alexander et al.'s generic cost model to SLM, covering pre- and post-processing steps plus a regression-based build-time estimate for mixed build jobs. It allocates build cost to parts by volume and build height so that parts of different size and complexity sharing one build each get a fair cost. Building parts simultaneously gave a 41% average cost reduction in the case study.

NRE.note: Geometry-data preparation and build-job assembly are costed per job and divided over the parts in it, which is recurring build prep with no redesign, reverse engineering or parameter development (Dogea et al. 2023 description).

Production.note: Per-part cost from preparation, job assembly, set-up, build (machine rate x build time plus material), removal, substrate separation and post-processing (Emerald abstract; Dogea et al. 2023).

QA_Qual.note: Two reviews reproduce the full cost equation as seven process-step terms (geometry-data preparation, job assembly, set-up, build, removal, substrate separation, post-processing), so qualification lies outside the model's documented scope (Costabile et al. 2017; Dogea et al. 2023).

QA_Insp.note: The reproduced equation has no inspection term, but inspection could sit inside the post-processing term and the paywalled paper could not be read to settle it (Costabile et al. 2017; Dogea et al. 2023; Emerald abstract).

Storage.note: Outside the documented scope: the model allocates SLM process-step costs to parts in shared build jobs, which does not involve inventory (Emerald abstract).

Shared_Capital.note: Build cost (machine hourly rate x build time) is allocated among parts from different projects sharing a build job by volume and build height, so filling the build space lowers unit cost (41% average reduction); the machine rate itself is given, not derived from capital (abstract; Costabile et al. 2017; Dogea et al. 2023).

Shared_Capacity.note: Pooling happens only within one machine's build jobs as a cost effect, with no lead-time or multi-site capacity effect (abstract; secondary descriptions).

Speed.note: Build time for a job is estimated by a linear regression on 24 builds (job volume, support area, layer-dependent fraction) and split among parts by an allocation algorithm, but only for cost; lead time is not reported (Costabile et al. 2017; Khanna et al. 2024).

tools.name: Lindemann et al. (2013) DMRC lifecycle-cost model with TD-ABC
tools.developer: C. Lindemann, U. Jahnke, M. Moi, R. Koch (Paderborn University, Direct Manufacturing Research Center)
tools.context: Lifecycle cost of AM vs. conventional manufacturing for end-use parts (wheel carrier, Formula Student upright); aerospace/automotive framing
tools.processes: L-PBF (SLM/DMLS)
tools.availability: Published model (SFF Symposium 2012 and 2013 papers); no public software
tools.description: Lifecycle cost model following the DIN/IEC 60300-3-3 phases: concept, design and development, production, installation, usage/maintenance, and disposal. Production is costed with time-driven activity-based costing across build-job preparation, build, part and support removal, and post-processing. Build rate, machine cost, material cost and utilization come out as the dominant drivers.

NRE.note: The design and development phase costs technical drawings, component design, QM planning, a prototype and test phase and production planning, and build-job preparation is a TD-ABC process (SFF 2013).

Production.note: TD-ABC of build-job preparation, build, part/support removal and post-processing with machine, material, personnel, energy, consumables and complexity factors per build job (SFF 2013).

QA_Qual.note: A prototype and test phase and QM planning are costed as design-and-development lifecycle elements, but material/process qualification or certification is not modelled beyond that lump (SFF 2013).

QA_Insp.note: Quality control is a TD-ABC production cost element bundled with post-processing (support removal, surface treatment), with no NDI/CT or coupon-testing line (SFF 2013; Khanna et al. 2024).

Storage.note: Usage-phase logistics include spare-part storage at about 22% of acquisition value, but AM's effect on stock levels is only discussed, not modelled (SFF 2013).

Shared_Capital.note: TD-ABC allocates machine cost by resource time with an explicit 75% utilisation assumption (about 673 parts/yr per machine), and utilisation is named a dominant cost driver, though it is not varied (SFF 2013).

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity appears only as an illustrative parts-per-year figure and predicted build rates; no pooling or contention is modelled (SFF 2013).

Speed.note: TD-ABC times each process (including build time from build rate) only as cost drivers; lead time is not modelled, and the EUR 100,000/day aircraft-on-ground cost is cited only as motivation (SFF 2013).

tools.name: Atzeni & Salmi DMLS vs. die-casting break-even model
tools.developer: E. Atzeni, A. Salmi (Politecnico di Torino)
tools.context: Aeronautical end-use component (landing-gear part); break-even batch size vs. high-pressure die casting
tools.processes: L-PBF (DMLS) vs. high-pressure die casting
tools.availability: Published model (Int J Adv Manuf Technol 62(9):1147-1155)
tools.description: Builds cost models for DMLS and high-pressure die casting of the same DfAM-redesigned aerospace part to find the volume at which AM becomes competitive. It concludes AM can compete for small-to-medium batches.

NRE.note: Pre-processing is costed per build as setup time times operator rate, but the DfAM redesign of the part is not shown as a one-time engineering cost (Khanna et al. 2024 review; abstract).

Production.note: Per-part DMLS cost is built up from material (volume x unit price), pre-processing, processing (machine cost over parts per build) and post-processing (operator time, heat treatment), against a die-casting model (abstract; Khanna et al. 2024).

QA_Qual.note: The abstract and two reviews that describe the model (Khanna et al. 2024; Baumers et al. 2017) do not mention qualification or certification, and no open full text was found (IRIS record has no file).

QA_Insp.note: The reviews list material, pre-processing, processing and post-processing (operator, heat treatment) terms without inspection, but absence cannot be confirmed without the full text (Khanna et al. 2024; Baumers et al. 2017).

Storage.note: The documented scope is a per-part production cost comparison by batch size against die casting, which excludes inventory (abstract; Khanna et al. 2024).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine cost (5-year straight-line depreciation, about 90% of AM part cost) is divided by the number of parts in a multi-part build that assumes the build space is used efficiently (Khanna et al. 2024; Baumers et al. 2017, Table 5).

Shared_Capacity.note: The model costs a single part on one DMLS route at different batch sizes, so capacity pooling across sites or users is outside its scope (abstract; reviews).

Speed.note: Neither the abstract nor the two reviews mention lead time or build-time reporting, though a comparison with die casting could treat tooling lead time; the full text could not be reached.

tools.name: Baumers et al. (2017) total-cost and capacity-utilisation model (IJPR)
tools.developer: M. Baumers, P. Dickens, C. Tuck, R. Hague (University of Nottingham), with L. Beltrametti and A. Gasparre on the 2017 paper
tools.context: Technology adoption: DMLS vs. machining+welding for a packaging-machine blower (2017); DMLS vs. EBM productivity and economies of scale (2016)
tools.processes: L-PBF (DMLS), EB-PBF (EBM)
tools.availability: Published models (Technol. Forecast. Soc. Change 102 (2016) 193-201; Int J Prod Res 55(23) (2017) 6957-6970; arXiv 1706.02090); in-house C++ packing/build-time tool not public
tools.description: Activity-based production cost models that combine direct costs with time-allocated indirect (machine and overhead) costs, voxel-based build-time estimates, and computational packing of the build volume. The 2017 version adds per-layer build-failure risk and the discounted value of design adaptation. It shows single-geometry builds overstate unit cost by 157% on average compared with full mixed builds.

NRE.note: Only per-build machine setup and unloading labour (180 min, about EUR 72 per build) is costed; design, redesign and re-validation costs are explicitly excluded (arXiv full text).

Production.note: Unit cost is built from material, energy, build-time-allocated indirect cost, setup labour and 37 min/part post-processing labour, inflated for build-failure risk; the 17-4PH blower costs about EUR 56-58 per unit in mixed builds (arXiv full text).

QA_Qual.note: Re-validation and qualification costs are explicitly omitted, which the authors say may be significant (arXiv full text).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection is only folded into 37 min/part of manual post-processing labour together with support removal, surface finishing and washing, and the scope statement elsewhere lists inspection as excluded (arXiv full text).

Storage.note: In-process inventory, warehousing and logistics costs are explicitly excluded (arXiv full text).

Shared_Capital.note: Indirect machine cost (about EUR 23/h) is allocated by build time and volume share, and filling unused build volume with other geometries ('fungible' capacity) cuts unit cost, so capital is spread with an explicit utilisation and multi-part-build assumption (arXiv full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Build-volume utilisation is modelled by packing other parts into the same build, but on one machine with no effect on lead time; scheduling and lead time are left to future work (arXiv full text).

Speed.note: Lead time is explicitly excluded from scope and named as future work (arXiv full text).

Same paper - full text (arXiv PDF)
