tools.name: Laureijs/Fuchs (CMU) process-based cost model: metal AM vs. forging
tools.developer: R. E. Laureijs, J. Bonnín Roca, S. P. Narra, C. Montgomery, J. L. Beuth, E. R. H. Fuchs (Carnegie Mellon University; E. R. H. Fuchs lab, Engineering & Public Policy)
tools.context: GE jet-engine bracket (design from public GE competition), commercial aviation, 1,000-12,000 brackets/yr; AM part redesigned ~80% lighter (1.66 kg saved). A footnote notes that military field repair, where forged spares cannot be sent for, would change the comparison.
tools.processes: Ti-6Al-4V by L-PBF (DMLS, EOS M290) and EBM (Arcam S12; Q20 discussed) vs. forging + heat treatment + grinding + multi-axis milling + wire EDM
tools.availability: Journal article: ASME J. Manuf. Sci. Eng. 139(8):081010, 2017, doi:10.1115/1.4035420. The full text was readable on the ASME Digital Collection page; supplementary input tables were not.
tools.description: Process-based cost model built on data from 14 anonymous firms (AM producers, powder and equipment suppliers, a university lab) and the Forging Industry Association. The AM route is modelled from the build step through stress relief (DMLS only), wire EDM, HIP, shot peening and destructive testing. At 1,000/yr the AM bracket costs about $3,200 vs. about $400 forged. With a 10-year fuel-saving NPV ($1,300 base, up to $3,000 per bracket), AM is competitive at 2,000-12,000/yr. Powder price and batch size (set by build orientation) are the top sensitivities. Cutting destructive testing from 1 part in 8 to 1 in 100 saves about $150/bracket at 10,000/yr, and about $410 when combined with vertical builds. FAA configuration control is modelled as 'one machine, one part' dedication of the AM machines.

NRE.note: Explicitly excluded: the model assumes the design is already optimised and converted to STL and starts at the build step, so redesign enters only as the lighter geometry (ASME full text as read in the earlier pass; the ASME page could not be reopened this session).

Production.note: Per-bracket cost for DMLS, EBM and forging is built up from process-step inputs, reject rates and best/base/worst ranges across 1,000-12,000 brackets/yr (ASME full text, Figs. 4-7; ScienceGate abstract).

QA_Qual.note: FAA configuration control is modelled only as a 'one machine, one part' dedication rule that raises AM machine cost per part at low volume; certification activities themselves are not costed and recertification is discussed only in words (ASME full text).

QA_Insp.note: Destructive testing is modelled as a yield loss (base 1 part in 8, swept to 1 in 100, worth about $150/bracket at 10,000/yr), but testing labour, equipment and AM NDI/CT are not costed (ASME full text, Fig. 8; ScienceGate abstract on reduced testing).

Storage.note: Inventory and spares are not analysed; lead-time reduction appears only in the introduction and a footnote on military field repair (ASME full text).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine cost per part depends on annual volume and batch size per build (set by vertical vs horizontal orientation, Fig. 9), with AM machines dedicated to the bracket while forging equipment is shared (ASME full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Production is modelled at a single facility with no pooling of capacity across sites or users (ASME full text).

Speed.note: Time value is not modelled; the lifecycle benefit is fuel saving from weight reduction, not availability or lead time (ASME full text; ScienceGate abstract).

tools.name: Bonnín Roca (CMU) process-based cost model + facility-location model for decentralized metal AM
tools.developer: J. Bonnín Roca, P. Vaishnav, R. E. Laureijs, J. Mendonça, E. R. H. Fuchs (Carnegie Mellon University EPP; Universidade de Lisboa / IN+ via CMU Portugal; Bonnín Roca now at TU Eindhoven). M. G. Morgan is not a co-author of this paper; he co-authored the team's regulation papers.
tools.context: Commercial-aviation maintenance spare parts. Case is a non-flight-critical titanium jet-engine bracket (the GE-competition bracket from Laureijs et al. 2017) supplied to airports, under current-technology, performance-improvement and equipment-cost-drop scenarios.
tools.processes: Metal AM of Ti-6Al-4V (powder-bed; specific machine not visible in accessed text) with post-processing including HIP
tools.availability: Journal article: Additive Manufacturing 28 (2019) 136-151, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2019.04.010 (paywalled; abstract, keywords and section snippets accessed). Related CMU dissertation: Bonnín Roca (2017) 'Leaders and Followers: Challenges and Opportunities in the Adoption of Metal Additive Manufacturing Technologies' (CMU repository record; PDF host blocked this session).
tools.description: A location-dependent process-based cost model (local labour and land costs) feeds an uncapacitated facility-location MILP. The MILP picks the cost-minimising number and location of AM sites, trading production scale economies against transport and inventory costs. The optimal number of sites barely changes across technology-improvement scenarios, and as demand grows the factory moves toward the highest-demand airports. Decentralisation pays only for non-critical parts that can share the same equipment with minimal certification requirements, at combined volumes in the tens of thousands per year. At lower volumes it pays only for parts that need no HIP. Expensive post-processing equipment is what favours centralisation.

NRE.note: The abstract and section snippets do not say whether design, reverse-engineering or build-preparation cost is included; no open full text or dissertation PDF could be reached (the CMU repository PDF is not fetchable), so this stays unconfirmed (ScienceDirect abstract; IN+ seminar abstract).

Production.note: A process-based cost model of AM production, with HIP as a post-processing step that drives the result, feeds the location optimisation (ScienceDirect abstract; IN+ seminar abstract).

QA_Qual.note: Certification works as a scoping condition: decentralisation pays only for non-critical parts on shared equipment 'with minimal certification requirements', and no qualification cost term is visible (ScienceDirect abstract).

QA_Insp.note: The abstract and snippets do not mention inspection or testing, and whether the predecessor Laureijs destructive-testing yield is carried over could not be checked without the full text (ScienceDirect abstract).

Storage.note: Inventory cost is an explicit term traded off against production and transport cost when choosing the number and location of sites (ScienceDirect abstract); the inventory formulation itself is not visible.

Shared_Capital.note: Production scale economies are traded off against the number of sites, and parts that share the same equipment, or skip costly HIP equipment, favour decentralisation (ScienceDirect abstract; IN+ seminar abstract).

Shared_Capacity.note: The optimisation sets the number and location of AM sites serving airports, but the accessed text shows no capacity contention or effect on lead time or service level (ScienceDirect abstract and snippets).

Speed.note: Lead-time reduction appears only as a motivation in the introduction, and whether lead time enters the inventory or transport cost terms cannot be seen in the abstract and snippets, so the earlier Partial rested on inference (ScienceDirect abstract and introduction snippet).

tools.name: Paderborn DMRC Trade-off Methodology (TOM), 2017 version (Kruse, Reiher & Koch)
tools.developer: C. Lindemann, T. Reiher, U. Jahnke, R. Koch; A. Kruse (Paderborn University, DMRC)
tools.context: Workshop-based screening of existing parts, mainly aerospace (ESA projects; 90% overlap with independent expert selections)
tools.processes: Metal and polymer PBF (aerospace metal focus)
tools.availability: Published method + Excel workbook (TOM matrix) used in workshops; not publicly downloadable
tools.description: Three-phase workshop (information, assessment, decision) in which non-experts and AM experts score candidate parts in a trade-off matrix. Criteria cover size limits, part class, assembly suppression, post-processing need, material applicability, design rules, property improvement and processing time, then material change, buy-to-fly, lead time and an AM-vs-milling cost ratio. Redesign and economic evaluation follow, and the 2017 revision adds knock-out gates and four value categories.

NRE.note: The decision phase gathers redesign requirements (black-box principle, InformationForms) and compares redesign approaches, but redesign and data-preparation effort are not costed (SFF 2014).

Production.note: An AM-vs-milling cost ratio and an early cost-calculation module give a first production-cost estimate without a documented build-up, and a full cost comparison is only planned in the 2017 version (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).

QA_Qual.note: Material applicability (industry use, public data) and space-specific requirements are scored and printable material is a knock-out gate, with no certification step (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).

QA_Insp.note: Full papers read; post-processing need is scored but quality inspection is not a criterion (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).

Storage.note: Avoiding tooling and tool warehousing is mentioned and the 2017 questionnaire asks about spare-part and tool management strategy, with no inventory criterion or calculation (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).

Shared_Capital.note: Full papers read; machine availability in-house or at providers is only a size-feasibility check and the TOM has no investment criterion (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).

Shared_Capacity.note: Full papers read; equipment availability is checked only for build-chamber size, and capacity sharing is not addressed (SFF 2014).

Speed.note: Lead, process and post-processing time and time-criticality are scored criteria on a 1-5 scale, not computed outputs (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).

tools.name: VTT/Aalto digital spare parts program (DIVA / DIVALIITO): screening, metal PBF cost tool, qualification workflow
tools.developer: M. Salmi, J. Partanen, J. Tuomi, S. Chekurov, N. Kretzschmar et al. (Aalto University); S. Metsä-Kortelainen, A. Jussila et al. (VTT)
tools.context: Finnish industrial spare-parts portfolios (198,638 and 17,182 items); crisis-preparedness motivation; Patria Aviation among funders
tools.processes: Metal PBF, DED (repair), polymer PBF
tools.availability: Published project report (DIVA final report, VTT/Aalto) + companion survey paper (Kretzschmar et al. 2018, Applied Sciences 8(10):1837); MATLAB cost tool described, not public
tools.description: Four-phase spare-part classification adapted from Knofius et al.: technical (material, size), photo-based geometry review, ranking, then economic (price, resupply lead time, annual consumption, MOQ). Only ~2% of one firm's items were feasible. It adds an STL-based metal PBF cost tool and illustrative AM vs. conventional business cases that include downtime. Its cost tool was later released as AMDSP 2.0, which is listed separately.

NRE.note: 3D-model availability is a technical screening criterion (though it could not be assessed systematically), and digitisation and redesign are not costed (DIVA report).

Production.note: The STL-based metal PBF cost tool sets orientation and supports automatically and splits cost into machine amortisation (8-yr depreciation), work and material with 74% powder packing, up to 95% recycling and 10% follow-up time; cases include an Inconel 718 pin at about EUR 55 vs EUR 90 (DIVA report).

QA_Qual.note: DIVALIITO sets out a six-step qualification workflow based on DNV GL CG-0197 (MPS and test plan, notified-body review, qualification build with witness specimens, component and powder test lists), but it is not tiered by part class or costed (2020 report; DIVA report).

QA_Insp.note: Hardness, porosity, Charpy, tensile, chemistry and microstructure tests on printed parts and witness specimens are listed, but not costed or set by part class (DIVA report; 2020 report).

Storage.note: The cost tool accepts storage and transport costs, and the enclosure business case quantifies stock reduction from printing on demand: average stock 10 vs 1 pcs, storage cost EUR 100 vs EUR 1, plus logistics-to-stock costs (DIVA report Table 4).

Shared_Capital.note: The PBF cost tool depreciates the printer over 8 years, but no utilisation, operating-hours or parts-per-build input is described (74% is the powder packing ratio), and spreading capital through service providers' wider customer base is mentioned only qualitatively (DIVA report).

Shared_Capacity.note: Five supply-chain models (OEM, maintenance provider, 3D database operator, printing service provider and end-user centric) and platform networks of AM service providers are described qualitatively, with no capacity model (DIVA report; 2020 report).

Speed.note: The enclosure business case quantifies downtime (EUR 1,000/h) and delivery time (20 vs 19 days) to show AM can be cheaper overall, and re-supply lead time is a screening criterion (DIVA report Table 4).

tools.name: Klahn-Leutenecker-Meboldt (ETH Zurich) design-strategy and indicator method
tools.developer: C. Klahn, B. Leutenecker, M. Meboldt (ETH Zurich; inspire AG)
tools.context: Identifying components where AM redesign adds most value; two industrial cases
tools.processes: L-PBF (SLM) and SLS
tools.availability: Published method (Procedia CIRP 36 (2015) 230-235; ICED 2015 DS80-4)
tools.description: Separates a manufacturing-driven strategy (substituting AM for an existing process, possibly later in the lifecycle) from a function-driven strategy (redesign for performance). It proposes indicators for parts that gain most from AM through process advantages vs. design advantages.

NRE.note: The strategy choice sets how much redesign is warranted (function-driven designs need major redesign to return to conventional production), but redesign effort is not quantified (Procedia CIRP full text).

Production.note: Cost is a screening outcome and a reason for the manufacturing-driven strategy, and the cases compare quoted unit costs by lot size (SLS about EUR 6.88 vs EUR 107.83 for prototype moulding at 25 units), but there is no cost model (Procedia CIRP Fig. 4; ICED 2015 Table 1).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification is not part of the strategies or indicators; the CIRP case mentions only customer testing of 50 SLS parts (Procedia CIRP and ICED 2015 full texts).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection is not addressed in either paper (Procedia CIRP and ICED 2015 full texts).

Storage.note: Inventory, spare parts and obsolescence are not among the indicators or strategies; reduced inventory appears only in a background list of general AM benefits citing Wohlers (ICED 2015 full text, Sec. 2, 5.1; Procedia CIRP).

Shared_Capital.note: AM machine investment is not discussed; the papers note only that AM avoids part-specific tooling and CAM investment (Procedia CIRP and ICED 2015 full texts).

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity is not addressed beyond a remark on growing build rates and service-provider competition (Procedia CIRP and ICED 2015 full texts).

Speed.note: The manufacturing-driven strategy uses AM for time reasons, citing about 3 weeks for prototype moulds and 3 months for series tooling in the case, but time is not computed or valued (Procedia CIRP; ICED 2015).

tools.name: Purdue/Virginia Tech Decision Engine for AM in defense acquisition
tools.developer: W. Tsutsui, Q. Shi, I. Walter, A. Wei, C. Williams, D. DeLaurentis, J. Panchal (Purdue University; Virginia Tech)
tools.context: Sustainable defense acquisition; 6061 aluminium part, replicated or topology-optimized; 100-part lot
tools.processes: Hybrid WAAM, metal binder jetting, sand binder jetting (printed molds), L-PBF vs. casting
tools.availability: Published model + software prototype (NPS Acquisition Research Symposium, SYM-AM-23-069); JSON-driven decision engine
tools.description: Expected-utility engine that ranks AM and conventional routes on total cost, total time and part mass, with a bounding-box go/no-go check. Cost comes from a Gibson et al.-style model (prorated machine purchase, operation, material, labour). Hybrid WAAM ranked highest in both scenarios.

NRE.note: Per-batch human time for printer facilitation is costed as labour, but the topology-optimised redesign enters only through lower mass and its design, CAD/CAM or file-preparation effort is not costed (NPS paper SYM-AM-23-069, cost model and Table 3).

Production.note: Cost per alternative is built from prorated machine purchase, machine operation, material (feedstock price times mass) and labour from human time, with build time from scan length and process parameters and a ±10% uncertainty (NPS paper, Table 3).

QA_Qual.note: The full paper models no qualification or certification term; only a note that the hWAAM part needs heat treatment (NPS paper).

QA_Insp.note: The full paper models no inspection or testing term (NPS paper).

Storage.note: Inventory reduction appears only as a general AM benefit in the introduction and the decision engine does not evaluate it (NPS paper).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine purchase is prorated into cost and parts per batch (5-8) are listed, but the proration basis (life, utilisation or parts per machine) is not stated and machine sharing is not modelled (NPS paper, cost model and Table 3).

Shared_Capacity.note: The full paper does not model machine counts, shared machines or pooled capacity; build volume is only a go/no-go check (NPS paper).

Speed.note: Total time for the 100-part lot (machine time from scan length plus human time) is computed and weighted 0.3-0.4 in the utility, but lead time, queueing and availability are not modelled (NPS paper, Table 3).

tools.name: Zaman et al. integrated material & AM process selection (Ashby + AHP)
tools.developer: U. K. uz Zaman, M. Rivette, A. Siadat (Arts et Métiers ENSAM, LCFC Metz); S. M. Mousavi (Shahed University, Tehran)
tools.context: Aerospace drilling grid; database of 134 machines from 38 vendors
tools.processes: Database includes SLM, EBM, LENS, LMD, EBAM; the case study screened only polymer processes
tools.availability: Published method (Robotics and Computer-Integrated Manufacturing 51:169-180); open author copy
tools.description: Translates requirements, screens materials and processes with Ashby material indices, then ranks them with AHP (validated with SAW) on function, cost and environment. Criteria include machine cost, labour cost, build speed, accuracy and build volume.

NRE.note: Design or engineering effort is not a criterion or cost term in the method; a longer design cycle is mentioned only in the literature review (ENSAM author copy).

Production.note: Per-part material cost is computed with the Yim and Rosen model (support, recycling, volume, price, density), while machine cost and labour cost enter only as AHP criteria, so no full per-part cost is built up (ENSAM author copy, Eq. 1, Table 11).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification and certification are not addressed anywhere in the method (ENSAM author copy).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection is not in the method; metrology and quality control appear only as challenges in the literature review (ENSAM author copy).

Storage.note: Inventory is not addressed anywhere in the method (ENSAM author copy).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine cost is an AHP ranking criterion (7.9% global priority), but it is not amortised and sharing or utilisation is not modelled (ENSAM author copy, Table 11).

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity is reflected only as machine build volume; throughput and shared capacity are not modelled (ENSAM author copy).

Speed.note: Build speed (printing speed on a 50x50x20 mm reference part) is the most heavily weighted machine criterion (26.9%) and 'time constraints' are noted as requirements, but no build or lead time is computed (ENSAM author copy, Table 11).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine maintenance enters as a fixed rate (e.g. $20k/yr, $3.5/h), but machine purchase, depreciation, utilisation and parts per build are not modelled (packing index left to future work) (Aston accepted manuscript).

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity sharing is not addressed anywhere in the full method (Aston accepted manuscript).

tools.context: Metal laser-sintering job shop with mixed-geometry builds; validated against Baumers' build B01 on an EOS M270

tools.description: Step-wise cost model (data preparation, build-job assembly, setup, building, removal) with skill-specific labour rates and OEE-adjusted times. NRE.note: Per-build preparation (orientation, supports) and build-job assembly are costed from operator and workstation rates (Eq. 18-19); redesign is mentioned in the introduction but no one-time redesign, reverse engineering or parameter development is modelled (UNISA preprint).

QA_Insp.note: Quality control is named as a post-processing phase but explicitly neglected in the cost calculation; production rejects enter only as the quality loss in the OEE time adjustment (UNISA preprint, Eq. 7-8).

Storage.note: Inventory is not addressed; the model covers one build job in a job shop (UNISA preprint, full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Build-chamber capacity utilisation and adapted utilisation are computed for the mixed build (Eq. 25-26), but the model covers one machine and one build with no queue, scheduling or cross-site pooling, which the authors leave to future work (UNISA preprint).

Speed.note: Outputs completion time per geometry in days from assembly, setup, build and removal times (Eq. 16), but post-processing, queueing and delivery are excluded and time is not valued (UNISA preprint).

tools.context: Titanium-alloy parts; single-part and 15-geometry mixed batches
tools.processes: L-PBF (DMLS)

tools.description: Production cost = energy + labour + material + overhead, where overhead covers machine amortisation, maintenance and administration by build time. Speed.note: The model computes build and scan time (t_build) to drive energy, gas and overhead costs, a print-time-only time model; lead time or availability is not reported or valued (MDPI full text).

tools.name: Dias et al. (2022) WAAM process-based cost model (Sustainability)
tools.developer: M. Dias, J. P. M. Pragana, B. Ferreira, I. Ribeiro, C. M. A. Silva (Instituto Superior Técnico, University of Lisbon)
tools.context: WAAM + finish milling vs. machining from solid and vs. die casting for a case part (316L)
tools.processes: WAAM (arc DED) + milling; vs. machining, die casting
tools.availability: Published model (Sustainability 14(9):5197, open access); MSc thesis with Excel process-based cost model
tools.description: Excel process-based cost model of setup, deposition and machining. Fixed costs cover equipment annualised and scaled by utilisation, building and overhead; variable costs cover wire, baseplate, gas, labour, energy and a scrap credit. WAAM beats machining from solid at all volumes studied and beats die casting up to ~2,000-2,300 parts, with buy-to-fly as the most sensitive parameter.

NRE.note: Pre-processing (3D modelling, planning) and post-processing are explicitly excluded from the cost model so the routes can be compared fairly, so no design or engineering cost is included (Sustainability full text, sec. 2).

Production.note: Per-part cost vs annual volume is built from wire, baseplate, gas, labour, energy, equipment, tooling, building and overhead for WAAM and the conventional routes (Sustainability full text).

QA_Qual.note: Full text read; qualification or certification is not part of the model (Sustainability full text).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection falls in the post-processing stage that the model explicitly excludes (Sustainability full text).

Storage.note: Full text read; inventory is not addressed (Sustainability full text).

Shared_Capital.note: Machinery is annualised over its life and scaled by a utilisation rate set by cycle time, annual production, rejection rate and uptime for non-dedicated machines (Sustainability full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: The model sizes the number of WAAM-plus-machining sets needed to reach annual production at 240 x 8 h/yr uptime, so capacity is modelled, but at one site and with no effect on lead time (Sustainability full text).

Speed.note: Deposition (from wire feed speed), inter-layer cooling and machining times are computed per part, but only to allocate cost; lead time is not reported (Sustainability full text).

tools.name: NIST SP 1176 / Thomas & Gilbert AM cost review and taxonomy
tools.developer: D. S. Thomas, S. W. Gilbert (National Institute of Standards and Technology)
tools.context: Economics of AM adoption across manufacturing; cites the F-18 spare air-duct centralized vs. distributed case
tools.processes: All AM (metal and polymer)
tools.availability: Published report (NIST SP 1176), free
tools.description: Literature review that sorts AM costs into well-structured costs (material, machine, build-envelope utilisation, build time, energy, labour) and ill-structured costs (build failure, setup, inventory, transport, supply-chain vulnerability). It gives conceptual supply-chain cost equations but no new calibrated model.

NRE.note: The reviewed per-part models carry per-build setup labour (Hopkinson and Dickens setup times of 10-120 min) and preparation at about 3-9% of cost (Lindemann), but design cost is only noted as the exception to cost-free customisation and no one-time engineering is modelled (NIST SP 1176, Secs. 3.3, 3.2, Table 3.1).

Production.note: The report sets out per-part cost models from machine, material, labour, build time and post-processing (Hopkinson and Dickens; Ruffo et al. C = material x mass + indirect rate x build time) and its own total-cost decomposition for AM vs traditional (NIST SP 1176, Secs. 4.1, 4.3).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification and certification are not treated as cost items anywhere in the full report (NIST SP 1176).

QA_Insp.note: Quality assurance is named as a concern needing standard methods to evaluate accuracy, surface finish and feature detail, and build failure is listed as an ill-structured cost, but neither is costed (NIST SP 1176, Secs. 3, 3.3).

Storage.note: Inventory is quantified only at the macro level (holding cost of $52 billion at an assumed 25% of inventory value) and appears as a finished-goods inventory term in the cost decomposition, but AM's effect on stock is not modelled (NIST SP 1176, Secs. 3.1.1, 4.3).

Shared_Capital.note: Utilisation and multi-part amortisation appear only in summaries of other studies (Hopkinson and Dickens; Ruffo); the report's own cost equations have no amortisation or utilisation term, and it says only that filling the build chamber lowers unit cost (NIST SP 1176, Secs. 4 and 6).

Shared_Capacity.note: Centralised vs distributed production is discussed by quoting Khajavi et al.'s F-18 case ($1.0M vs $1.8M per year) and Holmström et al., not computed by the report (NIST SP 1176, Sec. 3.1.2).

Speed.note: Time appears as a conceptual term in the 'total advantage' equations and in narrative on lead time and supply disruption, with no lead-time calculation or value of time (NIST SP 1176, Secs. 3.1.2, 3.1.4, 4.4).

Shared_Capital.note: AM machine capital is absent from the full text and limited AM equipment capacity is named as future work; unit cost is a single per-option input (accepted manuscript).

Shared_Capacity.note: Single-item, single-stock-point model; limited AM equipment capacity and multi-item approaches are left to future work (accepted manuscript, conclusions).

Speed.note: Expected backorders over review period plus lead time are computed and costed, with CM lead times of 4-12 weeks and AM lead time equal to total production time (accepted manuscript, Eq. 3, Table 6).

tools.name: Peron failure-rate-uncertainty AM vs CM spare parts model with inspection tools
tools.developer: Mirco Peron, Andrea M. Coruzzolo, Rob Basten, Nils Knofius, Francesco Lolli, Fabio Sgarbossa
tools.context: Spare parts with intermittent demand; AM failure rates uncertain because the technology is new; evaluates porosity assessment and in-situ monitoring.
tools.processes: Metal AM (porosity/in-situ monitoring implies powder-bed metal); exact process not verified
tools.availability: International Journal of Production Economics 278:109438; open-access PDF linked on UNIMORE IRIS (abstract seen).
tools.description: Periodic-review Poisson inventory model with materials-science-based failure-rate uncertainty showing AM is penalized far more than CM by uncertainty; porosity assessment or in-situ monitoring pays off only if it cuts uncertainty by ~5-6 percentage points.

NRE.note: The 2024 abstract does not mention design or one-time engineering cost, and the same authors' 2022 IFAC precursor (full text) has only holding, backorder and production cost terms; the 2024 open-access PDF on UNIMORE IRIS could not be fetched (URL rejected by the proxy), so whether the extension adds NRE is not shown.

Production.note: The 2024 abstract says the model weighs AM's high production costs against inventory savings, but the full text could not be opened, so whether unit cost is computed or entered is not confirmed; the same authors' 2022 precursor uses per-technology unit costs (abstract; IFAC 2022).

QA_Qual.note: AM failure-rate uncertainty derived from fatigue data, attributed to the newness of the process, acts as a proxy for missing qualification data and its cost penalty is computed, but no qualification activity, test set or cost is modelled (2024 abstract; 2022 IFAC precursor).

QA_Insp.note: Porosity assessment and in-situ monitoring are costed as investments and the model computes the uncertainty reduction that justifies each (about 5 and 6 percentage points) (UNIMORE IRIS abstract).

Storage.note: Holding cost (about 30% per year of unit cost) is computed on expected on-hand stock under the optimal order-up-to level for AM and CM, quantifying AM's inventory reduction (2024 abstract; 2022 IFAC precursor, Eq. 1).

Shared_Capital.note: Neither the 2024 abstract nor the 2022 precursor full text includes AM machine capital (unit production cost is a single input), but the 2024 full text could not be fetched to confirm the extension adds none.

Shared_Capacity.note: A single-item periodic-review inventory model with fixed lead times (0.1 weeks for AM), so capacity shared across sites or users is outside its documented scope (2024 abstract; 2022 IFAC precursor).

Speed.note: The 2024 abstract names AM's short lead time as the source of its inventory savings, but the full text could not be opened, so whether backorders or lead time are computed is not confirmed; the 2022 precursor computes backorder cost (abstract; IFAC 2022).

tools.name: Ahlsell automotive slow-moving spare parts AM supply chain cost model
tools.developer: Levin Ahlsell, Didar Jalal, Patrik Jonsson (Chalmers); Siavash H. Khajavi, Jan Holmstrom (Aalto)
tools.context: Automotive OEM; 14 slow-moving spare parts; European central distribution centre; outsourced centralized AM.
tools.processes: Polymer (e.g., FDM) and metal AM via supplier quotes
tools.availability: Open access, Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing 7(1):8.
tools.description: Total supply chain cost model (production price, inbound/outbound transport, ABC-based warehousing, and service costs incl. vehicle-off-road downtime, badwill, lost sales) over the part life cycle; 3 of 14 parts show savings; metal AM parts cost ~1,756% more and need 72-99% cost cuts to break even.

NRE.note: The model explicitly leaves out the cost of developing or adjusting 3D drawings and the engineering labour of redesign; production cost is only the supplier purchase price (Chalmers full text, method and Discussion).

Production.note: Part-specific unit prices for each technology are model inputs (AM prices from supplier quotes on 3D drawings, annual quantity and material; TM prices from the OEM database), which meets the per-technology unit-cost input test even though the AM price has no build-up (Chalmers full text).

QA_Qual.note: The model explicitly excludes the cost of quality controls to approve a spare part and has no qualification term (Chalmers full text).

QA_Insp.note: Quality-control cost is explicitly excluded, and quality-check time is also left out of the AM lead-time estimate (Chalmers full text).

Storage.note: ABC-based warehousing cost (capital cost on stock value, goods-in, overhead, building and more) is computed from average inventory, which differs by method: TM one-shot lifetime buy versus AM annual replenishment with a one-piece safety stock (Chalmers full text, Table 4).

Shared_Capital.note: AM production is outsourced and machine capital sits inside the supplier price (with margin), so capital and its sharing are outside the model's scope (Chalmers full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Only one centralised outsourced AM supplier is modelled and its capacity never constrains lead time; the authors state a dispersed AM supply chain was not investigated (Chalmers full text).

Speed.note: Vehicle-off-road penalty cost, badwill and lost sales are computed from service level, with the AM stockout penalty set by the AM lead-time input and the TM penalty at the maximum fee (Chalmers full text, service cost equations).

tools.name: Strong two-stage p-median model for metal AM post-processing hubs
tools.developer: Danielle Strong, Michael Kay, Brett Conner, Thomas Wakefield, Guha Manogharan (Penn State and collaborators)
tools.context: US metal AM supply chain: siting hubs that combine heat treatment and machining for near-net metal AM parts (US counties, NAICS data). Not spare-parts specific.
tools.processes: Metal AM plus post-processing (stress relief/heat treatment, machining)
tools.availability: Additive Manufacturing 25:469-476; abstract seen.
tools.description: Two-stage p-median facility location model choosing hub locations and capacities and assigning demand across machine shops and heat-treatment facilities, minimizing fixed, operating and transport costs; 22 hubs grow to 35 as demand rises.

NRE.note: Only the abstract was reachable (Elsevier paywall; no open copy, thesis or repository text found); it lists total cost as fixed, operational and transport costs and does not mention design or engineering cost.

Production.note: Operational costs of hybrid-AM processing at hubs enter the total cost, but at hub level with no part-level build-up (Penn State Pure abstract).

QA_Qual.note: Only the abstract was reachable and it does not mention qualification, so whether it is modelled cannot be established.

QA_Insp.note: Only the abstract was reachable; it covers heat treatment and machining but does not say whether inspection is in the operational costs.

Storage.note: Only the abstract was reachable and it does not mention inventory, so whether it is modelled cannot be established.

Shared_Capital.note: The p-median model trades fixed hub costs against operational and transport costs when choosing hub locations and capacities (22 hubs growing to 35 with demand) (Penn State Pure abstract).

Shared_Capacity.note: Outputs include hub capacity utilisation and demand assignment across machine shops, heat-treatment facilities and hubs, but the abstract shows no effect on lead time or service (Penn State Pure abstract).

Speed.note: Only the abstract was reachable; it reports transport cost but not lead time or delivery time, so whether speed is modelled cannot be established.

tools.name: Barz two-stage capacitated facility location model with AM buy-to-fly ratio
tools.developer: Andreas Barz, Tobias Buer, Hans-Dietrich Haasis
tools.context: Generic two-stage supply network (700 generated instances); not spare-parts specific.
tools.processes: AM represented only by material efficiency (buy-to-fly ratio 2-20), a metal-aerospace concept
tools.availability: Open access, Logistics Research 9:13.
tools.description: Two-stage capacitated facility location problem showing that lower buy-to-fly ratios (AM) cut transport costs and shift production sites closer to customers, with the site count roughly unchanged.

NRE.note: The objective has only first- and second-stage transport costs and site-opening fixed costs, so design or engineering effort is not modelled (open-access full text).

Production.note: Production costs are explicitly excluded: the paper states direct production costs are independent of the site and are not considered in the experiments (open-access full text).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification is not part of the model, whose only AM parameter is the buy-to-fly ratio in the flow-balance constraint (open-access full text).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection is not part of the model, which costs only transport and site opening (open-access full text).

Storage.note: Storage of raw materials or final products at production sites is explicitly forbidden, so inventory is not modelled (open-access full text).

Shared_Capital.note: Fixed costs of opening capacitated production sites are traded against transport cost, but these are generic site costs rather than AM machine capital, and economies of scale are explicitly excluded (open-access full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Site capacities (100-500 units) constrain single-sourcing assignment of customers to sites, but the model has no lead-time, delivery-time or service-level effect (open-access full text).

Speed.note: Lead time, delivery time and service level are absent; the paper lists slower production time only as future work (open-access full text).

tools.name: Doudnikoff NCSU/USMA military spare parts network model (extends McDermott et al.)
tools.developer: Letai M. Doudnikoff (advisor Brandon M. McConnell), North Carolina State University
tools.context: Isolated military repair-part sustainment network (remote DC/service locations); demand representative of US Army Alaska (USARAK).
tools.processes: Generic AM, with fixed-cost range cited for metal AM machines
tools.availability: Open NCSU MS thesis.
tools.description: MILP inventory policy plus Monte Carlo simulation (60 periods) for first-machine placement and isolated-network studies; distributed first machine lowers operating and transport cost, but no-AM is cheapest once AM fixed cost is included; returns to added AM capacity diminish.

NRE.note: The MILP objective covers TM and AM production, transport, carrying and backorder costs only, and part specifications are not modelled, so no design or engineering cost appears (NCSU thesis, ch. 3).

Production.note: AM per-part production cost is a model input but is set equal to TM cost for simplicity (Assumption 4), a lumped unit cost with no build-up from machine time or material (NCSU thesis, ch. 3).

QA_Qual.note: The thesis assumes equal build quality for AM and TM (Assumption 3), which takes qualification out of scope (NCSU thesis, ch. 3).

QA_Insp.note: No inspection or testing term appears in the cost objective, and build quality is assumed equal to TM (NCSU thesis, ch. 3).

Storage.note: The MILP sets order-up-to levels and charges inventory carrying cost at DCs and service locations, with reorder points set from a service-level parameter (NCSU thesis, ch. 3).

Shared_Capital.note: AM fixed cost per machine per day ($121/$241/$512 in Table 3.1, with sensitivity) is charged by the number of machines in the network, and centralized vs distributed placement and added capacity are traded off; variable machine cost is not modelled and the $2,000-5,000 metal figure is only a footnote (NCSU thesis).

Shared_Capacity.note: AM capacity per node and period constrains output (one part type per period), and a centralized AM node at the DC serves several service locations, so capacity contention drives backorders; total capacity is split evenly when distributed (NCSU thesis, ch. 3-4).

Speed.note: Transport lead times (7 periods TM-to-DC, 2 periods DC-to-SL) drive reorder points, and backorders and backorder penalty cost are model outputs (NCSU thesis).

sources.title: Doudnikoff (2021) NCSU MS thesis
Earlier version: NCSU/USMA AM spare parts network model (McDermott, Winz, McConnell)

earlier_versions: McDermott, Winz, Hodgson, Kay, King & McConnell 2021 (Journal of Defense Analytics and Logistics 5(2):179; from McDermott's 2020 NCSU MS thesis, with the Winz et al. 2020 readiness-vs-cost working paper): the original Monte Carlo + Croston/SBA intermittent-demand + MILP (s,S) model comparing no-AM, centralized and distributed AM. It found centralized AM wins for lumpy demand and distributed for stable demand. Doudnikoff 2021 reuses this model and its 1-1-4 network and modifies it for isolated military sustainment networks, first-machine placement and AM fixed-cost/capacity trade-offs.

tools.name: Coyle naval aviation AM sustainment screening + DES (NPS)
tools.developer: David M. Coyle (Naval Postgraduate School)
tools.context: US Navy aviation spares (Navy-managed consumables, FRC-manufactured items, DLA Class IX NMC items; 10,162 items screened); sample 17-4PH part with 545-day procurement lead time.
tools.processes: Metal: DMLS/L-PBF (EOS M290), 17-4PH stainless
tools.availability: Open (DTIC AD1046824).
tools.description: Top-down screen of Navy aviation inventory for AM candidates followed by an Innoslate discrete-event simulation (adapted from Jedeck 2015) comparing local stock, OEM order and local AM for one part: AM $3,145 in ~10 days vs OEM $7,005 in 545 days; at quarter print speed AM costs 17% more but stays far faster.

NRE.note: The DES assumes a 3D CAD file, PMI and a complete TDP already exist; reverse-engineering cost and time (SD-22's three to six months is cited) are omitted from the model and flagged as possibly decisive, with PLM/digital thread recommended (full thesis, Sec. V.B.1, VI).

Production.note: Per-part build-up for local AM: setup $100, machine run $550.10 for an 18.6 h build, removal $100, post-processing $1,000 and feedstock at $47.62/lb, as triangular distributions, with half- and quarter-print-speed sensitivity (full thesis, Tables 3-4, Sec. V.B.3).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification of AM and reverse-engineered parts is identified as a gap and future research but is not modelled or costed (full thesis, Sec. VI.A, VI.C).

QA_Insp.note: Final inspection is a per-part activity in the AM branch at $400 and 1 day (full thesis, Table 4).

Storage.note: Holding cost for the local-stock branch is computed as h = i x c (10% of the $7,004.77 unit cost, $700.48 per unit per year) and compared with the order and AM branches (full thesis, Sec. V.B.3.a).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine time is priced as a single run cost ($550.10 for 18.6 h, from Ray 2017 ABC models) with no depreciation, utilisation or multi-part-build input (full thesis, Table 4).

Shared_Capacity.note: One part per print run on one EOS M290 at the FRC, with no queue, capacity contention or multiple sites in the DES (full thesis, Sec. V.B).

Speed.note: The DES outputs time per activity and a Gantt chart for each supply branch (AM about 10 days vs. 545 days for an OEM order, about 30 minutes for a local pull), and long lead time is a candidate selection criterion; readiness is not dollarised (full thesis, Sec. V.C, VI.A).

tools.name: Busachi/Erkoyuncu (Cranfield, Babcock) AM framework and decision support for Royal Navy support services
tools.developer: Alessandro Busachi, John Erkoyuncu, Paul Colegrove (Cranfield University); Richard Drake, Chris Watts, Stephen Wilding (Babcock International)
tools.context: UK Royal Navy platforms; AM 'Rapid Availability Support System' located in-supplier, in-port, support vessel, on-platform or forward base.
tools.processes: Metal AM (technology selection is a framework phase; team focus on WAAM/DED and PBF)
tools.availability: Open (core.ac.uk / Cranfield); Int. J. System Assurance Engineering and Management 9(3):657-674.
tools.description: Soft-systems framework with eight phases (mission, platform, configuration, critical-to-availability parts, AM technology, DfAM, manufacturing configuration, dynamic simulation) and availability equations in which on-platform AM removes administrative and procurement delay; authors state benefits still need quantification.

NRE.note: Design time is an explicit DSS input and output (DesTim, Table 10) that the thesis says may lead to high costs, and the FDM model costs bidding and geometry preparation at a high level; 3D scanning for parts without CAD is a framework step (PhD thesis sec. 7.2; Procedia CIRP 2018; IJSAEM 2018).

Production.note: Per-part WAAM cost is computed from welding, deposited material, substrate, shielding gas, setup and non-productive costs using machine, engineering and machining rates, e.g. GBP 75,732 for case component 1 (PhD thesis ch. 5 Eqs. 4-15, sec. 8.2).

QA_Qual.note: Part qualification is named as the main constraint and is a framework phase, but no qualification cost or time is modelled, and expert reviewers flagged qualification as missing (IJSAEM 2018; PhD thesis secs. 6.2, 8.1).

QA_Insp.note: QA appears in the process map and a 3D scanner for QA is listed in the FDM cost breakdown, but the thesis has no inspection cost term and says scanner activities still need to be modelled; WAAM NDT methods are only listed (PhD thesis sec. 5.4; Procedia CIRP 2018).

Storage.note: Lower platform inventory and freed space are cited as benefits, but no inventory equation exists (IJSAEM 2018; PhD thesis sec. 8.3).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine rate is investment divided by utilised time times utilisation rate with overheads (Eq. 6), and setup cost is spread over batch size (Eq. 14) (PhD thesis ch. 5; Procedia CIRP 2018 Eq. 1).

Shared_Capacity.note: AM location configurations (in-port, support vessel, forward base, on-platform) are compared and change logistic delay time, but no machine count, capacity limit or queue is modelled, so platforms never contend for a shared facility (IJSAEM 2018; PhD thesis secs. 7.1, 8.1).

Speed.note: The DSS computes travel time, logistic delay time, downtime and operational availability from distance, platform speed and delay inputs, e.g. availability 96.47% to 99.25% when LDT falls from 661 h to 6.7 h; the IJSAEM paper itself gives these equations only conceptually (PhD thesis Eqs. 16-21, Table 18).

tools.name: Strieby USMC expeditionary metal AM cost-effectiveness analysis
tools.developer: LtCol Stephen F. Strieby, USMC (Naval Postgraduate School, Acquisition Research Program)
tools.context: USMC ground expeditionary metal AM for distributed naval operations (ExMan unit).
tools.processes: Metal: hybrid wire-arc AM (3D Hybrid Solutions), liquid metal (Xerox ElemX), metal FFF (Markforged Metal X), bound metal deposition (Desktop Metal Studio System 2)
tools.availability: Open (NPS-LM-23-263, dair.nps.edu).
tools.description: Cost-effectiveness ratio (total system cost / parts produced over a 5-year life, from representative print times) for four metal AM processes with sensitivity on print and sintering times; recommends hybrid wire-arc AM.

NRE.note: The MCO 4700.4 design, test-fit and approval workflow is described and design time per unique part is named as a using-unit cost, but it is not monetised in the CEA (NPS report, ch. V).

Production.note: Cost per part is purchase price divided by lifetime operating hours times a representative production time per process; material, labour and maintenance are excluded and parts are not specific (NPS report, ch. V, Tables 14-15).

QA_Qual.note: The CEA assumes all parts are approved and all printers meet qualification standards, but the report describes the MCO 4700.4 design, test-fit and approval workflow and recommends a standardised test print to verify printers and set an accepted engineering risk; nothing is costed (NPS report, ch. V-VI).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection and NDT are not discussed or costed anywhere in the CEA (NPS report, full text).

Storage.note: Raw-material inventory is excluded and spares inventory is not modelled; only general reductions in 'logistical supply lines' are expected (NPS report, ch. V-VI).

Shared_Capital.note: Each system's purchase price is amortised over 15,600 lifetime operating hours (12 h/day, 5 days/week, 5 years) and the parts produced in that time, a utilisation and volume assumption; maintenance is assumed zero (NPS report, ch. V).

Shared_Capacity.note: Assumes an in-theatre printer can be tasked by any organisation in the task force with a prioritisation process, but no queue or contention is modelled; a queuing study of XFAB numbers for a service level is future work (NPS report, ch. V-VI).

Speed.note: Representative production time per process sets parts produced and is the main sensitivity, but lead time, readiness and availability are explicitly not computed (NPS report, ch. V).

tools.name: NASA-STD-6030 Additive Manufacturing Requirements for Spaceflight Systems (2021)
tools.developer: NASA (Marshall Space Flight Center; NASA Engineering and Safety Center)
tools.context: Crewed spaceflight hardware (with tailoring guidance for non-crewed and aero via NASA-STD-6032); widely referenced by DoD and industry as a template for classification-driven AM QA
tools.processes: Metal L-PBF (powder) and DED (wire or powder) permitted for Classes A, B and C; polymers restricted to Class B/C or C only
tools.availability: Free public PDF on standards.nasa.gov
tools.description: Classifies each AM part by consequence of failure (Class A/B/C, plus Exempt), then structural demand and a points-based AM risk score (inspectability, removable as-built surfaces, supports, wall thickness) into subclasses A1–A4/B1–B4, and tailors the QA requirements (QMP, material property suite, witness testing, NDE, preproduction articles, part process qualification) to each class.

NRE.note: Requires a registered Qualified Metallurgical Process (QMP, per machine), a Part Production Plan and a Qualified Part Process frozen after the AM Readiness Review, so parameter development and build preparation are mandatory deliverables, but none is costed (NASA-STD-6030 Sec. 4-5, AMR-47/48).

Production.note: No per-part production cost content; the standard is a requirements document (NASA-STD-6030 text).

QA_Qual.note: Prescribes qualification by class in countable form: QMP-A/B/C scaled to part class, a lot-mature material property suite needing at least 5 feedstock lots and 10 build/heat-treat lots for A/B (removed for C), six tensile coupons to qualify Class C, and a preproduction article evaluation for every Class A/B part (AMR-31); no costs are given (NASA-STD-6030 Sec. 4-5).

QA_Insp.note: Sets per-build witness testing by class (independent builds: 6 tensile for A1-B4, 2 for C, plus microstructure, HCF and chemistry by subclass; continuous builds: 4 tensile for A1-B4) and full surface and volumetric NDE for Class A and B (AMR-17, AMR-19), removed for Class C (NASA-STD-6030 Tables 5 and 7).

Storage.note: Inventory reduction is not addressed; serialisation is mentioned only for managing part and inventory risk (NASA-STD-6030 text).

Shared_Capital.note: Spreads one-time qualification across parts without numbers: a QMP registered to a machine can produce parts of equal or lower class, sub-QMPs inherit a parent QMP on equivalent machines, and lot-mature design values apply to parts of all classes built under an equivalently controlled QMP (NASA-STD-6030 Sec. 5, AMR-47/48).

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity shared across sites or users is not addressed (NASA-STD-6030 text).

Speed.note: Part lead time or availability is not addressed; schedule appears only as programmatic risk when witness results lag production (NASA-STD-6030 text).

tools.name: USAF Structures Bulletin EZ-SB-19-01: Durability and Damage Tolerance Certification for AM Aircraft Structural Metallic Parts
tools.developer: U.S. Air Force, AFLCMC/EZ (Engineering Directorate)
tools.context: USAF aircraft structural parts under ASIP (MIL-STD-1530); directly applicable to sustainment replacement parts
tools.processes: Metal AM generally (not process-specific); discusses HIP, stress relief, Ti porosity
tools.availability: Public (Distribution A); hosted in the Dayton Aerospace USAF Structures Bulletins library
tools.description: Sets durability and damage-tolerance certification requirements for metal AM structural parts by ASIP category (Fracture Critical Traceable/Non-Traceable, Durability Critical, Normal Controls), using equivalent initial damage size at category-specific exceedance probabilities and validated NDI capability. It recommends gaining experience in order of escalating criticality (NC, then DC, then FC).

NRE.note: Requires demonstrated process control (machine qualification, software version control, periodic requalification, strictly controlled parameters), which presumes parameter development, but none of it is costed (EZ-SB-19-01, secs. 2, 3.2).

Production.note: Full bulletin read; cost appears only as stability and supportability criteria ('predictable costs', 'cost-effective' inspection), and part cost is not addressed (EZ-SB-19-01).

QA_Qual.note: Sets class-specific analysis criteria (EIDS exceedance 1e-1 for NC, 1e-3 for DC/FC, 1e-7 for FC damage tolerance), but test frequencies, EIDS test counts and dissection plans are 'as approved by the procuring agency', so the campaign cannot be costed by class (EZ-SB-19-01, secs. 2.2, 3.3, 4).

QA_Insp.note: Requires NDI capability with POD at 95% confidence, coupons from production parts, dissection or validated in-process monitoring, and dimensional verification for all parts, with frequencies left to the procuring agency and no split by category (EZ-SB-19-01, secs. 3.3-3.5).

Storage.note: Full bulletin read; inventory and spares are not addressed (EZ-SB-19-01).

Shared_Capital.note: Recommends gaining experience on NC, then DC, then FC parts, with DC parts pursued once EIDS data mature, so qualification data is built up and reused across parts without costs (EZ-SB-19-01, secs. 2.2, 4).

Shared_Capacity.note: Full bulletin read; machines appear only for traceability and EIDS variation across machines, not capacity sharing (EZ-SB-19-01, secs. 3.7, 4.1).

Speed.note: Full bulletin read; it says only that cost-effective inspection and repair methods should be available or developed 'in a timely manner', and part lead time is not addressed (EZ-SB-19-01).

tools.name: USAF Flight Systems Bulletin EN-FSB-25-01 (Preliminary Qualification Data Requirements for Metallic AM) and Part Family Qualification approach
tools.developer: U.S. Air Force (approach presented by M. Benedict at TMS 2026; issuing office not stated in the public abstract)
tools.year: Unknown (bulletin number suggests 2025; the public abstract gives no date)
tools.context: USAF airworthiness; explicitly motivated by spare-parts shortages and long lead times
tools.processes: Metallic AM (unspecified)
tools.availability: Bulletin not accessed; conference abstract public
tools.description: Separates material qualification from part certification and defines a standard minimum data set for screening new AM processes, materials and vendors on stability, producibility and predictability. It replaces 'point qualification' of each part with 'Part Family Qualification'.

NRE.note: The bulletin explicitly separates material qualification from part certification and covers preliminary data to screen new processes, materials and vendors, so one-time part engineering is outside its documented scope (TMS 2026 abstract).

Production.note: Per-part production cost is outside the documented scope of a qualification-data bulletin (TMS 2026 abstract).

QA_Qual.note: Defines a standard minimum data set to judge material stability, producibility and predictability and whether further qualification investment is worthwhile, and calls point qualification 'slow and expensive', but no costs or test counts are public (TMS 2026 abstract; the bulletin itself is not posted).

QA_Insp.note: Only a conference abstract describes the bulletin and it does not list the data set's contents; an Army RFI cites EN-FSB-25-01 only by number and a USAF vendor-qualification article does not mention it, so whether NDI or CT is required is not established (TMS 2026 abstract; Govly RFI 2026; Military & Aerospace Electronics).

Storage.note: Spare-part shortages are named only as motivation; inventory is outside the documented scope of a qualification-data bulletin (TMS 2026 abstract).

Shared_Capital.note: Moves from requalifying each part after any machine or process change to Part Family Qualification, which spreads qualification across a family of parts; qualitative only (TMS 2026 abstract).

Shared_Capacity.note: Print capacity is outside the documented scope of a qualification-data bulletin (TMS 2026 abstract).

Speed.note: The abstract says AM can overcome lead times of up to years and that Part Family Qualification aims to cut the time of full material qualification, a time-saving claim with no lead time computed (TMS 2026 abstract).

tools.name: NAVSEA AM qualification framework: Guidance letter Ser 05T/2018-024 severity levels, T9074-AX-GIB-010/100 material selection requirements, and PBF/DED Technical Publications
tools.developer: Naval Sea Systems Command (NAVSEA 05T, AM Technical Warrant Holder); DED tech pub developed with NSWC Carderock and EWI
tools.year: 2018 (guidance letter); 2020 (PBF Tech Pub); 2021 (DED Tech Pub, anticipated)
tools.context: Navy surface ships and submarines; waterfront/shipboard and depot AM
tools.processes: Metal L-PBF and DED; polymers (separate approved-materials lists)
tools.availability: Guidance letter publicly posted (NCMS AMMO); Tech Pubs not publicly accessed; public briefings (NRC, NSRP)
tools.description: Part failure-consequence severity (NAVSEA 5100.12-M Levels 1–7/N/A) determines whether material selection requirements and process/material qualification apply, whether a Technical Data Package is needed, and who approves. The process Tech Pubs then prescribe procedure qualification, part verification builds and a production conformance test plan.

NRE.note: Prescribes one-time engineering deliverables by part class (a NAVSEA-approved TDP for severity Levels 1-6, and an approved DED Procedure before procedure qualification) but puts no cost or effort on them, so it is a requirement rather than a cost term (guidance letter; DED tech pub).

Production.note: The letter says only that AM enables 'cost-effective, on-demand manufacturing of critical parts'; per-part costing is outside the framework, and NAVSUP's separate cost/part tool is being integrated into TDP development (Ser 05T/2018-024; Rettaliata 2020).

QA_Qual.note: Severity level sets the required qualification: Levels 1-5 invoke T9074-AX-GIB-010/100 and process/material qualification, Levels 1-6 a risk assessment that sets the approval authority, and the Tech Pub prescribes countable steps (procedure qualification build, PQTR, sacrificial part verification build with witness coupons, test reports); no costs (Ser 05T/2018-024; Hovanec 2021).

QA_Insp.note: Conformance testing per build is required, NDE test types are set by material group with MIL-STD-2035 Class 1 acceptance, but production NDE and destructive-test schedules are set part by part in each Production Conformance Evaluation Plan rather than by severity class, with no counts or costs (Ser 05T/2018-024; Hovanec 2021).

Storage.note: The guidance letter's documented scope (severity, qualification, approval) does not address inventory (Ser 05T/2018-024).

Shared_Capital.note: Procedure qualification is done once per process/material combination and then applies irrespective of part geometry while essential elements are kept, so qualification is reused across parts, but this is not costed (Hovanec 2021).

Shared_Capacity.note: Neither the guidance letter nor the Tech Pub briefing addresses capacity shared across ships, depots or users (Ser 05T/2018-024; Hovanec 2021).

Speed.note: The letter claims only that AM 'can shorten the design-to-production cycle', with no lead-time or readiness calculation (Ser 05T/2018-024).

tools.name: DNV-ST-B203 Additive manufacturing (Edition 2025-11)
tools.developer: DNV (formerly DNV GL)
tools.year: 2017 (DNVGL-CG-0197); first ST-B203 edition reported as 2019 (not confirmed); editions Dec 2022 and 2025-11
tools.context: Oil & gas, maritime and energy; used for spare-part and supplier qualification
tools.processes: Metal PBF and DED (inspection and test plan appendices); 2025 edition also covers polymers
tools.availability: Via DNV standards portal (standards.dnv.com/Veracity); full ST-B203 text not accessed; CG-0197 (2017) read
tools.description: Assigns parts to AM categories AMC 1–3 by criticality (an informative appendix guides AMC selection). The category sets the qualification route: AMC 1 needs a facility audit and a build process qualification, and AMC 2/3 add part family qualification. Appendices give inspection/test plans and NDT guidance.

NRE.note: The standard has an informative appendix on design of AM parts and build process qualification fixes the build process, but neither is costed (DNV ST-B203 pages).

Production.note: The documented scope (procurement, qualification, quality management, production testing and inspection, plus design and carbon-footprint appendices) contains no cost estimation (DNV ST-B203 pages).

QA_Qual.note: The AM category sets countable qualification steps (AMC 1: facility audit plus at least one BPQ per material; AMC 2/3: plus part family qualification) per DNV certification-services slides, and CG-0197 calls part-by-part certification 'costly, time consuming'; exact AMC criteria and test counts were not seen because the standard is paywalled.

QA_Insp.note: The standard defines inspection and test plans for PBF and DED and NDT acceptance criteria, with quality approaches scaled to part criticality (DNV pages; 2022 release); the class-by-class production testing (C1 visual only; C2/C3 add per-build tensile, impact, surface and volumetric NDT and dimensional checks) rests on Peron, Cantini & Coruzzolo (IFAC 2023), which is closed access and could not be re-opened in this pass.

Storage.note: The standard's documented scope has no inventory element; DNV's release mentions digital spare parts only as a general AM benefit (DNV pages).

Shared_Capital.note: Manufacturers prequalify per facility, per-material BPQ and per part family, and the part-family guidance 'may extend the validity of qualifications' across parts; no numbers (DNV slides; DNV 2022 release).

Shared_Capacity.note: The documented scope does not address capacity shared across sites or users (DNV ST-B203 pages).

Speed.note: The standard has no time or lead-time element; DNV's release mentions AM's lead-time benefit only in general terms (DNV pages).

tools.name: API Standard 20S Additively Manufactured Metallic Components (AM Specification Levels AMSL 1/2/3)
tools.developer: American Petroleum Institute
tools.context: Petroleum and natural gas equipment; presented as aiding supply-chain resiliency and spares
tools.processes: Metal PBF, DED (incl. DED-arc), binder jetting
tools.availability: Paid standard; full text not accessed
tools.description: Specifies process qualification and production control for AM metallic components at three AM Specification Levels. Each higher level raises technical, quality and qualification requirements, and the level is assigned by the product specification, purchaser or manufacturer according to consequence of failure, service severity and inspectability.

NRE.note: Summaries say the manufacturer must establish and qualify the machine, parameters, feedstock and post-processing (essential AM variables, aligned with ASME IX QW-600 in the 2nd edition) before production, a prescribed parameter-development activity with no cost (Inspenet summary; World Oil 2025).

Production.note: The documented scope is process qualification, production control, marking and documentation requirements, which plainly excludes per-part cost estimation (Normservis and Techstreet scope listings).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification requirements rise with AMSL, assigned by consequence of failure, service severity and inspectability, and require representative coupons, mechanical testing and metallography, but per-level test counts could not be verified because the full text is paid; the standard may meet the Yes bar (Inspenet summary; scope listings).

QA_Insp.note: NDE methods (RT, UT, PT, MT, CT, dimensional) are named and the 2nd edition adds an NDT annex on how AMSLs apply with example acceptance criteria, but class-specific inspection scope was not verified (Inspenet summary; World Oil 2025).

Storage.note: The scope (process qualification, production, marking, documentation) excludes inventory; spares appear only as candidate applications (scope listings; Inspenet).

Shared_Capital.note: No summary, scope listing or announcement says whether one process qualification can cover several parts or part families, and the full text was not accessible.

Shared_Capacity.note: The scope (process qualification, production control, marking, documentation) excludes capacity shared across sites or users (scope listings).

Speed.note: The requirements scope excludes lead time; shorter supply times near the asset are cited only as motivation in summaries and announcements (Inspenet; World Oil 2025).

tools.name: FAA AM Roadmap and risk-based certification framework (Gorelik briefings)
tools.developer: Federal Aviation Administration (AM National Team; M. Gorelik, Chief Scientist for Fatigue and Damage Tolerance)
tools.context: Civil aviation certification (CFR Parts 25, 33, etc.)
tools.processes: Metal AM generally (PBF emphasized)
tools.availability: Public briefings (FAA REDAC, NRC, National Academies, ASTM); views stated as the author's own
tools.description: Ties regulatory scrutiny to part criticality and maps the qualification path to criticality and volume: point-design certification for low-criticality, high-margin parts; part-family qualification as volume grows; model-enabled qualification later. It gives indicative figures for the barrier to entry and qualification timelines.

NRE.note: Process development is lumped into an indicative barrier-to-entry figure (about $1M for equipment alone vs '$10's of M' realistic, also covering qualification, process controls, characterisation, design data and QA/NDI), with no separate NRE term (Gorelik 2016 National Academies deck).

Production.note: Production cost appears only as background (about 50% of operating cost is labour and 20% depreciation, with powder expected to become the largest item), quoted rather than computed by the framework (Gorelik 2016 National Academies deck).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification paths (point design, part family, model-enabled) are mapped to criticality and volume only qualitatively, but the briefing gives building-block specimen counts, cost and time by test level (e.g. 5,000-100,000 coupons, $8-15M, 2 yrs) and alloy-introduction timelines of 10-15 years, not set by part class (Gorelik 2016 deck; FAA REDAC 2017 roadmap).

QA_Insp.note: NDI capability is a top-5 challenge, probabilistic fracture mechanics with inspection POD and zone-based evaluation are proposed, and a research task will develop POD for CT and laser ultrasonics, but no inspection cost or part-class scope is set (Gorelik 2016 deck; FAA REDAC 2017 roadmap).

Storage.note: The briefings are a certification and research framework whose scope excludes parts inventory, and neither deck mentions it (FAA REDAC 2017 roadmap; Gorelik 2016 deck).

Shared_Capital.note: Part-family qualification is proposed as volumes grow, which implies spreading qualification across parts, but no numbers are given (FAA REDAC 2017 roadmap).

Shared_Capacity.note: The framework's certification scope excludes print capacity and neither deck mentions it (FAA REDAC 2017 roadmap; Gorelik 2016 deck).

Speed.note: The only times given are qualification and alloy-introduction timelines; part lead time or availability is outside the framework's scope (Gorelik 2016 deck; FAA REDAC 2017 roadmap).

tools.name: CMU adaptive regulatory framework for metal AM in aviation (Bonnín Roca et al. 2017)
tools.developer: Carnegie Mellon University, Engineering and Public Policy (with Universidade de Lisboa / CMU Portugal)
tools.context: Commercial aviation regulation of safety-critical metal AM parts
tools.processes: Metal AM generally
tools.availability: Journal articles (Research Policy 46(7):1215–1233; Nature Materials 2016); only abstracts accessed
tools.description: Uses metal AM in aviation as a case study to propose adaptive regulation: standards revised periodically, and firms regulated differently according to their technological capabilities. It gives a general framework in which the right regulatory design depends on industry structure, safety requirements and sources of technological uncertainty.

NRE.note: The framework concerns how regulators revise standards and treat firms of differing technological capability; one-time part engineering cost is outside its documented scope (Research Policy 2017 abstract via TU/e and IDEAS records).

Production.note: Per-part production cost is outside the documented scope of a regulatory-design framework (Research Policy 2017 abstract).

QA_Qual.note: Proposes adaptive certification regulation with periodically revised standards and requirements that differ by firm capability, a qualitative framework with no costs or test counts in the abstract (Research Policy 2017 abstract).

QA_Insp.note: Only abstracts could be read (the full paper and the author's 2017 CMU dissertation PDF were not reachable); the work addresses certification standards, so whether it treats inspection or NDE requirements is not established.

Storage.note: Inventory is outside the documented scope of a regulatory-design framework (Research Policy 2017 abstract).

Shared_Capital.note: Only abstracts could be read (full paper and dissertation PDF unreachable); regulating firms by capability could let qualification carry across parts or users, but no source read shows the paper treating this.

Shared_Capacity.note: Print capacity pooling is outside the documented scope of a regulatory-design framework (Research Policy 2017 abstract).

Speed.note: Part lead time or availability is outside the documented scope of a framework for setting certification regulation (Research Policy 2017 abstract).

tools.name: Rapid qualification framework for powder-bed laser AM parts (Honeywell-led DARPA Open Manufacturing work; Peralta et al.)
tools.developer: Honeywell Aerospace-led team (Peralta, Enright, Megahed, Gong, Roybal, Craig) under DARPA Open Manufacturing
tools.context: Aerospace engine/structural parts; DARPA Open Manufacturing rapid qualification thrust
tools.processes: Laser powder bed fusion
tools.availability: Open access (Integrating Materials and Manufacturing Innovation 5:154–176)
tools.description: A probabilistic, risk-based qualification framework that runs ICME models (melt pool CFD, residual stress/distortion FE, microstructure/strength) with Bayesian calibration in a digital loop, adding physical tests only when the digital results do not show acceptable risk. In-situ monitoring and NDE feed the risk calculation.

NRE.note: ICME process models are used to identify the optimum process window and predict residual stress and deformation, narrowing parameter development, but engineering effort is not costed and no effort figures are given (IMMI 2016 full text).

Production.note: Production cost is not addressed anywhere in the paper (IMMI 2016 full text).

QA_Qual.note: A probabilistic risk framework decides when physical tests are needed; the 40% qualification-time, 20% cost and 40% testing reductions and certification-by-analysis rising from 10% to 20% are programme goals, not computed by a cost model, and no dollar figures are given (IMMI 2016 full text).

QA_Insp.note: Pyrometer quality metrics against a 95% limit flag off-nominal layers and X-ray CT/acoustic microscopy outcomes feed the risk calculation, but no inspection cost, scope or sampling plan is set and in-process data alone cannot accept a part (IMMI 2016 full text).

Storage.note: Inventory is not addressed (IMMI 2016 full text).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine capital and its sharing are not addressed; the remark that the framework allows interchangeability of components and AM processes does not describe sharing capital or qualification across parts (IMMI 2016 full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity is not addressed (IMMI 2016 full text).

Speed.note: The paper claims rapid qualification enables 'faster response to the market demands' and 'rapid procurement of qualified hardware' (40% qualification-time goal), but part lead time is not computed or valued (IMMI 2016 full text).

tools.name: NIST qualification pathways for AM materials, processes and parts (statistical, equivalence-based, model-based, 'qualify-as-you-go')
tools.developer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
tools.year: 2014-2025 (project page created March 2014; project completed; page last updated March 2025)
tools.context: Defense, aerospace and medical AM qualification; measurement science supporting regulators
tools.processes: Metal AM (emphasis on melting/re-solidification in powder bed processes)
tools.availability: Public project page and associated publications
tools.description: Frames three qualification routes with different testing burdens and develops measurement science (round-robin protocols, a public materials database, validated process models, in-process measurement) to make equivalence and model-based qualification viable and to spread the cost of statistical testing.

NRE.note: The project's documented scope is measurement science for qualification; part design files and run-parameter development are outside it (NIST project page).

Production.note: Production cost is outside the documented qualification scope and is not mentioned (NIST project page).

QA_Qual.note: Compares the testing burden of statistical, equivalence-based and model-based routes in words and cites full empirical qualification as 'many thousands of individual tests, costing millions of dollars and 5 to 15 years', with no model (NIST project page).

QA_Insp.note: 'Qualify as you go' uses pre-, in- and post-process measurements (including dimensional metrology of critical geometries) to show each part meets spec, as a concept with no scope or cost (NIST project page).

Storage.note: Inventory is outside the documented qualification scope and is not mentioned (NIST project page).

Shared_Capital.note: Aims to 'distribute the burden of testing' through round-robin protocols and a public materials database many contributors can add to, a qualitative sharing of qualification cost (NIST project page).

Shared_Capacity.note: Machine capacity is outside the documented qualification scope and is not mentioned (NIST project page).

Speed.note: Part lead time is outside the documented scope; the only time figure is the 5-15 years of empirical qualification (NIST project page).

tools.name: Seifi et al. qualification and certification pathway review (JOM, 2017)
tools.developer: Seifi, Salem, Beuth, Harrysson, Lewandowski (2016); Seifi, Gorelik, Waller, Hrabe, Shamsaei, Daniewicz, Lewandowski (2017)
tools.context: Aerospace and other critical applications
tools.processes: Metal PBF and DED
tools.availability: JOM (Springer); 2016 full-text content accessed via Springer; 2017 abstract only
tools.description: Compares statistically based qualification (e.g., AMS4999A), model-based qualification and ICME 'qualify-as-you-go' schemes for metal AM. The 2017 paper maps the standards landscape needed for a Q&C pathway and cites NASA's AM risk criteria (inspectability, surface removal, wall thickness).

NRE.note: Full texts read; design or engineering effort is not addressed (JOM 2016; NIST copy of JOM 2017).

Production.note: Full texts read; lowering production costs is named only as a general challenge, and part cost is not addressed (JOM 2016; NIST copy of JOM 2017).

QA_Qual.note: Gives costable counts for one route (AMS4999A: >50 tensile results per principal build direction for source qualification, >12 per direction on production parts) and says legacy qualification may cost millions and take up to 15 years, with any non-minor deviation triggering requalification; it is a review, not a model (JOM 2016).

QA_Insp.note: Discusses micro-CT and X-ray CT as leading NDT options, the lack of AM NDT consensus standards and NASA's inspectability risk criterion, with no costs or class-specific scope (JOM 2016; NIST copy of JOM 2017).

Storage.note: Full texts read; spares appear only as items needing defined NDT, and inventory is not addressed (NIST copy of JOM 2017).

Shared_Capital.note: The 2016 review names the lack of shared knowledge and materials test results across the AM community, and proprietary machine controls, as barriers to qualification, but pooling of qualification data is not costed (JOM 2016).

Shared_Capacity.note: Full texts read; capacity is not addressed (JOM 2016; NIST copy of JOM 2017).

Speed.note: The 2017 review claims AM could make essential parts on demand in days rather than months, as motivation only, with no time model (NIST copy of JOM 2017, p. 2).
