tools.name: Cost model for the economic evaluation of in-situ monitoring tools in metal AM (Colosimo, Cavalli, Grasso)
tools.developer: Politecnico di Milano
tools.context: Industrial L-PBF production (dental prostheses, machinery component, aerospace bracket cases); validated against an AM service bureau
tools.processes: Laser powder bed fusion
tools.availability: International Journal of Production Economics; author manuscript open on Polimi repository
tools.description: A per-part cost model comparing as-is production, in-situ monitoring, and monitoring with diagnosis. It uses scrap fraction, false-alarm and missed-detection rates, inspection time and monitoring equipment cost to find the scrap rates at which monitoring pays off, including a make-or-buy variant.

NRE.note: Build preparation (operator plus workstation/software rate times build-prep time, divided by parts per build) and machine setup are costed per build, but CAD development cost is explicitly excluded and there is no parameter-development term (Polimi author manuscript, Eqs. 9-10).

Production.note: Computes per-part cost from material, pre-process, LPBF process and post-process terms (e.g., 212.74 vs 192.99 EUR/part as-is vs monitoring), validated within about 10% of a service-bureau benchmark (Polimi author manuscript).

QA_Qual.note: The full paper has no qualification or certification cost term; certified medical materials are mentioned only as background (Polimi author manuscript).

QA_Insp.note: Per-part post-process inspection (operator plus metrology rate times inspection time, visual or CMM) is a cost term, combined with scrap fraction, Type I/II monitoring errors and 50k/150k EUR monitoring hardware to find break-even scrap fractions of about 0.02-0.2; CT is named as an optional extra and not included (Polimi author manuscript).

Storage.note: The full paper has no inventory, storage or holding-cost terms (Polimi author manuscript).

Shared_Capital.note: The L-PBF system is charged at an hourly rate from straight-line depreciation plus maintenance and space (EUR 600k over 5 years at a 55% load factor) and build cost is divided by parts per build, so machine capital is amortised into per-part cost (Polimi author manuscript).

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity shared across sites or customers is not modelled; the make-or-buy variant only blends in-house and service-bureau cost by the fraction outsourced, with no capacity or lead-time effect (Polimi author manuscript, Eq. 19).

Speed.note: The model computes average production time per part (pre-process, process and post-process, including scrapped builds) and annual throughput (about 4,585 vs 4,821 parts/year in the dental case), but has no lead time, delivery or value of availability (Polimi author manuscript, Eqs. 16-17).

sources.title: Colosimo, Cavalli, Grasso, A cost model for the economic evaluation of in-situ monitoring tools in metal AM (author manuscript)

tools.name: Process-based cost estimation model for metal AM spare parts with explicit qualification-test line items (Sheikh et al.)
tools.developer: Hamad Bin Khalifa University (Sheikh, Hadid, Padmanabhan, Elomri, Kerbache, Alabtah, Khraisheh)
tools.context: Oil & gas spare parts (impeller, repair clamp, eccentric gear wheel)
tools.processes: Bound Metal Deposition (Desktop Metal Studio System 2), 316L
tools.availability: Open-access conference proceedings (IEOM Paris 2025)
tools.description: Total part cost is the sum of design, material, manufacturing (print, debind, sinter), post-processing and 'part qualification' cost. The qualification term sums per-part tests for dimensions, corrosion, strength, hardness and density.

NRE.note: Design cost is an explicit term: 3D-scanner use (initial cost over annual usage hours times scan time), software licence spread over parts produced, and designer time times rate, $80-220 per part in the cases (IEOM full text, Eqs. 2-3, Table 3).

Production.note: Per-part cost is built from material (metal and ceramic rod weight times price), printing (setup labour, depreciation, maintenance and energy times print time), debinding, sintering and post-processing (heat treatment, machining, finishing) (IEOM full text, Eqs. 4-19).

QA_Qual.note: The 'part qualification' term is a flat per-part lump of test fees (dimensional $30, corrosion $50, strength $40, hardness $25, density $20); there is no material or process qualification campaign or approval (IEOM full text, Eq. 20, Table 3).

QA_Insp.note: Per-part test costs are explicit line items totalling $120-165 per part, about 11-20% of part cost; how the unit fees were derived is not explained (IEOM full text, Table 3).

Storage.note: Inventory or stock is not mentioned anywhere in the full paper (IEOM full text).

Shared_Capital.note: Printer and furnace capital enter as flat depreciation per hour times processing time with no utilisation, batch or volume input; only the 3D scanner is spread over annual usage hours (IEOM full text, Eqs. 3, 7-12).

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity, batching and distributed production are not modelled; the conclusion notes economies of scale are not accounted for (IEOM full text).

Speed.note: Lead time is not modelled; downtime and lead-time reduction appear only in the introduction and literature review (IEOM full text).

tools.name: In-situ NDE (INDE) with probability-of-detection framework for L-PBF (ORNL; Snow et al.)
tools.developer: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (Snow, Scime, Ziabari, Fisher, Paquit)
tools.context: L-PBF production quality assurance; DOE/ORNL MDF
tools.processes: Laser powder bed fusion
tools.availability: Journal article (Additive Manufacturing 78, 103817); ORNL publication record
tools.description: Detects 200–1000 µm subsurface flaws from fused process-monitoring data using machine learning, with XCT as ground truth, and generates POD/PFA curves and an a90/95 metric following NDE practice, so in-situ monitoring can be assessed as an inspection method.

NRE.note: The documented scope is in-situ flaw detection from fused process-monitoring data validated against XCT, which plainly excludes design-file or parameter-development cost (ORNL abstract).

Production.note: The documented scope is flaw detection and POD/PFA assessment, which plainly excludes per-part production costing (ORNL abstract).

QA_Qual.note: The abstract frames the method against the current qualification paradigm for critical L-PBF parts, which relies on expensive NDI and limits use cases, and the ORNL release quotes Snow that lacking a POD number makes parts hard to qualify and certify; no qualification cost or effort is modelled (ORNL abstract; EurekAlert release).

QA_Insp.note: Detection capability is quantified (POD/PFA curves, a90/95, flaws ~200-1000 um) but inspection cost is only claimed qualitatively as a 'less expensive alternative' to ex-situ XCT, with no cost or time figures (ORNL abstract; EurekAlert release).

Storage.note: The documented scope is an in-process flaw-detection method, which plainly excludes inventory (ORNL abstract).

Shared_Capital.note: The documented scope is flaw detection, which plainly excludes machine capital or its sharing (ORNL abstract).

Shared_Capacity.note: The documented scope is flaw detection on single builds, which plainly excludes pooled print capacity (ORNL abstract).

Speed.note: The documented scope is flaw detection; the release only says conventional evaluation demands more time and labour, and no lead time or availability is computed (ORNL abstract; EurekAlert release).

tools.name: VEXTEC VPS-MICRO model-assisted AM certification (AFWERX SBIR; AFRL QUASAR)
tools.developer: VEXTEC Corporation
tools.context: USAF/Space Force AM part certification; with AFRL/RQVS and Lockheed Martin
tools.processes: Metal AM (process not specified)
tools.availability: Commercial software; company announcements only
tools.description: Probabilistic microstructure- and defect-based fatigue software. It aims to predict EIDS distributions and part performance from specimen-level data so that part-level testing can be limited to validation ('risk-based certification').

NRE.note: VEXTEC lists 'AM Process Development' as a use, runs virtual sensitivity studies of build parameters on microstructure and claims 'significant cost/time savings', but engineering effort is not costed (vextec.com AM page; America Makes TRX webinar 2021).

Production.note: The AM page says VPS-MICRO can optimise post-build selective machining, which it says can be up to 20% of part cost, but the tool predicts fatigue risk and computes no part cost (vextec.com AM page and AM news feed).

QA_Qual.note: Model-assisted certification combines limited physical testing with fatigue simulation so parts are tested only when confidence is high, and a Phase III effort demonstrated reduced testing to qualify an LPBF component, but no test, cost or time reduction is quantified (vextec.com AM page; TRX webinar 2021).

QA_Insp.note: The SBIR framework links in-process monitoring and non-destructive part evaluation data to fatigue prediction, and the deck names NDE and post-process inspection as a cost driver, but no inspection cost or scope is set (TRX webinar 2021; vextec.com AM page).

Storage.note: VPS-MICRO is fatigue-performance prediction software; inventory is outside its documented scope (vextec.com software and AM pages).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine capital and its sharing are outside the documented scope of a fatigue-prediction tool; the deck names machine-specific allowables databases only as a burden of current practice (vextec.com software page; TRX webinar 2021).

Shared_Capacity.note: Print capacity is outside the documented scope of a fatigue-prediction tool (vextec.com software and AM pages).

Speed.note: VEXTEC says the testing burden 'has direct impacts on both the schedule and cost of AM part availability' and that its approach cuts long lead times and gives early confidence, but no lead time is computed (vextec.com AM news feed; TRX webinar 2021).

tools.name: NASA-CMU Additive Manufacturing Ecosystem for qualification of AM processes and materials in aviation
tools.developer: NASA Ames Research Center (K. Datta) and Carnegie Mellon University (A. Rollett)
tools.context: Aviation original and replacement parts (NASA ARMD)
tools.processes: Metal AM (process qualification focus)
tools.availability: NTRS/TechPort abstract
tools.description: A six-project research ecosystem for qualifying AM machines, which then supports certification of part production. It names qualification difficulty and cost as the main barriers.

NRE.note: The 'AM Flaw Management' and 'Qualification Aware Process Maps' projects develop processing windows with multiple qualified parameter points, a parameter-development activity, but no cost is given (TechPort data sheet).

Production.note: Names technology cost as a main barrier, notes post-processing can cost as much as fabrication, and targets lower manufacturing cost for short runs and replacement parts, with no cost model (TechPort data sheet).

QA_Qual.note: Builds a qualification ecosystem (porosity-limited processing windows, fatigue data, a data-driven qualification model, supplier training tiers) that links machine and process qualification to part certification, without costs (TechPort data sheet).

QA_Insp.note: The data sheet sets porosity limits and measures porosity effects on fatigue for qualification data but does not say whether per-part inspection is addressed, and no project outputs were found (TechPort data sheet).

Storage.note: None of the six listed projects (flaw management, process maps, post-processing, database analytics, training, scaling to production) addresses inventory (TechPort data sheet).

Shared_Capital.note: That machine qualification spreads across many certified parts and small suppliers is implied but not stated, and no machine cost or sharing is given (TechPort data sheet).

Shared_Capacity.note: The 'Scaling to Production' project configures production cells for hundreds to thousands of parts per year, but capacity shared across sites or users is not among the listed projects (TechPort data sheet).

Speed.note: Anticipates shorter time-to-production as a benefit, with no lead-time figures or model (TechPort data sheet).

tools.name: 3DXpert (build preparation with print time and cost estimation)
tools.developer: Developed by 3D Systems (TCT ties it to the 2015 Cimatron acquisition). tools.context: General metal AM production; no defense customer found in fetched sources

tools.availability: Commercial license; offered standalone or within Oqton MOS under Hubb ownership, and still bundled with 3D Systems metal printers
tools.description: Metal AM build-prep software (part positioning, supports, lattices, print strategies). Its Estimation Parameters dialog computes print time from published build rates (part/support/lattice rates, recoat time). It then costs material per cm3 and machine time at an hourly rate, reporting volume, time and cost for parts, supports and lattices plus total powder required.

NRE.note: The software performs build preparation (positioning, supports, print strategies, 'Automation, Quotation & Setup'), but no preparation, setup or engineering cost field exists in the estimation dialog (2019 estimation guide; oqton.com/3dxpert).

Production.note: Build cost is computed from material cost per cm3 for parts, supports and lattices plus machine time cost (hourly rate x total time from published build rates and recoat time); labour, setup and post-processing are not included and cost is totalled by category rather than allocated per part (2019 estimation guide).

QA_Qual.note: The AM Inspection feature is listed as 'Inspect, Adjust, Certify for future comparisons, generate reports', a build-certification step without any qualification costing (oqton.com/3dxpert).

QA_Insp.note: Build Inspection is listed to 'inspect and correct anomalies and defects' in running builds, but inspection is not costed in the estimation dialog (oqton.com/3dxpert; 2019 estimation guide).

Storage.note: 3DXpert is build-preparation software and the product page places inventory functions in the separate Manufacturing OS, so inventory is outside its documented scope (oqton.com/3dxpert).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine cost enters only as an hourly rate x total build time, with no amortisation, utilisation or per-part allocation of multi-part builds (2019 estimation guide).

Shared_Capacity.note: Documented scope is preparing individual builds; the product page describes no fleet, scheduling or multi-site capacity functions (oqton.com/3dxpert).

Speed.note: Print time is estimated from part, support and lattice build rates plus between-layer recoat time, a print-time-only model; lead time or availability is not computed (2019 estimation guide).

tools.name: Ansys Additive Prep (Cost Estimator)
tools.developer: Ansys, now part of Synopsys (ansys.com product pages redirect to ansys.synopsys.com); Additive Prep runs inside Ansys SpaceClaim
tools.context: General metal LPBF build preparation; no defense user found
tools.processes: Metal laser powder bed fusion. Cost data is built into SLM machine profiles only; other machine profiles show zero machine cost.
tools.availability: Commercial license (SpaceClaim-based Ansys additive tools)
tools.description: Build-preparation tool whose Cost Estimator prices the whole build job. Machine cost comes from build time (laser path and jump times plus recoater time per layer). Material is powder volume over the baseplate area times part height, times density, plus a material-loss %. A profit margin is added. Output is an 'Estimated Total Price' exportable to CSV.

NRE.note: Orientation, supports and scan-pattern build files are generated in the tool, but the preparation effort is not costed (Ansys help 2024 R2).

Production.note: The Cost Estimator prices a build job from scan-path build time times machine cost, powder volume times density plus a loss %, and profit, giving an Estimated Total Price; no labour, post-processing or per-part split is documented (Ansys help 2024 R2).

QA_Qual.note: The cost-estimator help lists only machine, material and profit terms, and the documented five-step build-preparation scope does not include qualification (Ansys help 2024 R2).

QA_Insp.note: The cost-estimator help lists only machine, material and profit terms, with no inspection step (Ansys help 2024 R2).

Storage.note: Additive Prep prepares and prices single build jobs, so inventory is outside its documented scope (Ansys help 2024 R2).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine cost (the largest contributor) is charged per build hour from the SLM machine profile and covers all parts added to the build volume, but no amortisation, utilisation or per-part allocation inputs are documented (Ansys help 2024 R2).

Shared_Capacity.note: Additive Prep prices one build job on one machine and does not address capacity shared across sites or users (Ansys help 2024 R2).

Speed.note: Build time is computed from laser path, jump and recoater times, but only to price machine time and rank orientations; no lead time or value of earlier delivery is output (Ansys help 2024 R2).

sources.title: Ansys Additive Prep help, Chapter 8: Estimate Costs of the Build Job (2024 R2)

QA_Insp.note: The documented selection, data and cost-estimator functions do not address per-part inspection or NDT (2026 R1 help).

Storage.note: The help index and pages show no inventory or stock feature; materials and process selection excludes inventory (2026 R1 help).

Shared_Capital.note: AM machines can be filtered by cost (purchase price) as a selection criterion; the Part Cost Estimator takes load factor and capital write-off time, but its coverage of AM processes is not documented (3DPI 2016; 2026 R1 help).

Shared_Capacity.note: No capacity, site or network feature appears in the help; production capacity is outside the selection scope (2026 R1 help).

Speed.note: The help index shows no lead-time feature and the AM data page mentions no lead time or build rate; lead time is outside the selection scope (2026 R1 help).

Eiger Fleet gives centralized control of distributed printers, users and a digital parts inventory (RBAC, SSO, API) and tracks KPIs for time and cost savings. Digital Source lets OEMs upload designs with locked process settings and encrypted build instructions, licensed to customers or approved print-service providers for on-demand 'manufacturer-certified' parts.

NRE.note: One-click automated print prep, and under Digital Source the OEM rather than the user prepares and locks process settings; NRE is not costed (Eiger page; Digital Source release 2023).

Production.note: Eiger computes a per-part cost when a part is sliced, but it is material cost only (labour and energy are planned), and the ROI dashboard sets the alternative cost at a flat 10x the Markforged cost (Markforged ROI tools blog).

QA_Qual.note: Digital Source lets vendors lock printing process requirements so users receive 'manufacturer-certified parts on demand', but no qualification cost or effort is modelled (Digital Source release 2023).

QA_Insp.note: The Eiger page lists 'quality control via automated part scanning plus intuitive measurement and reporting', but inspection is not costed (Eiger page).

Storage.note: Eiger has a digital part inventory and Digital Source claims 'reduced inventory costs', but stock effects are not computed (Eiger page; Digital Source release 2023).

Shared_Capital.note: The ROI dashboard tracks savings across the cloud-connected printer fleet and a separate Utilization Dashboard tracks printer utilisation, but printer capital never enters the cost, which is material only (Markforged ROI tools blog).

Shared_Capacity.note: Eiger Fleet manages distributed printers and a Utilization Dashboard reports printer utilisation and print time, and Digital Source licenses printing at approved service providers, but there is no queue or lead-time effect (Markforged ROI tools blog; Eiger page; Digital Source release 2023).

Speed.note: Digital Source claims on-site printing 'brings down the time it takes to receive the part', but the ROI tools compute cost savings only, not lead time or downtime (Digital Source release 2023; Markforged ROI tools blog).

tools.name: AMPOWER Additive Manufacturing Cost Calculator
tools.developer: AMPOWER (AM consultancy, ampower.eu)
tools.context: General industry; no defense user found
tools.processes: 7 metal AM technologies with 4 materials (incl. large-frame LB-PBF) and 3 polymer AM technologies
tools.availability: Commercial: EUR 5,900 perpetual enterprise license (delivery format not stated)
tools.description: Total-cost-of-ownership calculator. Inputs are part material, dimensions, volume, complexity, quantity and build utilization; outputs are cost per part broken down by process-chain step. Covers technician labor (machine prep, unpacking, support removal, optional data prep), heat treatment and consumables, all overridable. Also gives lead time per part, cost vs 1-10,000 parts/yr, service-bureau market price ranges, and side-by-side comparison of technologies.

NRE.note: Optional digital data-preparation time and cost is included as labour, but there is no reverse engineering, redesign or parameter development (AMPOWER product page).

Production.note: Per-part cost is broken down along the process chain (EUR/ccm or EUR/kg) from material, complexity, labour, heat treatment, consumables and pre/post steps (AMPOWER product page).

QA_Qual.note: The shop page lists the process-chain steps (material, data preparation, machine setup, printing, curing, unpacking, sintering, heat treatment) without qualification, but the Excel tool is user-customisable and its documentation is not public (AMPOWER shop and tools pages).

QA_Insp.note: The listed process-chain steps include no inspection step, but the tools page says the calculator is fully customisable with own processes, so whether inspection can be costed is not established (AMPOWER shop and tools pages).

Storage.note: The calculator's documented scope is per-part cost, production time and throughput by technology and annual quantity, which excludes inventory holding (AMPOWER product page).

Shared_Capital.note: Per-part cost depends on how well the build volume is utilised and on annual quantity (1-10,000/yr), with machine investment named as a main cost driver (AMPOWER product page).

Shared_Capacity.note: Annual throughput is output for production planning, so machine capacity is modelled, but there is no pooling across sites or users and no effect on lead time (AMPOWER product page).

Speed.note: The calculator outputs production time per part broken down along its process chain (data preparation to heat treatment), a partial time model that excludes queueing, inspection and delivery (AMPOWER product and shop pages).

tools.name: Ulu-Huang-Kara-Whitefoot (CMU) concurrent structure + process-parameter optimization for minimum-cost metal AM
tools.developer: E. Ulu, R. Huang, L. B. Kara, K. S. Whitefoot (Carnegie Mellon University, Mechanical Engineering)
tools.context: Design-stage optimisation of structural parts (cantilever, L-beam, bracket, table) for EBM. Cost inputs come from 14 US EBM Ti64 producers at >=13,500 units/yr.
tools.processes: EBM (electron-beam powder bed fusion), Ti-6Al-4V
tools.availability: Journal paper (ASME J. Mechanical Design per author page); author-hosted PDF
tools.description: Couples a process-based cost model (material with 1% scrap, machine investment and maintenance amortised over 7 yr at 7,000 h/yr, energy, labour, 3.5% reject factor) with SIMP topology optimisation. Beam power is chosen per element, so structure and process parameters are optimised together for minimum cost under compliance constraints. Concurrent optimisation cuts cost by up to ~15% and build time by ~21% vs. structure-only optimisation.

NRE.note: Setup time is a constant part of the costed build time (machine and labour per hour), but design effort, build preparation and parameter development are not costed; costs not affected by design or process variables are ignored (author PDF).

Production.note: Per-part cost from build time (scan passes, power, velocity), material with 1% scrap, energy and labour at $26/h, e.g. bracket $675 to $575; post-processing is excluded (author PDF, Table 2-3).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification is not addressed (author PDF).

QA_Insp.note: A single 3.5% reject-rate factor is defined as covering parts rejected in quality control and destructive testing; there are no separate inspection or test line items (author PDF, Table 2).

Storage.note: Inventory is not addressed (author PDF).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine investment ($1.1M) and maintenance are amortised over 7 years at a fixed 7,000 h/yr per hour of production time, while packing, batch size and production volume are explicitly excluded (author PDF, Table 2).

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity, queues or multiple sites are not addressed (author PDF).

Speed.note: Build time (setup, sintering, powder delivery, cooling) is computed and reported, e.g. 21% faster builds with concurrent optimisation, but this is print time only and is not linked to lead time or availability (author PDF).

tools.name: Nie-Jung-Kara-Whitefoot (CMU) part-consolidation optimization for minimum production cost/time with metal AM
tools.developer: Z. Nie, S. Jung, L. B. Kara, K. S. Whitefoot (Carnegie Mellon University)
tools.context: Aircraft aft-fairing assembly (48 components, 94 riveted interfaces) supplied by an aircraft-industry partner; decides which components to merge into AM parts
tools.processes: Ti-6Al-4V by EBM powder bed fusion and by wire-fed electron-beam DED; Al-6061 in comparison scenarios
tools.availability: ASME journal paper (J. Mechanical Design per file name); PDF hosted by CMU Whitefoot group; related US patent 'Tool for optimal part consolidation selection for AM' (not opened)
tools.description: Generates consolidation candidates from an interface connectivity matrix and removes structurally redundant ones with a 'closed-loop filter'. It then optimises build orientation for minimum support, places parts with a 2-D bottom-left layout, and estimates cost or time; a genetic algorithm searches large assemblies. Consolidating 17 components into 4 parts minimises cost (~20% lower unit cost); merging into 2 parts minimises time (~25%). Full consolidation is rarely optimal because support material and removal costs rise.

NRE.note: Build-job setup (labour and machine time per batch, set by the plate layout) is costed, but redesign of consolidated parts is excluded ('do not consider the topological redesign of parts after consolidation') and no engineering cost appears (CMU PDF).

Production.note: Unit cost from part and support material, machine and maintenance, scrap, energy, setup and support removal, plus assembly (machining, riveting) for unconsolidated interfaces (CMU PDF).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification is absent from the full paper's cost terms (CMU PDF).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection and testing are absent from the full paper's cost terms (CMU PDF).

Storage.note: The paper states its cost estimates exclude inventory; fewer part numbers could cut spares stock, but this is not modelled (CMU PDF).

Shared_Capital.note: The machine rate amortises investment (e.g., $1.1M for EBM) over a 7-year life and 7,000 operating hours per year plus maintenance, and parts are nested into batches by a 2-D layout, so capital is spread by a utilisation and multi-part-build assumption (CMU PDF, cost model and parameter table).

Shared_Capacity.note: The model prices one assembly's production and has no shared capacity, queueing or multi-site element (CMU PDF).

Speed.note: Unit production time (build, batch setup, support removal and assembly) is computed and is an alternative objective, but lead time, delivery and the value of availability are not addressed (CMU PDF).

sources.title: Nie, Jung, Kara, Whitefoot - Optimization of Part Consolidation for Minimum Production Costs and Time Using Additive Manufacturing (CMU-hosted PDF)

tools.name: Piili et al. (LUT/Aalto) laser PBF stainless-steel cost estimation by build scenario
tools.developer: H. Piili, A. Happonen, T. Väistö, V. Venkataramanan, J. Partanen, A. Salminen (affiliations not shown on the accessed record; record held by Aalto University)
tools.context: Generic stainless-steel parts on a research L-PBF machine equivalent to EOS M-series; extreme build scenarios (single part vs. full build)
tools.processes: L-PBF ('laser additive manufacturing'), stainless steel
tools.availability: Conference paper, Physics Procedia 78 (2015) 388-396, doi:10.1016/j.phpro.2015.11.053 (open access; only abstract and a review summary accessed)
tools.description: Estimates part cost from build time, machine, material and energy across build scenarios with optimised machine utilisation. Machine investment dominates while energy and material are minor, so time per part is the main lever. A secondary review reports that building as many parts as possible per build cut cost 81-92% vs. building singly.

NRE.note: Only the abstract and a review summary could be read (full text not reachable via Aaltodoc, UTU portal or core.ac.uk), and neither says whether design or build-preparation effort is costed.

Production.note: Part cost is estimated from calculated build times and machine, material and energy costs for each build scenario (Aaltodoc abstract).

QA_Qual.note: Only the abstract and a review summary could be read, and neither mentions qualification; the full paper was not reachable.

QA_Insp.note: Only the abstract and a review summary could be read, and neither mentions inspection or post-processing; the full paper was not reachable.

Storage.note: The documented scope is per-part cost by build scenario on one machine, which plainly excludes inventory (Aaltodoc abstract).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine investment dominates cost and is spread over multi-part builds under optimised machine utilisation; the MDPI review reports full builds cut cost 81-92% vs single parts and 40 concurrent items cut the machine-cost share by 6% (Aaltodoc abstract; MDPI 2024 review).

Shared_Capacity.note: The documented scope is build scenarios on one research machine, which plainly excludes capacity shared across sites or users (Aaltodoc abstract).

Speed.note: Build time per scenario is calculated and drives cost, a print-time-only time model; lead time or availability is not valued (Aaltodoc abstract).

tools.name: Barclift et al. (Penn State) CAD-integrated cost estimation and build-orientation optimization for metal PBF
tools.developer: M. Barclift, A. Armstrong, T. W. Simpson, S. B. Joshi (Pennsylvania State University)
tools.context: Design-stage cost estimate inside SolidWorks for a metal-printed automotive component. Distinct from the 2016 powder-reuse entry, whose depreciation model it reuses: this paper adds CAD-API support generation and build-orientation and packing effects.
tools.processes: Metal powder bed fusion
tools.availability: ASME IDETC/CIE 2017 paper DETC2017-68376 (43rd Design Automation Conf.); SolidWorks API macro (not public). Abstract only accessed.
tools.description: Pulls part volume and surfaces through the SolidWorks API and generates internal and external supports as solid bodies, then varies build orientation. This lets designers estimate build time and feedstock (including depreciation of reused powder) while designing. An imprecise support angle underestimates support volume by 34% and build time by 20%. Poor orientation and packing can push powder-depreciation cost to nearly twice the material cost.

NRE.note: The 2017 abstract automates support generation and orientation but does not say whether preparation or redesign labour is costed; the 2016 base model it builds on costs per-build geometry preparation and says redesign is not captured, but the 2017 full text (ASME, paywalled) could not be reached to confirm what it keeps (sciencegate abstract; Barclift et al. SFF 2016 full text).

Production.note: Estimates metal AM build cost per part from CAD geometry: build time, feedstock including generated supports, and reused-powder depreciation (sciencegate abstract; MDPI 2024 review).

QA_Qual.note: The abstract scopes the estimator to build time and feedstock cost inside CAD, which plainly excludes qualification, and the 2016 base model leaves powder acceptability to supplier-purchaser agreement (sciencegate abstract; SFF 2016).

QA_Insp.note: The abstract scopes the estimator to build time and feedstock, and the 2016 base model it extends does not cost inspection (sciencegate abstract; SFF 2016 Sec. 5.4).

Storage.note: A design-stage build-cost estimator inside CAD; inventory is outside its documented scope (sciencegate abstract).

Shared_Capital.note: Packing parts within the build volume is shown to change per-part powder-depreciation cost (computed), but machine capital is not amortised with a utilisation assumption; the 2016 base model uses a flat machine operating rate of $60/h and no machine depreciation (sciencegate abstract; SFF 2016 Table 1).

Shared_Capacity.note: A single-build, design-stage cost estimate; capacity shared across sites or users is outside its documented scope (sciencegate abstract).

Speed.note: Computes build time (an imprecise support angle underestimates it by 20%), a print-time-only time model; lead time and the value of availability are not computed (sciencegate abstract).

tools.name: Budinoff & Shafae geometry-to-cost process-based model for metal L-PBF design alternatives
tools.developer: H. D. Budinoff, M. Shafae (affiliation not shown on accessed page)
tools.context: Choosing among geometrically different design alternatives of the same function for L-PBF
tools.processes: Metal L-PBF plus post-processing
tools.availability: Journal article, Int. J. Adv. Manuf. Technol. 121:6125-6136 (2022); abstract accessed
tools.description: Process-based cost model of the L-PBF build and post-processing, applied to design alternatives. Costs differ by up to 14% between alternatives, with part mass and build time the strongest predictors. Higher complexity was linked to lower cost but not strongly to reject rates. Scrap and reject rates vary with geometry in conflicting directions.

NRE.note: Only the abstract was readable (the accepted manuscript in the Arizona repository could not be downloaded); it does not say whether design or build-preparation cost is in the model (Springer abstract).

Production.note: Process-based per-part cost of the L-PBF build and post-processing for each design alternative, differing by up to 14% (Springer abstract).

QA_Qual.note: Only the abstract was read; qualification is not mentioned, so whether it is costed cannot be established (Springer abstract).

QA_Insp.note: The abstract shows geometry-dependent scrap and reject rates in the model but does not say whether inspection or testing is costed (Springer abstract).

Storage.note: The documented scope is build and post-processing cost of design alternatives, which excludes inventory (Springer abstract).

Shared_Capital.note: Only the abstract was read; it does not show how machine cost is amortised or whether parts share a build (Springer abstract).

Shared_Capacity.note: The documented scope is per-part cost of design alternatives on one process, which excludes capacity pooling across sites or users (Springer abstract).

Speed.note: The model estimates build time for each design (with mass, the most influential cost factor, and found non-linear in complexity), a print-time-only partial time model, but lead time is not reported (Springer abstract; Brennan & Hanft, SFF 2024).

tools.name: Sartini et al. (UNIVPM) analytic cost model for bound metal deposition
tools.developer: M. Sartini, I. Bianchi, A. Vita, M. Germani, M. Mandolini (Università Politecnica delle Marche)
tools.context: Designer-facing cost estimate for metal material extrusion. Validated on a 17-4 PH tensile specimen on a Desktop Metal Studio System (estimate within 2% of actual).
tools.processes: Bound metal deposition (metal material extrusion + debind + sinter)
tools.availability: Open-access conference paper, DESIGN 2024 (Proc. Design Society), doi:10.1017/pds.2024.184
tools.description: Analytic per-part cost over pre-processing, printing, debinding and sintering. Each phase sums material, machine, labour, energy and consumables, driven by part and support geometry, material, batch quantity and accuracy. Sintering machine and energy dominate the validation case (EUR 565 estimated vs. EUR 576 actual).

NRE.note: Pre-processing labour for set-up and nesting (orientation, supports, slicing, file loading; nesting counted only for the first job) is costed, but CAD design and parameter development are not (Cambridge PDF).

Production.note: Per-part cost sums material, machine, labour, energy and consumables over printing, debinding and sintering from part and support geometry, accuracy setting and batch size, validated within 2% (EUR 565 vs 576) (Cambridge PDF).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification is not modelled; 'quality' is only an accuracy input that sets layer thickness and nozzle diameter (Cambridge PDF).

QA_Insp.note: No inspection or testing cost term appears in any phase (Cambridge PDF).

Storage.note: Inventory is not addressed in the full paper (Cambridge PDF).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine hourly rates cover depreciation, overhead and maintenance at a 57% load factor (4,993 h/yr), and set-up, debind and sinter costs are divided across parts in the batch, with mixed jobs allocated by volume (Cambridge PDF).

Shared_Capacity.note: The model prices one batch on one printer, debinder and furnace and has no shared or pooled capacity (Cambridge PDF).

Speed.note: Build time is computed from extruder path length and print speed, and debind/sinter times are fixed inputs, but these only drive cost; no lead time is aggregated or valued (Cambridge PDF).

tools.name: DeBoer-Diba-Hosseini AM cost calculator (FFF and metal bound powder extrusion)
tools.developer: B. DeBoer, F. Diba, A. Hosseini (Ontario Tech University; Fleming College CAMIIT)
tools.context: Feasibility of AM vs. traditional manufacture. Metal case is a topology-optimised double-cardan H-yoke in 17-4 PH on a Markforged Metal X.
tools.processes: Bound powder extrusion (metal) and FFF (polymer)
tools.availability: Open-access CSME 2021 congress paper
tools.description: Cost calculator covering machine (equipment cost over a payback period and operating hours, power, changeover and setup labour), material (adjusted for shrinkage), post-processing (wash, sinter, argon, debind fluid, loading labour), overhead and profit. In the H-yoke case about 85% of part cost was Metal X capital, so BPE was judged uneconomic unless weight is critical.

NRE.note: Per-print setup and material-changeover time are costed at the labour rate (Eq. 12), but design, CAD, file preparation and other one-time engineering are not included; the model starts from slicer G-code (UPEI PDF).

Production.note: Per-part cost is built up from machine time, electricity, material adjusted for shrinkage, wash and sinter post-processing and labour, plus overhead and markup, for the metal BPE route (UPEI PDF, Eqs. 1-16).

QA_Qual.note: The full paper has no qualification, certification or first-article cost term (UPEI PDF).

QA_Insp.note: The full paper has no inspection, testing or quality-control cost term (UPEI PDF).

Storage.note: The full paper does not address inventory or storage (UPEI PDF).

Shared_Capital.note: The hourly machine rate spreads purchase cost over a payback period in months, 21.5 working days per month and a user-set operating hours per day, which is a utilisation input; batch packing enters only through wash and sinter efficiency factors (UPEI PDF, Eqs. 6-7, 11).

Shared_Capacity.note: The full paper costs single parts on one machine and does not address shared or pooled capacity (UPEI PDF).

Speed.note: Print time is computed (from slicer G-code for FFF, scaled by speed, layer and nozzle ratios for BPE) and drives machine cost, but lead time or availability is not calculated (UPEI PDF, Eqs. 12-16).

tools.name: Reiher et al. (Paderborn DMRC) holistic approach: part selection through test and verification
tools.developer: T. Reiher, C. Lindemann, U. Jahnke, G. Deppe, R. Koch (Paderborn University, DMRC)
tools.context: Industrialising AM from candidate selection to verified part; space case (satellite reaction-wheel bracket). Extends the TOM matrix scored in the main file.
tools.processes: Metal powder-bed AM (alloy not named)
tools.availability: Journal article, Progress in Additive Manufacturing 2:43-55 (2017), open-access PDF
tools.description: Chains the TOM selection matrix (rough cost quote, knock-out criteria, scored sub-criteria) with topology-optimisation redesign, a manufacturing strategy (orientation, supports, thermal stress) and part marking. It adds a three-tier test scheme: part-independent material/process tests, witness specimens in every build, and part-specific NDT (CT, dimensional, surface) plus load tests. The bracket was 60% lighter with buy-to-fly reduced from ~50 to 1.5. AM was cheaper at the forecast volume, although post-processing and quality costs 'had a major impact'.

NRE.note: A redesign workflow is defined (system-context review, InfoForms, FE topology optimisation, voxel smoothing, NURBS re-intersection with the original CAD), but its effort is not costed (Springer full text).

Production.note: TOM computes a rough cost quote from quantities, current production cost, size, mass and material with depreciation-time and demand assumptions, and a costing tool compares production, self- and lifecycle costs, but the cost build-up and figures are not published (Springer full text).

QA_Qual.note: Prescribes part-independent material/process tests (tensile, SCC, crack growth, fatigue, powder checks), frozen parameters and SOPs, and part-specific tests at qualification loads, with no counts by class and no costs (Springer full text).

QA_Insp.note: Requires witness specimens in every build (at least tensile and density) and part-specific CT, dimensional and surface checks; quality costs are said to have 'a major impact' but are not itemised (Springer full text).

Storage.note: States that only raw material needs storing, reducing inventory, WIP and capital lock-up, and proposes on-demand JIT production at the assembly point, without quantification (Springer full text).

Shared_Capital.note: TOM's rough quote is calculated with depreciation-time and demand assumptions, and high machine prices are said to favour centralised production at almost full workload, but how capital is spread is not documented (Springer full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Discusses centralised vs distributed production: distributed sites need cheaper machines and more suitable parts, and low build rates require a small buffer inventory; nothing is modelled (Springer full text).

Speed.note: Claims on-demand JIT production can shorten overall lead time for the bracket, with no lead-time values (Springer full text).

tools.name: Siller et al. (TU Berlin) potential-assessment and adaptation method for AM of conventionally made components
tools.developer: N. Siller, S. Werner, V. Molina, D. Göhlich (Technische Universität Berlin, Institute of Machine Design and Systems Technology)
tools.context: Screening an existing portfolio for AM with stakeholder-weighted criteria. Demonstrated on an 11-part gas-turbine pilot-nozzle assembly for serviceability (direct spare replacement).
tools.processes: Powder bed fusion (metal L-PBF implied by cited standard and turbine case)
tools.availability: Open-access journal article, Research in Engineering Design 35:73-96
tools.description: A pass/fail prefilter (fits build space, material available, AM-sensitive features acceptable, no legal restriction, conventional production not much cheaper) is followed by 0-4 scored assessments. These cover in-process and post-process restrictions and 'opportunistic' economic, eco-social and functional drivers, weighted by utility analysis. An automatic 'AM adaptation potential' flags parts that minor redesign could make suitable. Below 40% overall means low suitability; above 65% means generally suitable. In the case, 5 of 11 parts failed the prefilter.

NRE.note: An automatic 'AM adaptation potential' score (high at 6 or above) flags parts that minor non-functional redesign could make suitable, but redesign effort is not costed (TU Berlin open-access PDF).

Production.note: Cost enters only as a prefilter check that conventional production is not significantly more cost-efficient and as a 0-4 'Reduces costs' driver (12% weight in the case); no cost is calculated (TU Berlin open-access PDF, Table 7).

QA_Qual.note: No qualification, certification or testing criterion exists; load-capacity simulation and tests follow the assessment outside the method (TU Berlin open-access PDF).

QA_Insp.note: Post-processing need is scored, but inspection or quality assurance is not a criterion (TU Berlin open-access PDF).

Storage.note: Table 7 scores 'Enables on-demand-manufacturing/build-to-order' (21% weight in the turbine case) and 'Secures/improves supply-chain activities' as 0-4 AM drivers, a qualitative proxy for stock avoidance; inventory is not named or costed (TU Berlin open-access PDF).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine capital is not a criterion; machine performance only adjusts geometric thresholds and build-space fit is a prefilter (TU Berlin open-access PDF).

Shared_Capacity.note: Machine capacity or utilisation is not scored; company capacity is mentioned only for scheduling backlogged parts (TU Berlin open-access PDF).

Speed.note: Table 7 includes 'Reduces lead time' as a 0-4 driver (weight 0 in the turbine case for lack of production-time data) and prefilter P9 asks whether the part can be produced or purchased especially fast; lead time is never quantified (TU Berlin open-access PDF).

tools.name: Lawand et al. (McGill/Chalmers/GKN) dynamic lifecycle-cost model for DED remanufacturing (repair/extend vs. replace)
tools.developer: L. Lawand, M. Panarotto, P. Andersson, O. Isaksson, M. Kokkolaras (McGill University; Chalmers University of Technology; GKN Aerospace Engine Systems)
tools.context: Aero-engine turbine rear structure. Choose between original, robust and 'adaptable' designs, where a stiffener is DED-deposited on-site mid-life to extend life instead of replacing the part.
tools.processes: Directed energy deposition (Inconel 718 stiffener)
tools.availability: Open-access journal article, Aerospace 7(8):110 (2020); model built in Simulink (not public)
tools.description: Present-value lifecycle cost over a 700-month service period, with nine categories: material, manufacturing (variable plus fixed tooling), transport (replacement only), fuel, replacement labour, failure-probability-based repair, inventory, salvage, and recertification (supplemental type certificate fee). Nested optimisation (MADS) picks the stiffener design and deposition time. Deposition timing dominates LCC, and the optimal design lifespan is 312-432 months.

NRE.note: The nine LCC categories contain no design, engineering or deposition-parameter development cost for the adaptable design; the only fixed manufacturing term is machine tooling (gamma_man, USD 20,000) (Chalmers full text, Eq. 2-11).

Production.note: Material (alpha_mat x weight), manufacturing (USD 3.33 per cycle plus fixed tooling), replacement labour and failure-probability-based repair are computed per design over the service period (Chalmers full text, Eq. 2-8, Table 1).

QA_Qual.note: The only certification term is a fixed EASA supplemental-type-certificate fee (gamma_recert = USD 9,977, Eq. 11); qualification testing, analysis or approval effort is not modelled (Chalmers full text).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection and NDT are not mentioned in the model or text (Chalmers full text).

Storage.note: Inventory cost C7 = alpha_inv x weight + beta_inv x design lifespan + gamma_inv is a costed LCC element, but it is held constant and has no deposition term, so AM's effect on stock is not modelled (Chalmers full text, Eq. 9).

Shared_Capital.note: DED machine capital is not modelled; only a fixed tooling cost and per-cycle manufacturing cost appear, with no sharing or utilisation (Chalmers full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity, sites or pooled resources are not modelled (Chalmers full text).

Speed.note: Downtime, lead time and availability are not modelled; transport is costed only for replacement (Chalmers full text, Eq. 4).

tools.name: Xu & Feng AM-based remanufacturing cost model (remanufacture vs. new manufacture)
tools.developer: Y. Xu, W. Feng (Cranfield University, School of Applied Sciences)
tools.context: End-of-life decision: remanufacture a specified component by an AM-based process or make a new one
tools.processes: AM-based remanufacturing (deposition process and metal not named in abstract)
tools.availability: Open-access article, Journal of Remanufacturing 4:4 (2014), doi:10.1186/2210-4690-4-4 (abstract only accessed; publisher full text blocked)
tools.description: Framework and cost-breakdown structure for an AM-based remanufacturing process, validated by expert judgement, with a case comparing remanufacturing cost against new manufacture.

NRE.note: Pre-production cost (reverse engineering plus data processing, from labour rate and working time) is an explicit cost element, about 44% of total in the slat-track case (Springer open-access full text).

Production.note: Per-component cost is built up from setup, wire deposition and grinding (material, shielding gas, wheels, depreciation, power, labour) and overhead, for repairing titanium slat-track lugs vs. milling a new part costed in SEER-MFG (Springer full text).

QA_Qual.note: No qualification or certification step or cost; expert judgement validates the cost model, not the part (Springer full text).

QA_Insp.note: Quality inspection and testing are not in the cost breakdown structure or the cost equations (Springer full text).

Storage.note: Only costs on the remanufacturing premises are considered; inventory and reverse logistics are explicitly left to system-level analysis (Springer full text).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine depreciation is charged as a function of operating time, with idle rates inflating depositing and grinding times, but there is no utilisation, volume or shared-use input (Springer full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity is not modelled; the scope is the cost of one remanufacturing job on the premises (Springer full text).

Speed.note: Computes depositing and grinding times (mass over deposition rate, adjusted for idle rate) to drive cost, a process-time-only model; lead time, delivery and downtime are not modelled (Springer full text).

tools.developer: F. Baffa (Università degli Studi di Firenze, doctoral thesis)
tools.context: Hybrid WAAM repair of a mould insert, compared with replacement. Remanufacturing viability across three supply chains and three materials (steel, aluminium, titanium).
tools.processes: Hybrid WAAM (wire-arc DED + machining)
tools.availability: PhD thesis; full text embargoed until 31 Dec 2026 (abstract only)
tools.description: Develops WAAM repair toolpath strategies, compares the sustainability of repair vs. replacement, and builds a mathematical model of remanufacturing viability (cost and energy) in closed-loop supply chains. It identifies feasible configurations and the parameters that most affect cost and energy.

NRE.note: The thesis is embargoed until 31 Dec 2026, and neither its abstract nor the abstract of the companion J. Cleaner Production 2024 paper says whether the effort of developing repair toolpath strategies is costed (FLORE records; the paper itself is closed access).

Production.note: Both abstracts describe a mathematical model that computes cost and energy of remanufacturing (hybrid WAAM repair) vs. new parts for steel, aluminium and titanium across three supply-chain scenarios, with remanufacturing volume and share of material preserved as the most influential parameters; the cost build-up itself is not public (thesis and JCP 2024 abstracts, FLORE).

QA_Qual.note: Only abstracts are public (thesis embargoed, JCP paper closed access) and neither says whether requalification of repaired parts is costed.

QA_Insp.note: Only abstracts are public and neither says whether inspection of the repaired insert is costed.

Storage.note: The JCP 2024 abstract compares a no-remanufacturing chain with direct and distribution-centre remanufacturing chains but does not say whether inventory is costed (FLORE abstract).

Shared_Capital.note: Only abstracts are public and neither says how WAAM or machining equipment cost is allocated.

Shared_Capacity.note: The three scenarios differ in how customer and manufacturer interact (direct or via a distribution centre), not in shared repair capacity, and the abstracts say nothing on capacity (FLORE abstracts).

Speed.note: Only abstracts are public and neither says whether repair vs. replacement lead time or downtime is valued.

tools.name: RAND 3D printing supply-chain impact matrix and fab-lab concept (PE-229)
tools.developer: RAND Corporation (Simon Véronneau, Geoffrey Torrington, Jakub P. Hlavka)
tools.context: DoD and commercial supply chains. Military examples include forward operating bases, ships, submarines and contested theaters.
tools.processes: Technology-agnostic. The proposed fab-lab has CNC milling, metal-alloy AM, plastic-composite AM and CT metrology.
tools.availability: Public RAND Perspective PE-229 (22 pp.)
tools.description: A two-by-two matrix in which the impact of 3D printing grows with site isolation and with ad hoc (unpredictable) demand. The paper proposes a four-machine fab-lab and a process flow: incoming inspection, CT, 3D rendering, AM or CNC, post-production, outgoing inspection, tracking and serialization, then return to service. It calls for a total supply-chain cost comparison but gives no cost model and does not rank parts.

NRE.note: CT metrology can 'generate a 3D printable design' from existing parts and characterising a part without a 3D diagram 'would take about one hour', a quoted estimate that is not costed (RAND PE-229 full text).

Production.note: Says a fab-lab vs centralized comparison 'must involve a total supply chain cost approach' and calls for a 'comprehensive cost-effectiveness evaluation', but gives no per-part cost (RAND PE-229 full text).

QA_Qual.note: Recommends 'rationalizing the certification and testing approach' for AM components, without steps or costs (RAND PE-229 full text).

QA_Insp.note: Incoming and outgoing inspection and CT defect scanning are steps in the fab-lab process flow, and CT is called 'relatively underappreciated', but inspection is not costed (RAND PE-229 full text).

Storage.note: Inventory and holding cost are not discussed, but the impact matrix uses demand variability (ad hoc vs steady) and obsolescence as criteria for where printing pays, a screening use (RAND PE-229 full text).

Shared_Capital.note: The proposed fab-lab is not costed and sharing its equipment is not discussed; pay-per-use appears only as background on civilian hobbyist fab-labs (RAND PE-229 full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: The matrix argues for forward fab-labs at isolated sites with ad hoc demand rather than central production and notes sizing needs a throughput estimate, without a capacity model (RAND PE-229 full text).

Speed.note: Quotes times only: a noncritical part 'in as little as 45 minutes' and readiness gains where items 'cannot otherwise be procured'; nothing is computed or valued (RAND PE-229 full text).

tools.name: RAND Europe AM and obsolescence management in defence (PE-171), with Cranfield obsolescence-resolution cost metrics
tools.developer: RAND Europe (eds. Jon Freeman, Giacomo Persi Paoli). Contributors from armasuisse S+T, US Army ARDEC (G. Di Benedetto) and Cranfield University (J. Erkoyuncu, R. Roy, S. Williams, P. Colegrove, F. Martina, A. Busachi). Funded by armasuisse S+T.
tools.context: Defence obsolescence management for in-service equipment, with Swiss, UK and US perspectives (including Fleet Readiness Center East examples)
tools.processes: Generic AM, with DMLS 4340 steel data and WAAM (Cranfield)
tools.availability: Public RAND Perspective PE-171
tools.description: A collection of expert perspectives, not a model. The nearest decision elements are a 'window of opportunity' test for obsolescence, a list of resolution options (same component, form-fit-function replacement, emulation, redesign), and Cranfield cost metrics (Table 2) for choosing 'the most cost effective solution'. The cost metrics are not AM-specific.

NRE.note: Cranfield Table 2 gives non-recurring obsolescence-resolution costs by integration level (emulation GBP 52,100 to 2.69m, minor redesign GBP 50,100 to 549,000), but these are generic survey figures, not an AM-specific NRE estimate; the US Navy RESTORE 'SCAN to CAD to FAB' workflow is described without costs (RAND PE-171, pp. 8, 13-14).

Production.note: AM costs are described in words as 'largely predictable' and needing to be competitive, and whether small batches can be made at constant cost is posed as a question; no unit figures (RAND PE-171, pp. 5, 13-14).

QA_Qual.note: Requalification of air/safety-critical components is one of the cost parameters folded into the generic Table 2 non-recurring costs per resolution approach, and ARDEC DMLS 4340 tensile data are reported, but there is no AM-specific qualification costing (RAND PE-171, pp. 10-14).

QA_Insp.note: Per-part inspection is not addressed; the only testing reported is ARDEC tensile testing for process qualification (RAND PE-171, full text).

Storage.note: Proposes digital storage of designs for on-demand remanufacture and notes stock ties up money; Table 2 prices 'existing stock' only as a GBP 300 resolution option, not as an AM inventory model (RAND PE-171, pp. 5, 8, 14).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine investment or its sharing is not discussed; investment appears only as R&D funding for the industrial base (RAND PE-171, p. 9).

Shared_Capacity.note: Raises a national 'strategic reserve of additive manufacturing capabilities' and mobile AM facilities for sustainment contracts, described qualitatively with no capacity or lead-time model (RAND PE-171, pp. 5, 15).

Speed.note: Cites FRCE repairs made with AM 'over a few days' instead of three or more weeks, and frames obsolescence as replacement time exceeding a window of opportunity, but time is not computed or valued (RAND PE-171, pp. 10, 12).

tools.name: Braunberger AFIT MODA and metal L-PBF cost model for AM vs DLA procurement (C-130 parts)
tools.developer: 1st Lt Trever J. Braunberger, USAF, Air Force Institute of Technology (committee: Maj John Situ, Maj Ryan Kemnitz, Alfred E. Thal Jr.)
tools.context: USAF legacy aircraft parts with long lead times. Six C-130 troop-seat, rack and beam parts were judged not flight-safety critical. Selection criteria: price of $1,000 or more, lead time of 70 days or more, and a printable material.
tools.processes: Metal L-PBF/DMLS (EOS M290; Ti-6Al-4V)
tools.availability: Open thesis (DTIC AD1102526; AFIT Scholar etd/3748). The MODA is presented as a user tool; no software release is noted.
tools.description: A nine-criterion multi-objective decision analysis. Weights: quality 21.0%, lead time 20.1%, readiness 18.3%, price 14.6%, airworthiness 7.3%, expected life 6.3%, strength 6.2%, weight 4.8%, quantity 1.5%. Score bands: 86–100% is an 'extremely good candidate'; below 60%, use traditional methods. It is paired with an Atzeni & Salmi-based cost model and a guide to AM lab set-up costs ($1.94M for one metal lab). Single-part AM builds averaged $3,174.96 against $2,486.83 DLA prices, 27.6% more. Table 4.3 shows two of six parts cheaper with AM, while the text says three. AM lead times were 9–16 days against 71 to 120+ days.

NRE.note: Pre-processing cost CPRE = (ET x EC) + (TS x CO) has an engineering-time term and the thesis defines NRE as reengineering incl. creating 3D data and programming, but ET/EC values are not given and the implied engineering cost is only ~$25-106 per part per build (Table 4.3, rising per part in multi-part builds, Table 4.4), while one-time reverse engineering (50-150 h, ~$10k), redesign (up to $1M) and parameter development ($150k+, 6+ months) are quoted from SMEs outside the cost model (DTIC full thesis, ch. 3-4).

Production.note: Per-part material, pre-processing, processing (build-time formula, depreciation, energy, maintenance) and post-processing (labour $21.9/h, heat treatment $85/part, test, machining) costs are computed for six parts and for batch builds (DTIC full thesis, Eq. 3-5, Tables 4.3-4.4).

QA_Qual.note: Airworthiness is a MODA criterion (7.3% weight) and parts need a strength test and Chief Engineer approval, but airworthiness approval cost or effort is not quantified and all six parts were chosen as non-flight-safety-critical (DTIC full thesis, ch. 2-4).

QA_Insp.note: Post-processing cost CPOS = (TPOS x CO) + CTEST + CHT + CMACH carries a per-build test-cost line item for the tensile test run after each build ($1,061 grips, test-sample volume in material), though CTEST is not reported separately and volumetric/NDI inspection is explicitly excluded (DTIC full thesis, Eq. 5 and assumptions).

Storage.note: The thesis notes that 'space does cost money' and that storage and transport savings differ by part and location, but calls them difficult to quantify and leaves them out of the equations (DTIC full thesis, ch. 2-3).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine depreciation (8-year amortisation, ~$1.105M M290 package) is charged per build hour and multi-part builds are costed explicitly, cutting per-part cost 33% (2 parachute racks) and 35% (3 bracket mounts); annual machine hours/utilisation are not stated and sharing across sites or users is not modelled (DTIC full thesis, Eq. 4, Tables 4.1 and 4.4).

Shared_Capacity.note: SME interviews call for an integrated network of printing sites for faster turn-around and note distributed production 'may be cost effective' with more automation, but no capacity pooling is modelled (DTIC full thesis, ch. 2 and 4).

Speed.note: AM lead time (9-16 days) is estimated per part against DLA lead times (71 to 120+ days) and scored in the MODA alongside a separate readiness criterion; time is quantified, not dollarised (DTIC full thesis, Fig. 4.2 and MODA).

sources.title: Braunberger (2020) Providing Rational for Further Funding Additive Manufacturing Efforts in the Air Force, AFIT thesis (DTIC AD1102526)

tools.name: Crean AFIT metal AM per-part cost model and AM capability fielding costs
tools.developer: Capt Ryan C. Crean, USAF, Air Force Institute of Technology (advisor Alan W. Johnson)
tools.context: USAF long-lead-time parts: 10 NIINs, of which 7 were costed (PLT+ALT 324–611 days). Screening: unit cost over $1,000, ALT+PLT over 180 days, fits the EOS M290 envelope, not flight-critical. Also costs fielding three levels of AM capability.
tools.processes: Metal L-PBF/DMLS (EOS M290; titanium, aluminum, steel); production and desktop polymer printers for fielding costs
tools.availability: Open thesis (AFIT Scholar etd/791; core.ac.uk PDF)
tools.description: An Atzeni & Salmi-based cost model (material, pre-processing, processing, post-processing) with a layer-based build-time formula. It matched UDRI builds within 0–5.3%. Single builds averaged $3,144.74 per part and maximum batches $2,615.95. Before NRE, only 1 of 7 parts was cheaper with AM in single builds, and 3 with batching. Fielding one metal capability costs about $1.52–1.66M per alloy family.

NRE.note: Build setup is costed ($90 per build: 2 h at $45/h) and an engineering-hours term sits in the pre-processing equation, but one-time NRE is excluded from per-part cost and only cited outside the model (AFLCMC's ~$1,000,000 and Tinker's ~40 h per reverse-engineered part) (full thesis, ch. III-VI).

Production.note: Per-part cost is built up from material (with waste factor), pre-processing, build time x machine depreciation per machine-hour, energy (3.2 kW), maintenance ($18k/yr), labour ($45/h), heat treatment ($100) and machining (full thesis, Eq. 1).

QA_Qual.note: Missing AM process specifications are discussed as a barrier and flight-critical parts are screened out, but qualification is not costed (full thesis).

QA_Insp.note: A per-build test cost is a line item in the post-processing term: one ASTM E8 tensile coupon per build at $300 ($200 machining, $100 test); volumetric NDI is excluded and the CMM appears only as fielding equipment (full thesis).

Storage.note: Holding-cost and inventory savings are said to vary by part and location and are deliberately left out of the model (full thesis).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine depreciation (EOS M290, ~$1.1M) is charged per machine-hour and spread across multi-part builds (up to 16 parts per build), cutting average cost from $3,144.74 single-build to $2,615.95 max-batch; sharing across users or sites is not modelled (full thesis).

Shared_Capacity.note: The conclusions recommend an enterprise-wide network of metal machines placed by demand, skills and proximity to other bases, but capacity and pooling are not modelled (full thesis, ch. VI).

Speed.note: AM build and post-processing hours are computed (e.g. 46.17 h for one part, 216.48 h for a 16-part build) and current PLT+ALT is reported, but AM lead time is not totalled or valued; NMC-S cost is suggested as future work (full thesis).

tools.name: AMPAT (Additive Manufacturing Process and Analysis Tool), NPS Navy Expeditionary AM capstone
tools.developer: Leslie J. Amodeo, Brian B. Dick, Charles P. Flynn, Rebecca A. Nagurney and Meagan B. Parker (NPS Systems Engineering capstone). Sponsor: Navy Expeditionary Combat Command (NECC).
tools.context: Navy expeditionary forces under DMO, LOCE and EABO: choosing AM equipment and informing where to disperse and preposition it
tools.processes: Database of at least 40 AM systems (data cut-off Mar 31, 2021); polymer/metal mix not verified
tools.availability: Excel/VBA tool described in DTIC AD1150790; whether the file is distributed is not stated
tools.description: The user filters a database of AM systems on attributes such as build size, material, process, footprint, print speed, cooling, print quality, post-processing, failure rate, operational availability and environment, then assigns weights. The tool outputs a normalized weighted ranking and plots, for example overall score against initial cost. It covers equipment only, not part selection.

NRE.note: The tool has no NRE attribute, but the report mentions an X-FAB 3D scanner for generating models from existing parts and recommends adding a library of parts and part specifications (DTIC AD1150790).

Production.note: Material cost per pound, consumable cost per 100 operating hours and component cost are weighted system attributes in the ranking, but per-part cost is not computed (DTIC AD1150790, Table 2).

QA_Qual.note: The tool has no qualification attribute; the report cites the DON objective to rapidly qualify and certify AM components and recommends AMPAT to help qualified SMEs judge AM technologies for DoD use (DTIC AD1150790).

QA_Insp.note: Print quality is a database attribute and the report says sailor-printed parts need a validation process, but inspection is neither scoped nor costed (DTIC AD1150790).

Storage.note: The report argues on-demand printing eases spare-part stocking; the tool's 'initial spares and inventory cost' attribute refers to the AM system's own spares, and part inventory is not quantified (DTIC AD1150790).

Shared_Capital.note: System initial cost (with maintenance and consumable costs) is entered per AM system and plotted against overall score, but machine cost is not spread over parts or users (DTIC AD1150790, Table 2, Fig. 38).

Shared_Capacity.note: The tool is meant to inform dispersion and prepositioning of AM systems across the fleet, but the team could not build a dispersion plan and capacity is not modelled (DTIC AD1150790).

Speed.note: Print speed, maintenance times and operational availability of each AM system are weighted ranking attributes and part lead-time cuts are argued qualitatively, but no part lead time or readiness is computed (DTIC AD1150790).

tools.name: Sasson & Johnson 3D printing supercenters concept
tools.developer: Amir Sasson, John Chandler Johnson (BI Norwegian Business School)
tools.context: Manufacturers with complex, varied bills of material; low-volume and out-of-production spares
tools.processes: Direct digital manufacturing (plastics first; metals named as a later expansion)
tools.availability: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management 46(1):82–94; open author version
tools.description: An invited conceptual paper. Firms use direct digital manufacturing (DDM) to separate out low-volume, disruptive parts even at a higher unit cost, then grow into regional multi-product 'supercenters'. These move spares inventory from finished goods at company plants to raw material at shared DDM facilities. There is no quantitative model; the authors call for cost comparisons and simulation studies.

NRE.note: Digital design (creation, modification, copying or scanning) is named as a phase of 3D printing and firms are urged to digitise and publish printable component files to control quality, but the effort is not costed (BI open author version).

Production.note: Higher DDM unit cost (energy and raw material) is accepted for low-volume parts because it stabilises plant operations, argued only in words with illustrative figures (BI open author version).

QA_Qual.note: A lack of safety and quality standards is cited as a constraint on adoption, and part quality is said to depend on the CAD model, but qualification is not otherwise treated (BI open author version).

QA_Insp.note: The full paper does not discuss inspection or testing of printed parts (BI open author version).

Storage.note: Spares inventory is argued to shift from finished goods at company plants to raw material at shared DDM supercenters, with no quantification (BI open author version).

Shared_Capital.note: Supercenters raise utilisation of printing capacity by serving other firms' demand and gain economies of scope in learning and raw-material purchasing, without numbers (BI open author version).

Shared_Capacity.note: Orders are 'redirected to center B' when center A is full, routed only when extra distribution cost is below customer queuing cost, but this pooling is described without a model (BI open author version).

Speed.note: Expedited low-volume orders are moved to DDM to avoid disrupting scheduled production, and local printing is claimed to cut lead time and delivery distance, without quantification (BI open author version).

tools.name: Strong et al. hybrid-AM hub facility-location model (uncapacitated and p-median, 2018)
tools.developer: Danielle Strong, Michael Kay, Brett Conner, Thomas Wakefield, Guha Manogharan (Penn State)
tools.context: US metal hybrid-AM supply chain: AM hubs that use the spare capacity of traditional machine shops (NAICS data). Not specific to spare parts.
tools.processes: Metal AM plus secondary processing (machining, grinding, heat treatment, HIP)
tools.availability: Additive Manufacturing 21:159–173, DOI 10.1016/j.addma.2018.03.010 (abstract read). Companion to the 2019 two-stage p-median entry already scored.
tools.description: An uncapacitated facility-location model places hubs by geography, demand and hybrid-AM processing cost. Hubs land at demand centroids, and location depends only on AM utilization rate. A constrained p-median model grows from 22 to 44 hubs as demand rises. Outputs are candidate US counties, fixed, operating and transport costs, and hub utilization. Transport cost was not a significant factor.

NRE.note: Only the abstract (via the record) and a trade summary were available; the full paper could not be reached (Penn State Pure blocked, Scribd copy empty), and neither mentions design or engineering effort.

Production.note: Hybrid-AM processing and operating cost enter the hub-location model at hub level rather than as a per-part build-up (abstract as summarised in the record).

QA_Qual.note: The abstract mentions meeting GD&T and property requirements but not qualification, and the full paper could not be reached.

QA_Insp.note: The abstract names post-processing steps but not inspection, and the full paper could not be reached.

Storage.note: Neither the abstract nor the trade summary mentions inventory, and the full paper could not be reached.

Shared_Capital.note: Fixed hub cost is traded against hub count (22 to 44 hubs as demand rises) with location driven by AM utilisation rate, and spare traditional-shop capacity is pooled into hubs (abstract as summarised in the record).

Shared_Capacity.note: Hub capacity utilisation is an output and the trade summary recommends expanding existing hub capacity, but no effect on lead time is reported (abstract; Assembly Magazine summary).

Speed.note: Neither the abstract nor the trade summary mentions lead or delivery time, and the full paper could not be reached.

tools.name: ISO/ASTM TS 52930:2021 Qualification principles: installation, operation and performance (IQ/OQ/PQ) of PBF-LB equipment
tools.developer: ISO/TC 261 and ASTM F42 (joint), adopted by CEN as CEN ISO/ASTM/TS 52930
tools.context: Qualification of metal laser powder bed fusion machines used for production parts; facility, personnel, process and material issues only insofar as they support machine qualification.
tools.processes: PBF-LB/M (metal laser powder bed fusion) only
tools.availability: Paid technical specification; scope pages public
tools.description: Recommended practices for IQ, OQ and PQ of PBF-LB/M machines and connected equipment. Feedstock qualification and post-processing beyond powder removal are excluded. The public scope gives no test list, sample sizes or tiering by part criticality.

NRE.note: The scope is machine IQ/OQ/PQ; process mapping, risk assessment and validation planning are stated to be prerequisites outside it, so one-time part engineering is excluded (ISO scope).

Production.note: Cost is outside the stated scope of machine qualification practices (ISO scope; TOC preview).

QA_Qual.note: Defines IQ, OQ and PQ of PBF-LB machines plus revalidation and a normative process-capability (SPC) annex, but no test counts or part-class tiering are visible (ISO scope; ANSI/iTeh TOC preview).

QA_Insp.note: Only scope and TOC were seen; post-processing beyond powder removal is excluded, but the PQ section and normative Annex A on process capability (SPC) may set ongoing part or specimen checks, so per-part inspection is not established (ISO scope; TOC preview).

Storage.note: Inventory is outside the stated scope of machine qualification (ISO scope).

Shared_Capital.note: Only scope and TOC were seen (including a revalidation section), so whether a qualified machine's IQ/OQ/PQ carries across parts or users is not established.

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity shared across sites or users is outside the stated scope of machine qualification (ISO scope).

Speed.note: Lead time is outside the stated scope of machine qualification (ISO scope).

tools.name: EASA CM-S-008 Additive Manufacturing, Issue 04 (3 Sept 2025)
tools.developer: European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA); revision discussed at FAA-EASA AM Workshop WG1
tools.context: Civil aviation type certification and production approval (CS-23/25/27/29/E/P/ETSO etc.); metallic and non-metallic AM. Guidance, not new requirements.
tools.processes: All AM processes (metallic and non-metallic)
tools.availability: Free PDF on easa.europa.eu
tools.description: Adopts the ASTM F3572-22 Class A-D scheme. Section 3 policy covers only new parts or repair-by-replacement of no/low criticality (Class C and D); higher classes are said to be hard to certify near-term. All AM parts need early authority engagement, a threat and design safety assessment, M&P specifications and process control documents, KPPs, statistically covered design values (A/B/C/D/S-basis per MMPDS/CMH-17), and machine OQ plus process PQ over multiple builds. Class C/D may use S-basis data, a minimal representative coupon set and simplified means of compliance; Class D may qualify for minor change approval. POA must treat a new AM process as a significant change.

NRE.note: Calls for identification of key variables and key process parameters and for M&P specifications supported by process control documents, a prescribed parameter-development activity with no effort or cost and no redesign or reverse-engineering content (CM text, Sec. 3.1.1-3.1.2).

Production.note: Per-part production cost is not addressed; the CM is certification guidance (CM text, full read).

QA_Qual.note: Tiered by class (Class C/D may use S-basis data, a minimal representative coupon set and simplified means of compliance; machine OQ and process PQ need statistical relevance over multiple builds), but no build or coupon counts are given and A/B are left case by case (CM text, Sec. 1.3.2, 3.1).

QA_Insp.note: No NDI, first-article, witness-coupon or production acceptance requirement is given for any class; NDT appears only in definitions and the POA section requires only conformity to design data (CM text, Sec. 1.3, 3.5).

Storage.note: Spares and inventory are not mentioned (CM text, full read).

Shared_Capital.note: Part families and machine equivalency are not covered; reuse is allowed only where a part falls within previous regulatory agreement (CM text, Sec. 1.3.2, 3.1.2).

Shared_Capacity.note: Production capacity is not mentioned; only organisational AM capability is required (CM text, Sec. 3.1.2).

Speed.note: Lead time and availability are not mentioned (CM text, full read).

FAA-EASA AM Event 2024, WG1 Qualification of AM parts (slides)
