tools.name: FAA Advisory Circular AC 33.15-3 Powder Bed Fusion AM Process for Aircraft Engine Parts (with FAA 2020 AM Report to Congress)
tools.developer: Federal Aviation Administration (Aircraft Certification Service)
tools.context: Engine part certification under 14 CFR 33.15 (materials); non-binding acceptable means of compliance. The Report to Congress describes the FAA's overall risk-based approach.
tools.processes: Metal powder bed fusion
tools.availability: Free PDFs on faa.gov
tools.description: Design values should be statistically based (MMPDS-level rigor) from a frozen process and stable feedstock. Specimens should span builds, build locations, orientations, thicknesses and powder lots, with debits for features and thermal exposure. Key process variables are frozen within validated windows; changes need requalification; each machine is validated separately. Powder reuse limits are required, ISO/IEC 17025 labs are expected, and periodic destructive sampling is based on SPC. No sample sizes are given. There are no criticality tiers beyond noting that life-limited parts need more (33.14/33.70). The 2020 report says acceptable risk is set by part criticality but defines no formal tiers.

NRE.note: Requires identifying key process variables, running parametric studies to set their tolerances and freezing the process (one-time engineering), with no effort or cost given (AC 33.15-3 secs. 8.1, 8.1.3).

Production.note: The AC's scope is material and process compliance under 14 CFR 33.15, which plainly excludes production cost; the 2020 report does not cost parts either (AC 33.15-3; FAA 2020 report).

QA_Qual.note: Prescribes qualification elements (MMPDS-rigour design values from specimens spanning builds, locations, orientations and powder lots; per-machine validation; requalification on process change) but gives no specimen counts and no part-class tiers (AC 33.15-3 secs. 6.1-6.4, 11.5-11.6).

QA_Insp.note: NDI (including CT) is one option alongside process monitoring, proof testing and periodic destructive sampling set by SPC, with no quantities or class-specific scope (AC 33.15-3 secs. 10.3-10.9, 11.4.2).

Storage.note: Inventory is outside the AC's materials-compliance scope; the 2020 report mentions spare parts only as case-by-case applications (AC 33.15-3; FAA 2020 report sec. 4.2).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine investment is outside scope, and each machine needs its own process validation, so qualification is not shared across machines (AC 33.15-3 sec. 11.5).

Shared_Capacity.note: Production capacity is outside the AC's scope and is not discussed in the 2020 report (AC 33.15-3; FAA 2020 report).

Speed.note: Lead time is outside the AC's scope; the 2020 report notes schedule savings only as background on why industry uses AM, not as part of the approach (AC 33.15-3; FAA 2020 report secs. 4.2, 5).

tools.name: MMPDS Volume II guidelines for AM allowables (2026 handbook edition)
tools.developer: Battelle (MMPDS Secretariat) with the MMPDS General Coordinating Committee (FAA, DoD, industry)
tools.year: 2021-2026 (AM data guidelines presented 2021-2023; Volume II first released 1 July 2024; 2026 edition 1 July 2026; no AM allowables published yet)
tools.context: Aerospace design allowables for process-intensive metals (incl. AM); used by FAA, DoD services and OEMs. Note: CMH-17 Volume 7 (AM) covers non-metallic materials only (due end of 2026), so it is out of scope here.
tools.processes: Metal AM (L-PBF IN718, Ti-6Al-4V, 6061-RAM2 and others in work)
tools.availability: MMPDS handbook is licensed/paid; guideline slides public
tools.description: Volume II adds C-basis (lower of spec minimum or T99), D-basis (T90) and S-basis allowables for AM metals, each requiring 'further showing'. Mandatory S-basis minimums: 30 samples per strength property from 3 heats, 3 manufacturing lots, 3 machines and 3 build cycles (fewer for modulus and density). Recommended D-basis: 100 samples, 10 heats, 10 lots, 5 machines, 10 builds. C-basis: 100 samples, 10 heats, 20 lots, 5 machines, 20 builds. If no parametric fit is possible, 299 samples are needed. C-basis needs 20 builds or lots, against 10 lots for conventional A-basis. Lot-release values are being derived for several AMS AM specs.

NRE.note: Part design, reverse engineering and parameter development are outside the scope of a handbook framework for generating and analysing material allowables data (SAE Mobilus Volume II page; Hall slides 2021/2023).

Production.note: Per-part production cost is outside the scope of a material-allowables handbook (SAE Mobilus Volume II page; Hall slides 2021/2023).

QA_Qual.note: The Volume II draft sets costable data minima per allowable basis (S-basis 30 samples, 3 heats, 3 lots, 3 machines, 3 builds; D-basis 100/10/10/5/10; C-basis 100/10/20/5/20, or 299 samples without a parametric fit), but basis is not tied to part class: S-basis for low-criticality parts was still under FAA-EASA discussion (Hall, AMSC 2021 and NRC 2023).

QA_Insp.note: Battelle is deriving lot-release values for AMS AM specs (7024, 7030, 7036, 7038, 7039), which must carry lot acceptance criteria for composition and mechanical properties; per-part inspection or NDI is not addressed (Hall, NRC 2023).

Storage.note: Inventory is outside the scope of a material-allowables handbook (SAE Mobilus Volume II page; Hall slides).

Shared_Capital.note: A published handbook allowable built from data across several machines, heats and builds is one dataset reused by all users of the spec, and AMS 7032 machine-qualification data feed MMPDS, but the sharing benefit is not quantified (Hall, AMSC 2021 and NRC 2023).

Shared_Capacity.note: Print capacity is outside the scope of a material-allowables handbook (Hall slides 2021/2023).

Speed.note: Part lead time or availability is outside the scope of a material-allowables handbook; the slides mention only that two to five alloys are added per year (Hall, NRC 2023).

tools.name: JMADD: Joint Metal Additive Database Definition (America Makes project 5511.001), public B/A-basis allowables framework for L-PBF Ti-6Al-4V
tools.developer: Wichita State University NIAR (presenter; fabrication and testing) with Battelle, Auburn University, Beehive Industries, EOS, Boeing and Penn State CIMP-3D; America Makes project funded by OSD ManTech (AFRL agreement FA8650-20-2-5700)
tools.context: Shared public material database, specifications and process control document so each user does not have to regenerate allowables; NCAMP-style B-basis (T90) and A-basis (T99) datasets.
tools.processes: L-PBF Ti-6Al-4V on EOS M290
tools.availability: Datasets and specs intended to be public (B-basis report scheduled April 2024); briefings public
tools.description: Budget: $4.24M ($1.8M government + $2.44M cost share) over Oct 2020 to Oct 2024. Inputs: three fabricators, three powder suppliers, 19 feedstock lots in Qual 1 and 10+ heats. About 1,733 specimens were defined for Qual 1, covering tension, shear, compression, bearing and fracture toughness, with a CT subset of 216. Qual 2 uses 60 builds. The overall program was described as about 3,600 specimens. Planned follow-ons are machine equivalency (GE M2 vs EOS M290, 18-24 months) and fatigue curves (360 specimens, 8 builds, 24 months).

NRE.note: JMADD's documented scope is a public material and process specification with statistically based allowables for L-PBF Ti-6Al-4V, so part design files and part-specific build preparation are outside it (NIAR briefing AFRL-2024-1140 as read earlier; FAA REDAC 2022 slides).

Production.note: JMADD is an allowables database and specification effort, so per-part production cost is outside its documented scope (FAA REDAC 2022 slides; NIAR briefing).

QA_Qual.note: Gives a lump cost ($4.24M) and a costable test matrix for material allowables only (about 1,733 Qual-1 specimens across tension, shear, compression, bearing and fracture toughness, 60 Qual-2 builds), with no part-class qualification counts or cost model (NIAR briefing; FAA REDAC 2022 slides).

QA_Insp.note: Specifies lot-release tensile testing per build and CT of a 216-specimen subset, which is lot-level acceptance rather than per-part production inspection cost (NIAR briefing).

Storage.note: JMADD is an allowables database and specification effort, so parts inventory is outside its documented scope (FAA REDAC 2022 slides; NIAR briefing).

Shared_Capital.note: Its purpose is publicly available allowables so each user need not regenerate them, with a planned machine-equivalency follow-on, but the saving from this reuse is not quantified (FAA REDAC 2022 slides; NIAR briefing).

Shared_Capacity.note: JMADD does not address print capacity; its scope is material data and specifications (FAA REDAC 2022 slides; NIAR briefing).

Speed.note: JMADD does not address part lead time or availability; its scope is material data and specifications (FAA REDAC 2022 slides; NIAR briefing).

tools.name: MASAAG Paper 124 Issue 2 (2022): qualification and certification of AM parts for military aviation
tools.developer: Military Aircraft Structures Airworthiness Advisory Group (MASAAG), UK Ministry of Defence
tools.context: UK military aircraft structures, engines and systems; advisory guidance to Type Airworthiness Authorities (not regulation).
tools.processes: Metal AM (with a separate polymer chapter)
tools.availability: Free PDF on gov.uk
tools.description: Grade A structural parts and Critical engine parts get the full recommendations: the MCRI (Military Certification Review Item) process, a PCD supplied with airworthiness documentation, B-basis allowables per failure mode with minimum coupon and batch counts, and a test pyramid up to component tests. Grade B is at the designer's discretion. Non-critical parts need a consequence-based subset agreed with the TAA. Statistical guidance: about 100 measurements for direct A/B values, 30 as an interim B-value. NDI detectable crack size is linked to inspection intervals for inspection-based fatigue substantiation.

NRE.note: NRE-type activities are recommended without counts or cost: a Process Control Document for critical parts, recorded build parameters and qualified build files, calibration builds on any machine new to the part or after an alloy change, and possible redesign for AM residual stress (MASAAG 124, Exec. Summary, 6.2-6.4, REC6.5, REC6.8).

Production.note: The guidance does not address production cost; cost appears only as the aim of powder reuse to keep material cost down (MASAAG 124, 6.4.1.3; full text read apart from part of the polymer chapter).

QA_Qual.note: Grade A structures get countable requirements (B-basis per failure mode, minimum coupon and batch counts in Table 3-3, a 15-coupon mean fallback, 100 or interim 30 measurements, MCRI, PCD, test pyramid), while Grade B and non-critical parts get TAA-agreed subsets, so counts exist for the top class only (MASAAG 124, 3.1.6, 3.6.1, REC3.3, Exec. Summary).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection scope is set by part class and per build: each Grade A (and Class 1/Group 1 engine) AM part gets inspection of 100% of its surface with part-specific POD, and every powder-bed build carries a witness set of a density cube, powder capsule and tensile coupons (MASAAG 124, REC3.7, REC4.8, REC4.10, REC5.6, REC6.43).

Storage.note: Parts inventory and spares are not addressed; storage appears only for feedstock degradation (MASAAG 124, REC6.2; full text read).

Shared_Capital.note: Reuse is described without numbers: process qualification may later cover several parts 'at least within the same part family', parameters may be fixed for a part or part family, machines other than the qualified ones need pre-qualification builds, and parts are placed to maximise parts per build (MASAAG 124, 4.7.2.2, 6.3.3.3, REC6.8, REC7.18).

Shared_Capacity.note: The guidance does not address print capacity across sites or users; moving parts between machines is treated only as a pre-qualification requirement (MASAAG 124, REC6.8; full text read).

Speed.note: Lead time and availability are not addressed in the guidance (MASAAG 124; full text read).

sources.title: MASAAG Paper 124 Issue 2 (gov.uk)

tools.name: Lloyd's Register LR-GN-046 guidance notes for AM metallic parts (June 2024)
tools.developer: Lloyd's Register (with TWI for the 2016/2017 editions)
tools.context: Classification/certification of metallic AM parts for ships, offshore structures and machinery; 2024 edition refocused on marine and offshore.
tools.processes: 2017: laser metal deposition, L-PBF, WAAM; 2024 edition scope details not seen
tools.availability: 2024 edition via free Regs4ships sign-up; 2017 edition PDF circulated publicly
tools.description: The 2017 edition is goal-based with no fixed part categories. Testing depends on design code, criticality and a functional study. Five certifiable stages (design, materials, manufacturing, post-processing, inspection/testing) can be certified separately by different organisations. Minimum per part: 100% visual and 100% dimensional examination. NDE methods are set by quality level, complexity and criticality. For PBF, good practice is a density block, retained-powder capsule and one tensile set per build. Build parameters are machine-specific. The 2024 edition adds facility approval but its categories were not seen.

NRE.note: Requires a manufacturing plan for each AM part design and machine-specific build-parameter qualification, and lists reverse engineering as a suitability criterion, none costed (2017 edition text secs. 3, 7.1.1, 10; the 2024 text sits behind Regs4ships sign-up and was not read).

Production.note: Material cost, production size and shipping time and cost are listed among the criteria for deciding whether AM is suitable, with no cost calculation (2017 edition text sec. 3).

QA_Qual.note: Five separately certifiable stages and machine-specific parameter qualification, but testing is set by design code, risk matrix and a functional study agreed case by case, with no class-specific counts (2017 edition text secs. 4, 5, 9.3; 2024 page lists facility approval and qualification only by name).

QA_Insp.note: Sets costable minimums for every part and build (100% visual and 100% dimensional examination, a mandatory powder capsule per build, density block and tensile set as good practice) but leaves NDE extent to complexity, criticality and agreement (2017 edition text secs. 7.2.2, 9.1).

Storage.note: The 2017 text does not mention inventory or spares, and the 2024 edition's scope (manufacture, testing and certification) plainly excludes it (2017 edition text; LR guidance notes page).

Shared_Capital.note: Says stage certification reduces effort on later contracts and that using pre-certified organisations cuts part certification cost, a qualitative reuse of qualification (2017 edition text sec. 4).

Shared_Capacity.note: Production capacity and pooling are not addressed in the 2017 text and fall outside the documented certification scope (2017 edition text; LR guidance notes page).

Speed.note: Lead time and shipping time are suitability criteria, and pre-certified organisations are said to shorten certification lead times, not quantified (2017 edition text secs. 3, 4).

tools.name: ABS Requirements for Additive Manufacturing
tools.developer: American Bureau of Shipping (ABS)
tools.year: 2018 (Guidance Notes, Sept 2018); 2021 (Guide, April 2021); Requirements edition date Unknown (a linked PDF file name suggests July 2022)
tools.context: Marine and offshore classification; approval of AM facilities and AM parts; ABS also supports NSRP/US Navy shipbuilding AM work.
tools.processes: Metal powder bed fusion and directed energy deposition
tools.availability: Free on ABS website (2021 Guide PDF not accessible in this session); 2018 Guidance Notes PDF public
tools.description: The 2018 Guidance Notes define four maturity stages: feasibility, verification of a cradle-to-grave file, pre-production validation builds witnessed at hold points, and production with monitoring. Qualification depth scales with the part's ABS Tier of Approval; specimen counts are agreed case by case. A critical process-parameter change triggers requalification. A 2023 ABS briefing describes AM Test Levels 1-3 set by risk (likelihood x consequence, consequence mapped to ISO 5817 classes). It lists standard approval tests and rapid-qualification options: in-situ monitoring replacing NDT, reduced scope using existing data, and part- or feature-family qualification. It states only that approval cost is high.

NRE.note: The feasibility and verification stages require design review and checks of converted build files (units, origin, pre-distorted vs resulting geometry) before any build, but this effort is not costed (ABS Guidance Notes 2018 full text; current Requirements portal blocked).

Production.note: Per-part production cost is outside the scope of classification requirements for AM facility and part approval (ABS Guidance Notes 2018 full text).

QA_Qual.note: Staged qualification with ABS-witnessed hold points, depth correlated with the part's Tier of Approval and 2023 Test Levels set by risk, but 'the amount and type of testing varies on a case-by-case basis' with no class-specific specimen counts (ABS Guidance Notes 2018; Qiao ABS slides 2023).

QA_Insp.note: Production NDE must address defect types, locations and probability of detection, a test artifact in each build is recommended and in-situ monitoring may partly replace NDT, but inspection frequency is agreed case by case by criticality with no class-specific scope (ABS Guidance Notes 2018; Qiao ABS slides 2023).

Storage.note: Inventory is not addressed in the guidance text; the 2023 slides mention spare and obsolete parts only as cases where standard qualification is ill-suited (ABS Guidance Notes 2018 full text; Qiao ABS slides 2023).

Shared_Capital.note: ABS proposes qualification by part family, design-feature family or material group and reduced scope using recognised data, though qualified processes 'may be specific to the serial number of a particular AM machine'; no numbers (Qiao ABS slides 2023; ABS Guidance Notes 2018).

Shared_Capacity.note: The guidance notes that a single AM service provider can serve multiple clients and part types, acting as several qualified factories 'under one roof', but capacity or lead time is not modelled (ABS Guidance Notes 2018 full text).

Speed.note: The guidance states AM's value lies in producing 'a low number of complex parts faster than traditional manufacturing methods' and that early detection of failed builds may cut production time, but no lead time is set or valued (ABS Guidance Notes 2018 full text).

tools.name: Indian Register of Shipping Classification Notes: Additively Manufactured Metallic Parts for Marine and Offshore Applications
tools.developer: Indian Register of Shipping (IRClass)
tools.context: Marine and offshore class approval of AM metallic parts; criticality by service (essential vs habitability).
tools.processes: Metal PBF and DED (powder and wire)
tools.availability: Free PDF on irclass.org
tools.description: Parts are 'class items' (must meet IRS Rules; IRS approves feedstock and manufacturer) or 'certified items' (meet industry/OEM standards; manufacturer qualifies feedstock and design). Criticality is set separately: critical = primary/secondary essential services, non-critical = habitability. Qualification specimen counts are tabulated per category. PBF: tensile 5 (class) vs 3 (certified critical), impact 3 sets vs 1, hardness 6 vs 3, microstructure 4 vs 2, density 3 vs 3. DED tensile: 6 vs 3. Coupons and components get visual and surface NDT; components also get embedded-flaw NDT. Production sampling frequency is set in an agreed inspection and test plan.

NRE.note: Requires CAD model or drawing review and approval for class items, an engineering-analysis report for topology-optimised redesigns and AMPS qualification over a parameter range, without costable effort by class (IRClass CN, secs. 1.6.2, 3.2.3, 5.1.2).

Production.note: Full classification notes read; production cost is outside the scope of a class approval document (IRClass CN, July 2025).

QA_Qual.note: Tables 19-21 prescribe qualification specimen counts per test for certified-critical vs class items and per process (e.g. PBF tensile 3 vs 5, hardness 3 vs 6), which are directly costable (IRClass CN, July 2025).

QA_Insp.note: Requires 100% visual examination and NDT of every delivered part with component-level embedded-flaw inspection, but NDT extent and production test frequency follow an agreed NDT plan or ITP and do not differ by category (IRClass CN, sec. 7.3, Tables 19-20).

Storage.note: Full classification notes read; inventory is not addressed (IRClass CN, July 2025).

Shared_Capital.note: Certified-critical items may be approved as a part family with a risk analysis, and a serial-number change within the same machine model is not a change of machine, so qualification is reused across parts and machines without numbers (IRClass CN, secs. 6.4, range of approval).

Shared_Capacity.note: Full classification notes read; capacity sharing is not addressed (IRClass CN, July 2025).

Speed.note: Full classification notes read; lead time is not addressed (IRClass CN, July 2025).

tools.name: AIA Recommended Guidance for Certification of AM Components, Rev. A (Oct 2025)
tools.developer: Aerospace Industries Association (AIA) Additive Manufacturing Working Group, with FAA participation
tools.context: Civil aviation metal AM certification (14 CFR 2x.603/605/613, 23.2260, 33.15, 35.17; higher-criticality references 2x.571, 33.14, 33.70); industry consensus, not FAA policy.
tools.processes: L-PBF, EB-PBF, DED (wire and powder)
tools.availability: Free PDF on aia-aerospace.org
tools.description: Criticality is set by FMECA rather than ASTM F3572 classes, and requirements scale with consequence of failure. Higher criticality brings fatigue and damage-tolerance allowables, tighter KPV control, more frequent machine maintenance and stricter requalification. Inspection development needs limits of detection and POD. Performance qualification ends in first-article inspection, and witness coupons are built into production for high-criticality parts. Every machine serial number is qualified independently, though PCDs can be reused. Equivalency is shown statistically. Requalification triggers include software, firmware, component or relocation changes. A section on part-family allowables exists but was not read.

NRE.note: Requires process development (DOE varying up to 8-10 parameters), a parameter set per material and machine model, and fixed PCDs, without costing them (AIA 2025, secs. 6.3, 6.4, 7.2).

Production.note: Notes only that maximising parts per platform generally lowers cost per part (AIA 2025, sec. 6.9.3).

QA_Qual.note: Requirements scale with FMECA criticality (KPV control, maintenance frequency, part-family scrutiny, PQ per machine serial number), but no class-specific test counts are set (AIA 2025, secs. 3, 6-8).

QA_Insp.note: Every part from every machine gets 100% dimensional verification and critical parts keep 100% sampling of select witness coupons until the process is stable, but NDI extent and acceptance criteria are left to criticality with no fixed scope (AIA 2025, secs. 6.5, 13, 14).

Storage.note: Full guidance read; inventory is not addressed (AIA 2025).

Shared_Capital.note: PCDs can be reused across machines and test data pooled across a part family once similarity is shown, but every machine still needs full PQ and no costs are given (AIA 2025, secs. 7.3, 8.2.2).

Shared_Capacity.note: Machine equivalency is treated as a qualification requirement, not capacity pooling; shared capacity is not addressed (AIA 2025, sec. 7.3.2).

Speed.note: Full guidance read; lead time and schedule are not addressed (AIA 2025).

tools.name: Peron/Cantini qualification-cost model for AM vs conventional spare parts (Cantini et al. 2025)
tools.developer: Peron (NTNU), Cantini (Politecnico di Milano / Univ. Firenze), Coruzzolo and Lolli (Univ. Modena e Reggio Emilia), De Carlo (Univ. Firenze)
tools.context: Spare parts make-vs-buy between AM and conventional manufacturing, with qualification tests by criticality class (DNV-ST-B203 classes). Case: scale-model aircraft landing gear, DMLS vs high-pressure die casting.
tools.processes: Metal powder bed fusion (DMLS) vs high-pressure die casting
tools.availability: 2023 paper open access (IRIS UNIMORE); 2025 PPC paper abstract only
tools.description: Adds three qualification cost blocks to a production-cost comparison. Build process qualification is one-time for all classes (12 tensile, 3 impact, plus hardness, microstructure, porosity, chemistry and visual). Part qualification is one-time and C3 only, covering the full test set including surface and volumetric NDT and dimensional checks. Production testing is per build job: full set for C3, reduced for C2, negligible for C1. A CM batch shares one production test, while each AM build job needs its own. Test prices run from $10 (visual) to $150 (hardness or volumetric NDT), plus $20 per part for transport. Reported break-even quantity below which AM wins: 42 parts without qualification, 42 for C1, 8 for C2, 6 for C3. Sharing a build job among 4 parts raises the C3 break-even to 9. The 2025 extension embeds qualification costs in a spare-parts inventory cost model with holding and backorder costs (abstract only).

NRE.note: The 2023 full paper costs no AM design-file or parameter preparation and lists 'different design routines and related costs' as future work; its only one-time production cost is the CM fixed cost ($22,366), and the 2025 abstract adds no design cost (IFAC 2023 full text; PPC 2025 abstract).

Production.note: Explicit per-part unit costs by technology are model inputs (AM $560.55/part; CM $22.68/part plus $22,366 fixed), taken from Atzeni & Salmi 2012 rather than computed from geometry (IFAC 2023 full text).

QA_Qual.note: One-time build-process qualification (all classes) and part qualification (C3 only) test sets are priced per test by DNV criticality class (IFAC 2023 full text, Eqs. 2-3, Table 4).

QA_Insp.note: Per-build-job production testing is priced by class (full set C3, reduced set C2, visual only C1), with a batch-sharing rule for CM and per-test-job transport cost (IFAC 2023 full text, Eqs. 4-6).

Storage.note: The 2023 paper has no inventory terms; the 2025 paper is titled for spare-parts inventories and its abstract says prior models compare production, holding and backorder costs, but the full text (no file on IRIS UNIMORE or Polimi; DOI blocked) was not read, so whether it computes holding cost is not established.

Shared_Capital.note: One-time qualification cost is amortised over part quantity (break-even N) and tests are shared across parts in a build job (4 parts per job raises the C3 break-even from 6 to 9), but machine capital is not modelled (IFAC 2023 full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Machine capacity is not discussed in the 2023 full paper, and the 2025 abstract does not mention capacity (IFAC 2023 full text; PPC 2025 abstract).

Speed.note: The 2023 paper uses AM's shorter lead time only as motivation; the 2025 abstract names backorder costs in prior models, but its full text was not reachable, so whether the extension computes backorders or lead time is not established.

tools.name: Verna et al. quality-inspection cost model for low-volume and AM production (2022)
tools.developer: Politecnico di Torino (Verna, Genta, Galetto, Franceschini)
tools.context: Choice of offline inspection strategy for low-volume production, with metal L-PBF case studies (AlSi10Mg).
tools.processes: Metal L-PBF/SLM (AlSi10Mg; EOS M290 in 2022 case)
tools.availability: Author manuscripts open on IRIS PoliTo; journal versions paywalled
tools.description: A probabilistic model per output characteristic covering defect probability p, false-alarm α, missed-defect β, inspection cost, necessary and unnecessary repair cost, and external failure cost. It yields D_tot (expected undetected defects) and C_tot (quality cost) to compare inspection strategies (2020). The 2022 paper adds quality costs to a per-part production cost model, with a return-on-inspection metric (ROII). In the L-PBF case, production cost was 18.56 €/part and quality-related costs were 14.40-31.69 €/part across three alternatives. In 2020, the most effective strategy cost about 4x the cheapest (€168.81 vs €42.36) with fewer undetected defects. CT was mentioned but not modeled.

NRE.note: Per-job AM system setup (2.5 h) and software job preparation (1.5 h) are costed (2.97 EUR/part pre-process cost), but no one-time design or parameter development is included (2022 manuscript).

Production.note: The 2022 model computes per-part material and manufacturing cost from powder, machine, operator, and pre- and post-process times (18.56 EUR/part in the L-PBF case) (2022 manuscript).

QA_Qual.note: Full manuscript read; qualification is not modelled, and only inspector skill affecting error rates is discussed (2022 manuscript).

QA_Insp.note: Per-part inspection cost (operator plus equipment rate x inspection time, e.g. 3.38-12.50 EUR/part) is traded against detection errors and repair and escape costs across inspection strategies (2022 manuscript).

Storage.note: Full manuscript read; inventory is not addressed (2022 manuscript).

Shared_Capital.note: The L-PBF system is charged at about 38 EUR/h from a 700 kEUR price depreciated over five years at 50% utilisation (plus maintenance, rent, overheads), and job cost is divided over 60 parts per job (2022 manuscript).

Shared_Capacity.note: Full manuscript read; shared capacity is not addressed (2022 manuscript).

Speed.note: Build time (18 h/job) and handling times are fixed inputs used only for cost, and lead time or throughput is not modelled (2022 manuscript).

tools.name: CT vs electromechanical-impedance per-specimen verification cost estimate for metal AM (Strutner et al.)
tools.developer: Virginia Tech (Strutner, Tenney, Tarazaga, Williams) with Northrop Grumman (Kwas); NSF award 1635356
tools.year: Unknown (SAMPE conference paper; neither the NSF PAR record nor the PDF gives a date; latest reference is 2018)
tools.context: Low-cost NDE screening of AM parts as an alternative to CT.
tools.processes: Electron beam melting Ti-6Al-4V (Arcam A2X)
tools.availability: Open on NSF PAR
tools.description: Builds a simple per-specimen CT cost estimate. In-house 220 kV CT: $600k capital over 5 years x 2,000 h, i.e. $60/h, scaled to $240/h at a 25% duty cycle. A 2-hour scan therefore costs $480 machine time, plus about $1,000 analysis labour (about 8 h), for about $1,480 per specimen. A service bureau costs about $2,300 ($450/h + $1,000 labour + $400 shipping). Larger parts may cost 5-10x more to analyse. The EMI alternative is estimated at about $324 per specimen (about 90 min).

NRE.note: No design, parameter-development or other one-time engineering cost appears in the full paper (NSF PAR full text).

Production.note: Section 3.4.1 builds each EBM specimen's cost from powder ($160), machine time ($188, from a $1.5M Arcam A2X depreciated over 5 years of 4,000 h and a quarter share of a 10 h build) and de-caking labour ($600), giving at least $947 each (NSF PAR full text, sec. 3.4.1).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification or certification cost is not discussed; EMI is presented only as post-production screening (NSF PAR full text).

QA_Insp.note: Explicit per-specimen inspection cost build-up: in-house CT $1,480 (capital at 25% duty cycle, 2 h scan, $1,000 analysis labour), service bureau $2,300, EMI $324 now and $103 with a clamp-on system (NSF PAR full text, Table 3).

Storage.note: Inventory is not discussed in the full paper (NSF PAR full text).

Shared_Capital.note: Equipment capital is amortised with explicit utilisation assumptions: the $600k CT at a 25% duty cycle ($240/h) and the AM machine over 4,000 h/yr with a quarter-build share per specimen (NSF PAR full text, sec. 3.4).

Shared_Capacity.note: No capacity contention is modelled; the paper only notes that one CT specimen is scanned per day and that external vendors may be used without enough volume (NSF PAR full text).

Speed.note: Scan (2 h) and analysis (about 8 h) times feed the inspection cost only; part lead time, turnaround or availability is not computed (NSF PAR full text).

tools.name: Multivariate equivalency testing framework for AM requalification (Lynch et al., UTEP) with R package MultivariateEquivalency
tools.developer: University of Texas at El Paso W.M. Keck Center and collaborators (Lynch, Villalobos, Valadez Mesta, Gomez Guillen, Mireles, Wicker)
tools.context: Screening whether a changed AM process (new machine, parameter set or measurement workflow) remains equivalent to a qualified reference, before formal requalification.
tools.processes: L-PBF (validation on AconityMIDI+ and SLM280 HL)
tools.availability: Journal article (MDPI J. Manuf. Mater. Process., doi:10.3390/jmmp10070229, open access per publisher); open-source R package
tools.description: Feature-wise equivalence tests on percentile bins of the reference process, with family-wise error control across measured attributes. Simulations map trade-offs among power, detectable effect size, feature count and fabrication/measurement cost. Validation used 40 observations per process and three geometric features. The authors position it as a requalification screen, not a replacement for formal qualification.

NRE.note: Full text read; the framework screens equivalence after a machine, parameter or measurement change and does not cost design or parameter development (JMMP full text).

Production.note: Full text read; per-part production cost is not modelled, and an illustrative artifact cost ($4,165) enters only as a requalification input (JMMP full text, sec. 6).

QA_Qual.note: The framework minimises a composite cost of artifact fabrication and measurement over sample size and feature count for the requalification screen, so qualification test effort is an explicit cost output; the $424,500-$1,269,255 figures in the paper are the cost of a conventional tensile-test procedure it compares against (full text).

QA_Insp.note: Full text read; measurement cost applies to requalification samples, and per-part production inspection is not addressed (JMMP full text).

Storage.note: Full text read; inventory is not addressed (JMMP full text).

Shared_Capital.note: The framework is meant to show that a candidate machine, facility or workflow stays equivalent to a qualified reference, so a qualified baseline can be extended to new machines, but that reuse is not costed (JMMP full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Full text read; capacity is not addressed (JMMP full text).

Speed.note: Full text read; sequential stopping cuts requalification sample sizes by up to 67.5%, but part lead time or availability is not addressed (JMMP full text).

tools.name: NAVAIR Additive Manufacturing Capability initiative: licensed Material Process Combination (MPC) qualification data packages (Colibrium Additive contract) and FRCE depot certification
tools.developer: Naval Air Systems Command (NAVAIR AM Team) with Colibrium Additive (GE Aerospace); Fleet Readiness Center East (FRCE) depot
tools.year: 2026 (FRCE first certified metal AM parts reported April 2026; Colibrium MPC award reported May 2026)
tools.context: Naval aviation sustainment: buying pre-generated qualification data (material property data, process parameters, specifications, design allowables) so organic NAVAIR sites can qualify metal AM parts faster.
tools.processes: Metal L-PBF (Colibrium M Line and M2 machines); alloys AlSi7Mg, IN718, 316L, CoCr, Ti64, adding 17-4PH and 7050-RAM2
tools.availability: Program described in trade press and Navy news only; no public NAVAIR AM airworthiness requirements document found
tools.description: NAVAIR licenses six alloy Material Process Combinations. Each includes characterization data and curves, optimized parameters, consolidated material and process specifications, and design allowables for the tested properties, plus thin-wall fatigue characterization and workforce training. FRCE, working with the NAVAIR AM Team and Fleet Support Teams, qualified, produced and certified its first metal AM parts in under six months, which it called the fastest such effort in NAVAIR. The parts were an AH-1Z pylon fitting, a V-22 landing-gear door stop fitting and a C-130 blanking plate, in aluminum, described as non-flight-critical. No contract value, cost or tiered criteria are public.

NRE.note: The Colibrium package supplies optimized process parameters, manufacturing process instructions and consolidated specifications, removing part of the parameter-development NRE, but this work is not costed separately within the contract (GE Aerospace release Apr 2026; TCT).

Production.note: The GE release, trade coverage and Navy story give a contract value but nothing on per-part production cost, so whether production cost is treated is not established.

QA_Qual.note: NAVAIR's $31M Colibrium contract buys six alloy MPC packages (property data, parameters, specifications, design allowables, thin-wall fatigue data) plus four printers and training as one lump, and FRCE certified its first parts in under six months; there is no tiered or per-part qualification costing (GE Aerospace release; TCT; Navy.mil).

QA_Insp.note: The sources say only that parts meet the same quality requirements as conventional parts and that training covers quality teams, so per-part inspection is not described (Navy.mil; GE release).

Storage.note: The Navy story describes in-house, on-demand production of parts hard to get through traditional supply chains but says nothing about inventory (Navy.mil).

Shared_Capital.note: The releases say the licensed data, four printers and training build in-house capability to produce NAVAIR components at scale, but reuse of an MPC package across parts or sites and machine sharing are not stated (GE release; TCT).

Shared_Capacity.note: The Navy story names FRCE, Lakehurst, NAVAIR HQ and Fleet Support Teams as collaborators but describes no sharing of machines or capacity (Navy.mil).

Speed.note: Releases claim shorter lead times for critical components and less aircraft downtime, and FRCE's certification took under six months, but no part lead time is computed or valued (GE release; Navy.mil).

tools.name: ROK procedure for applying 3D-printed repair parts in operational units (DMSMS / FMECA / localisation screening with DT&E-OT&E qualification)
tools.developer: S. Yoo (ROK Ministry of National Defense), J. Hur (ROK Naval Academy), H. Lee (ROK Navy Force Support System Project Group)
tools.context: Weapon-system repair parts, Republic of Korea armed forces (2016-17 Army pilot; 2018 development plan of seven items; F-15K example)
tools.processes: PBF and DED named; processes used for the defence parts not stated; the 2016-17 Army pilot judged most metal parts unsuitable, mainly on strength
tools.availability: Open-access journal paper (Journal of Aerospace System Engineering 13(1), in Korean)
tools.description: Qualitative screening built on existing parts-localisation procedures. Candidates come from three pools: DMSMS-tracked obsolete parts, FMECA risk level 2-3 parts with poor MTBF/MKBF/MRBF, and foreign-sourced parts with high import-substitution value. Each passes DT&E, an installation test, OT&E and a military-suitability determination before being catalogued in a parts database. The programme (since 2017) was extended by a 2025 industry-defence ministry agreement.

NRE.note: The paper describes 3D scanning, reverse modelling and CAD design changes in the printing workflow and has approved parts catalogued with their design data for future production, but this effort is not costed or used in screening (full paper, Korean).

Production.note: Ease of manufacture and cost prioritise the localisation pool and an F-15K HPT cover plate is cited at 90% lower purchase cost, but there is no cost model (full paper, Korean).

QA_Qual.note: Specifies a feasibility review, DT&E, installation test, OT&E (if needed) and a military-suitability determination before cataloguing, but with no class-specific test counts or burden figures (full paper, Korean).

QA_Insp.note: Refers to KCL national quality guidelines that assess printouts for dimensions, mechanical and chemical properties and reliability, with no per-part inspection cost or class-specific scope (full paper, Korean).

Storage.note: The full paper gives no inventory or stock analysis or claim; it argues only that localised production speeds logistics for obsolete parts (full paper, Korean).

Shared_Capital.note: The full paper proposes a Defense Center for 3D printing and service-level training but does not address sharing machine investment across units (full paper, Korean).

Shared_Capacity.note: The full paper gives no printer counts or capacity and no sharing of printing capacity between units or services (full paper, Korean).

Speed.note: FMECA risk 2-3 and MTBF/MKBF/MRBF screening targets parts whose failures cut mission capability, and an F-15K case cut procurement by more than 30 days, but lead time or availability is not computed (full paper, Korean).

tools.name: Satair/Airbus AM spare-part pre-assessment and RapidSpares recertification route
tools.developer: Satair (Airbus aftermarket subsidiary) AM team with Airbus RapidSpares design offices; production at Airbus Filton Reference Manufacturing shop
tools.year: 2015-2020 (AM team since c. 2015; first certified metal flying spare 2020)
tools.context: Civil aircraft spares for the Airbus fleet: AOG and non-procurable parts
tools.processes: Titanium metal AM at a process-qualified shop (process not named in fetched sources); polymer parts also
tools.availability: Corporate practice; described only in press releases
tools.description: When a part becomes non-procurable or an AOG order arrives, Satair's AM team runs a short pre-assessment and hands candidates to Airbus RapidSpares design offices for redesign and recertification. In the A320ceo wingtip fence case, AM beat both re-tooling the casting and redesigning for machining. Satair reports more than 300 AM-certified part numbers.

NRE.note: The pre-assessment compared non-recurring cost of AM against re-tooling the casting and redesigning for machining, with AM NRC 45% lower in the wingtip-fence case, a case outcome with no published method (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).

Production.note: Printing the four-part shipset in one 26-hour build is said to reduce cost per piece, but no per-part cost or cost model is given (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).

QA_Qual.note: RapidSpares re-certified the former cast part within five weeks via a new certification process and the parts ship with EASA Form 1 from a shop process-qualified in 2019, a case outcome rather than a modelled qualification burden (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).

QA_Insp.note: The press releases say post-processing steps make the part airworthy but say nothing about inspection or testing, and no fuller description of the route is public (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020; TCT 2020).

Storage.note: The route is triggered when a part is no longer procurable (here, out of production with supplier mould losses), so obsolescence works as a screening trigger, but stock levels or holding cost are not discussed (Satair press release 2020; TCT 2020).

Shared_Capital.note: Four parts are printed together 'to reduce the cost per piece and the printing time per part' in a process-qualified shop with more than 300 AM-certified part numbers, but machine cost or utilisation is not quantified (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).

Shared_Capacity.note: The press names the Filton Reference Manufacturing shop and notes four more customers requested the same part, but says nothing about how print capacity is shared or allocated (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).

Speed.note: The route is AOG-triggered and machining redesign was rejected because its 'cost and lead-time implications were not competitive'; total lead time was shorter but no figure is given or computed (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).

tools.name: Leonardo Aircraft Division AM spare-part candidate criteria (safety, feasibility, lead time >180 days, unscheduled removal rate band)
tools.developer: Leonardo S.p.A. Aircraft Division Customer Support (Caselle, Turin) with Politecnico di Torino (A. Pochettino MSc thesis; builds at IAM@PoliTo)
tools.context: Military aircraft spares and logistic support (C-27J, M-346, M-345), Italy
tools.processes: L-PBF (EOS M270) in AlSi10Mg and Ti6Al4V
tools.availability: Public MSc thesis
tools.description: Four screening criteria: non-safety-critical (binary); feasibility (geometry, material, volume, cost); procurement lead time over 180 days; and unscheduled removal rate of 0.050-0.500 per 1,000 flight hours. They yielded three use cases: a C-27J main landing gear bracket, an M-346 clevis and an M-345 connector. Leonardo reports more than 100 metal AM parts qualified and flying. This is separate from the earlier pass's Viano business-model entry for the same division.

NRE.note: The bracket CAD was rebuilt in SolidWorks from the drawing and Al 2024 was substituted by AlSi10Mg; the effort is described but not costed (full thesis, ch. 1-2).

Production.note: The feasibility criterion requires AM to be more cost-effective than conventional manufacturing at small to medium volumes, a filter; per-part costs (EUR 69-105 from AMOtool, whose calculation is not shown) are estimated only after selection (full thesis, Table 1.1 and ch. 3).

QA_Qual.note: Safety-critical parts are excluded by a binary gate, and the work relies on Leonardo's existing certification path (AlSi10Mg already certified); qualification is not costed (full thesis, ch. 1).

QA_Insp.note: Each order is built in two copies and the second, the first article, undergoes dimensional, chemical-physical and mechanical testing, but tests are not costed (full thesis, ch. 1-3).

Storage.note: On-demand production near the user is presented as a way to digitise the warehouse and reduce inventory, without quantification (full thesis, ch. 1).

Shared_Capital.note: Read in full: the four documented criteria (Table 1.1) and the rest of the thesis contain no machine investment or utilisation element (the thesis notes only that precise criteria definition is outside its scope); a post-selection AMOtool estimate fills a build platform (16, 14, 68 parts) without showing its calculation (full thesis).

Shared_Capacity.note: Read in full: neither the four documented criteria nor the rest of the thesis discusses print capacity, sites or pooling; parts were built on one EOS M270 at IAM@PoliTo (full thesis).

Speed.note: Procurement lead time over 180 days and an unscheduled removal rate of 0.050-0.500 per 1,000 FH are screening thresholds, with AOG/AOCP as motivation; lead time is not computed (full thesis, Table 1.1).

EDF says it has not yet entered an industrial phase.

NRE.note: Worn obsolete parts are 3D-scanned to get a digital model and rebuilt, with material and process chosen per part, but the effort is not costed (EDF R&D pages).

Production.note: Lower manufacturing and sourcing cost and cost gains from cold spray are claimed in words, with no figures or method (EDF R&D pages).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification and use-case identification are named as the main obstacles; RCC-M does not yet cover AM and parts must match conventional mechanical properties, so EDF began with parts with few regulatory requirements (EDF R&D pages).

QA_Insp.note: Inspectability of AM parts is named as a main unknown, with NDT methods being adapted or developed, but inspection is not costed (EDF R&D page, 'les benefices pour la production').

Storage.note: EDF says it now stores only powder or wire, with part designs kept in a digital catalogue for on-demand production; no stock or holding cost is quantified (EDF R&D page, 'une revolution des modes de production').

Shared_Capital.note: EDF reports 'significant investments' in a cold-spray lab and a WAAM lab, but no source says whether machine cost or sharing enters part decisions (EDF R&D pages).

Shared_Capacity.note: EDF Hydro works with external partners (CIH, Institut de Soudure) and two EDF labs, but capacity or pooling is not discussed (EDF R&D pages).

Speed.note: Claims manufacturing lead time cut by a factor of 3-4, shorter cold-spray interventions and lower hydro unit unavailability costs, with no lead-time model (EDF R&D pages).

tools.name: Siemens Energy (Siemens Industrial Turbomachinery) Finspang AM burner repair and spares programme
tools.developer: Siemens Industrial Turbomachinery AB, Finspang (now Siemens Energy); Materials Solutions, Worcester (acquired 2016)
tools.context: Industrial gas turbine burner repair and spares, Sweden
tools.processes: L-PBF (EOS M270/M280, modified for burner-tip repair)
tools.availability: Corporate practice; trade press and Siemens software case material
tools.description: Problem-driven adoption: eroded burner tips are repaired by machining off the worn section and reprinting it, instead of buying new burners. A digital thread (NX, Teamcenter, MOM tracking powder reuse) supports the work. No formal part screening or business-case method is published.

NRE.note: Redesign of the burner head to combine many welded parts into one unit, with lattice and thin-wall weight reduction (22%, goal 50%), is described but not costed (Siemens blog).

Production.note: Repair is presented as a lower-cost alternative to new burners and AM as cutting material use and cost, with no cost model or figures (Siemens blog; Metal AM).

QA_Qual.note: Repaired burners are re-certified, with endurance over the required duty cycles as 'the true test'; the process is not described or modelled (Siemens blog; Metal AM).

QA_Insp.note: Burners were inspected after 20,000 operating hours, an AM monitor checks layer images for deviations, and automated 3D scanning and in-line/off-line monitoring are named as needs; inspection is not costed (Metal AM; DN Siemens feature).

Storage.note: Envisions turbines linked to a diagnostic centre where spare parts are ordered and printed on demand to minimise downtime; no stock effect is quantified (Metal AM; Siemens blog).

Shared_Capital.note: Press reports a 2016 automated facility with eight new machines and plans for more, but no source says whether investment or machine sharing enters any part decision (Metal AM; Siemens blog).

Shared_Capacity.note: The Siemens AM Network 'links part designers and AM production service providers together', with no capacity model (Metal AM).

Speed.note: Burner repair turnaround cut 70% and lead times 'reduced by up to 90 percent' are reported outcomes, not computed by any decision method (Metal AM; DN Siemens feature).

tools.name: GE annual part audit and per-part ROI screen for casting-to-AM conversion (LM9000 bleed air adapter caps)
tools.developer: GE Aviation (now GE Aerospace) with GE Additive; parts for Baker Hughes LM9000 turbines
tools.context: Aeroderivative land/marine gas turbine parts and spare-part sourcing, US
tools.processes: L-PBF (Concept Laser M2 Series 5), CoCr
tools.availability: Internal practice; one trade-press account
tools.description: In GE's 2020 annual part audit, the team reviewed hundreds of purchased castings, found 180 suitable for AM, and calculated ROI for each. It chose four CoCr bleed air adapter caps as the most profitable and checked them against quotes from four outside vendors. Reported results: ~35% lower manufacturing cost and 10 months from identification to prototypes.

NRE.note: Available engineering resources were a factor in narrowing nine candidates to four, and the caps needed only minor printability tweaks and a build-plate re-layout, but engineering effort is not reported as a cost term (The Fabricator 2021; 3DPI 2021).

Production.note: Teams calculated per-part ROI with internal production and financial models whose inputs are not documented, and compared AM with vendor casting quotes (about 35% lower) as a case result (trade press).

QA_Qual.note: Candidates were screened on whether the material was well characterised and previously used on the M2 machines, and printed parts matched cast quality within weeks, but no formal qualification effort or cost is described (The Fabricator 2021; 3DPI 2021).

QA_Insp.note: Two trade-press accounts describe the screen (post-processability, machining and brazing) but neither mentions inspection or whether it enters the ROI; no GE source is public (The Fabricator 2021; 3DPI 2021).

Storage.note: The press mentions de-risking the caps' supply chain for future spares as vendors drop materials or moulds become too costly, but not whether inventory is assessed; no GE source is public (3DPI 2021; The Fabricator 2021).

Shared_Capital.note: The team re-laid the build plate to fit four parts instead of three in about the same print time, spreading machine time across more parts, but machine investment or utilisation is not stated as an ROI input (The Fabricator 2021).

Shared_Capacity.note: Pandemic downtime freed machine and post-processing time at GE's Auburn additive facility for the project, a qualitative note on shared plant capacity with no capacity or lead-time model (The Fabricator 2021).

Speed.note: Time to market is quoted from the case (10 months from identification to final prototypes vs 12-18 months for castings), not computed by the screen (3DPI 2021; The Fabricator 2021).

tools.name: Sandvik-Boliden on-demand printed drill-rig spare parts trial
tools.developer: Sandvik Mining and Rock Solutions with Boliden
tools.context: Underground mining drill-rig wear and repair parts (Garpenberg, Sweden; then Ireland)
tools.processes: Metal AM (process not named), printed at a Sandvik-managed facility in Italy
tools.availability: Press coverage only
tools.description: Proof-of-concept trial installing redesigned metal-printed parts on Boliden drill rigs to test local on-demand supply. The parts are bushes, brackets and drill parts replaced every 3,000-4,000 h. Costs, IP, warranty and liability are listed as open questions.

NRE.note: The trial prints 'a set of specially redesigned components', but redesign is not costed (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).

Production.note: Sandvik's release lists 'What will the costs be?' as an open question, so whether the trial assesses part cost cannot be established.

QA_Qual.note: Part performance is monitored in service at Garpenberg as proof of concept, with warranties and liabilities listed as unresolved; no qualification procedure is described (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).

QA_Insp.note: The release describes only in-service performance monitoring and does not mention inspection or testing of the printed parts.

Storage.note: Sandvik says it cannot tie up the capital that keeping all these parts in stock would need; not quantified (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).

Shared_Capital.note: The release does not say whether machine investment or its sharing is assessed.

Shared_Capacity.note: Parts are printed at one Sandvik-managed facility in Italy, local printing is raised, and who prints (OEM, miner or third party) is left open; no capacity model (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).

Speed.note: 'Shorter delivery times' are cited as a benefit, not quantified (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).
